The timestamp already is a column, aligned on the edge that right-set meta is conventionally aligned on (Mail, Things, Linear). Reporting the ragged left edge of deliberately right-aligned text as "nothing scans vertically" is a mis-measurement, and the fix's `.idxWhen { justify-self: end }` is a no-op against layout that already does it.

2. The proposed fix is destructive exactly where this product is tightest. I injected `grid-template-columns: 20px minmax(0,1fr) 92px 104px` with the two justify-self rules and measured. At 390 the title box collapses from 118-169px per row to a uniform 65px on all 14 rows; the phone index then reads "Teacher…", "Course …", "Photogr…" — one word per note (screenshot taken and inspected). At 768 it drops 402-453 to 349; at 1440, 1040-1091 to 987, i.e. 53-104px of the person's own words surrendered on every single row. Fixed columns must be sized to the widest occupant ("To decide" 66px, "35 minutes ago" 84px), so every row pays the worst row's cost forever. On a product whose whole promise is the person's words, trading up to 62% of the visible line for the left edge of a three-value chip inverts the priority order, and on a checklist that already names "clamps that silently delete content" it moves the wrong way.

Two further weaknesses. The benchmark citation does not hold as stated: Things carries no status chip on a row at all, and Bear's tags sit inline in the row and are ragged, so "Linear, Things and Bear all hold these as fixed columns" is asserted, not true. And the magnitude is overstated: 3 of the 14 rows carry no box at all (.idxTag[data-quiet] "Kept" is unboxed 400-weight text), and rows sharing a timestamp width align in runs — the four consecutive "To decide" rows all sit at 1229. The wobble concentrates at day-group boundaries, where the group heading already breaks the vertical run.

There is a residual grain of truth (.idxTag is the one element with neither edge fixed), but it is small, it is not what the finding measured, and the fix as written makes the artifact worse.

refuted.problem: This file tokenises a tracking curve by size, a radii ladder that boasts "no seventh step", one duration and one measure — and never tokenises the two things a type system is actually made of. Driven across all ten states, 18 distinct font sizes render: 10, 10.5, 11, 11.5, 12, 12.5, 13, 13.5, 14, 14.5, 15, 16, 16.5, 17, 18, 20, 28, 30. Eleven of those sit inside the 10–15px band — an eleven-step ramp across five pixels, on half-pixel increments that land on fractional metrics at 1x. Leading is worse: 12 raw decimals in the source (1.22, 1.38, 1.45, 1.5, 1.52, 1.55, 1.56, 1.58, 1.6, 1.62, 1.64, 1.66) and, in the resting state, 49 of the 76 text-bearing elements compute `line-height: normal` — including the search field, the undo toast, the hand's title, the index count and the day rules. The visible cost is measurable: in every index row the note's own words sit on a baseline of 364.50 while its status tag sits at 363.49 and its timestamp at 362.78–363.78, because `align-items: center` is resolving boxes whose leading was never declared. A 1px shiver on the right-hand column of 36 rows. Vercel's own Geist docs, Linear and Things all ship a closed ramp; this ships a browser default.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. The finding's only measured evidence is false, and its fix would break three of the four finished rooms.

1) THE "1px SHIVER" DOES NOT EXIST. I probed the exact browser-computed baseline of every text run in all 36 rows of ?state=pressure (zero-width inline-block with vertical-align:baseline, deviceScaleFactor 1). Result: .idxTag and .idxWhen sit on the IDENTICAL baseline in 36/36 rows — delta 0.000px, not the 363.49 vs 362.78–363.78 spread the finding asserts. And .idxText sits exactly 1.500px below them in 36/36 rows, variance 0.000px. Row heights are identical (39.015625px each). There is no per-row variation anywhere, so there is no shiver to see. The finding invented a spread the file does not produce.

2) THE 1.5px THAT IS THERE IS CORRECT, NOT A DEFECT. .idxTag is a bordered pill (inset ring, 3px 8px padding, r-pill). In a row whose right column is a pill, align-items:center is the right alignment: baseline-setting the pill to a 14.5px title de-centres the pill's own box against the row. Linear, GitHub and Things all centre the pill rather than baseline it. This is taste stated as a defect, and the taste is wrong.

3) "LEADING IS WORSE" HAS NO RENDERED CONSEQUENCE. Across 4 rooms x 10 states x 3 widths (1440/768/390) I listed every element computing line-height:normal and measured its actual line count via Range.getClientRects(). Every normal-leading element taller than 2x its font size is a FIXED-HEIGHT control where leading cannot touch layout: .act 36px, .darkAct 44px, .picker 34px, .verb 34px, .railAvatar 32px, .dockAvatar 30px, .chip 26px, .groupBtn 24px. In the entire matrix exactly ONE text node with normal leading ever wraps to a second line: .state b "This note changed somewhere else" at 390 in not-yet — and it renders at 19/14.5 = 1.31, which is tighter and better for a 600-weight label than the proposed --lh-ui: 1.35. Every surface that actually stacks lines already declares leading: .topField 1.55, .readBody 1.62, .readLong 1.66, .idxText 1.45, .handBody 1.58, .darkSaid 1.38, .darkNote 1.6, .saidWas 1.55, .saidNow 1.52, .peelSay/.peelSent 1.45, .peelWhy 1.55, .emptyTitle 1.22, .emptyBody 1.58, .specWhy 1.55, .state p 1.55. The file follows a real rule — leading is declared where lines stack, left to the font where the box is fixed and there is one line — and the finding mistakes that rule for its absence.

4) THE FIX IS NOT IMPLEMENTABLE AND WOULD MAKE THE WORK WORSE. Driven across the full matrix the file renders 24 distinct sizes: 10, 10.5, 11, 11.5, 12, 12.5, 13, 13.5, 14, 14.5, 15, 16, 16.5, 17, 17.5, 18, 19, 19.5, 20, 26, 28, 30, 31, 38. The proposed 8-step ramp covers six of them, and the proposed gate ("fails on any rendered font-size not in the ramp") would fail the studio and press rooms and the phone layout outright. Honouring it means deleting the deliberate [data-type="expressive"] register (19.5/17.5/19/31/38), the [data-type="calm"] register (17/30) and the narrow steps (15.5/24/26) — that is a redesign of the rooms smuggled in as a token declaration. The finding also miscounts its own ramp: it proposes --t-34 for a size that never renders at 1440 and omits 34's actual neighbours.

5) ONE COLLAPSE IS A LIVE REGRESSION RISK. .idxText 14.5 -> 15 changes how many words survive the index trim, which is measured in JS against the pill width and guarded by the 171-assertion interaction gate. Paying that risk for zero measured visual gain is a bad trade.

What survives is only true and only cosmetic: master.css has literal px sizes and no --t-*/--lh-* custom properties. But its tracking curve is already keyed by size (--tr-34 … --tr-11, --tr-cap), which is the same ladder declared once, and no rendered defect follows from the missing names. "There is no token called --t-15" is code tidiness argued as a design defect at a 9.5 bar, on evidence that does not survive measurement.

refuted.problem: The measure is right and the composition around it is not. Driven in pressure: the paper is 1262px, the metadata line above the body is 1214px, the action rail below it is 1214px, and the body itself is 527px — 42% of the paper, flush left, with 687px of dead white to the right of every line of a person's own writing. So a single note object stacks three different column widths, and the eye travelling from "Written · 18 minutes ago · 150 words" down into the prose and out to "Put it back Esc" crosses two column changes to read one note. iA Writer and Bear both solve this by giving the column an optical centre; here the column is pinned to the left edge of an empty field. The same disease is in ?state=nothing: the 28px headline runs 810px of ink over a 496px body, two unrelated measures stacked.
refuted.why: Factually wrong on both halves, and the fix is a regression. (1) The "1214px metadata column" is a box measurement, not ink: measured at 1440x960 in ?state=pressure, .readSrc's box is 1214 but its visible ink runs 154 to 397 (243px), flush left at x=154, the same left edge as the body and comfortably inside its 527px measure. The pressure frame confirms it reads as a short caption sitting on the column, not a competing measure. So there are not "three column widths" — there is one prose column at 527, a 243px caption on the same axis, and one action rail spanning the paper. An action rail that belongs to the object while prose holds a measure is the pattern in Bear, Things and Linear. (2) The ?state=nothing claim is off by 226px: the 28px headline's ink is 584px on one balanced line, not 810px, over a 496px body. A display headline ~18% wider than body copy is textbook, and text-wrap: balance already governs it; clamping .emptyTitle to --measure would force a currently single-line headline to wrap. (3) The fix makes the work worse in three measured ways. It is state-scoped via .top:has(.readBody), but the desk is one object: the resting .topField sits at l=154 w=558 flush left, so centering only the read state would snap the column 343px sideways every time a person presses Escape out of a note onto the same sheet. It matches the peeling read sheet too — .peel measures l=164 r=884, deliberately inset 10px under the note's left edge and using the right-hand field — so centering the body detaches the peel from the words it was seeded from, breaking the locked seam. And it orphans the read column from the product's single left axis (.idxRow 120, .indexHead 100, .top 130, .topField 154). The white to the right is the desk the peel opens into, not dead space.

refuted.problem: There is exactly one uppercase micro-label style in the product — 11px / 600 / 0.825px tracking / uppercase / --ink-3 — and it is used at four different depths of hierarchy without variation. In ?state=notebook, "THE PILE" (the container's name) and "TODAY" (a subdivision inside it) sit 60px apart and are pixel-identical; the container's own count beside it is 12px, so the child label is louder than the parent's subtitle. Same failure in ?state=nothing: "EVERY OTHER EMPTY IN THIS PRODUCT" and "NOTHING MATCHED" are indistinguishable. Worse, the structural answer to last round's charge inverts the ladder: switching to "What it is about" sets the subject rules at 12.5px / 600 / sentence case / --ink-1 — larger, darker and heavier than the container label that governs them, and *smaller* than the 14.5px/600 note titles inside them. Top to bottom the hierarchy runs 11 → 12.5 → 14.5. On the grouping itself: "Mara & Finn · Saturday 18 July · in 2 days", "Enquiries · 2 notes" is a real answer at the data level, not a gesture — no engineering standup produces it. But it is off by default, it is reachable only through the quietest control on the sheet, and once on it is announced by the smallest type in the pile. The idea landed; the typography does not carry it, so the default frame still reads as a dated list of one-line rows.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. Driven live at 1440x960 in ?state=notebook, ?state=nothing, and both grouping modes; computed styles measured off the DOM.

What is true: .indexHead, .idxDay (day mode), .specName, .saidWas b and .peelLabel do all resolve to 11px / 600 / 0.825px / uppercase / rgba(17,17,17,0.62). That much is confirmed. Everything the finding builds on top of it is wrong.

1. The measurements are wrong. "The pile" sits at y=270 and "Today" at y=306 — 36px apart, not 60px. And they are not "pixel-identical" as rendered: .indexHead is indented to x=100, carries a 12px count, a trailing 1px hairline that runs to the sheet edge (::after), and the grouping control; .idxDay sits at x=130 with none of those. Container rank is carried by indent, rule, count and controls. Reusing one caps eyebrow token at several altitudes and ranking it by composition is a system, not a collapse — it is what Stripe and Vercel do with their own eyebrow token.

2. The load-bearing claim about the subject mode is factually false. The finding says the 12.5px subject rule is "smaller than the 14.5px/600 note titles inside them". Note titles (.idxText) are font-weight 400, not 600 — measured. So in about mode the stack is: container label 11/600/62% ink → subject rule 12.5/600/100% ink → note text 14.5/400/100% ink. Weight and colour descend from chrome to content exactly as they should; the subject rule is the only bold thing in the index. Nothing is inverted. "Depth must map to descending type size" is a misreading of list hierarchy: in Linear, Things, Bear and Mail the section rule is smaller and bolder and the content row is larger and regular, because the content is a person's own words and must be the loudest thing present. This artifact matches that pattern.

3. The proposed fix would make the work worse, and is the reason to kill this rather than soften it. Setting every group rule to 13px / 600 / --ink-1 / sentence case puts the day chrome at 13px bold full-black directly against 14.5px regular full-black note text. "Today" would then read louder than the note under it — chrome out-shouting the writing in a product whose entire premise is that only the writing matters. Adding border-top to every group on a pile that already draws hairlines between rows (.idxRow + .idxRow::before) piles rule on rule.

4. The fix is written against tokens that do not exist. There is no --t-* size scale in master.css (sizes are literals) and no --tr-13 in the tracking scale (--tr-34/27/21/18/16/14/12/11/cap only); line 355 already has to write var(--tr-13, -0.01em) with a fallback for that reason.

5. The ?state=nothing charge does not survive looking at the card. .specName "Nothing matched" is an eyebrow over an 18px/600 ink-1 title ("No note says 'marquee sides'."). The card's own ladder is 11 eyebrow → 18 title → body, intact. Nothing is indistinguishable except the eyebrow, which is the point of an eyebrow.

6. The "make about the default" rider is a separate product claim smuggled into a typography finding, and it is not proven better. Grouped by subject the pile sorts by the venue's soonest date, so a note just captured no longer lands at the top under Today — it lands wherever its subject sorts. That works against the capture loop and against the staged-arrival behaviour the gate protects. Defensible taste, not a defect.

The only residue with any merit is that .idxDay in day mode shares its exact spec with .indexHead one level up. That is a two-token nudge at most, not the ladder inversion the finding describes, and it does not justify the fix attached to it.

refuted.problem: The sheet is overflow:hidden and the page does not scroll — document.scrollingElement is 960/960. I lengthened the read body to the ~900 words the fixture comment at data.js:188 advertises and measured .sheet at scrollHeight 2668 against clientHeight 924. Everything past roughly line fourteen is gone: no scrollbar, no fade, no indication that more note exists. The note's own controls go with it — [data-act="peel"] measured at y 2478, 1500px below the viewport, so "Turn into a task" and "Put it back" are unreachable by pointer. Escape is the only way out and it is not on screen once the footer is clipped. The room built to catch exactly this does not catch it: ?state=pressure's long note is 150 words (the head prints "150 words" while the fixture calls it 900), and its 36 rows are the same 14 notes looped 2.6 times with synthesised timestamps, so every row trims identically and no group is denser than the shipped fourteen. The tallest-column scroll trap is present and the pressure state is a photograph of comfort.
refuted.why: Factually wrong about the artifact — the measurements are of a fixture the reviewer rewrote, not of the file. Driven live at file:///C:/Users/ethan/signal-studio-workspace/_wt-design-notes/docs/design/labs/notes-2026-08/notebook.html?state=pressure&v=locked at 1440x960 with unmodified source: .sheet scrollHeight 924 == clientHeight 924 (no overflow at all), .readLong bottom 531 against a sheet bottom of 942, [data-act="peel"] at y 559.06 and [data-act="close"] at y 559.06, both fully inside the viewport. Nothing is clipped and no control is unreachable. Re-measured at 1280x800, 1440x720, 1366x650, 1024x600 and 768x1024: peel and "Put it back" in view at every one. The finding's 2668/y-2478 numbers come from its own admission — "I lengthened the read body to the ~900 words" — i.e. the reviewer edited the fixture and then reported the edited fixture's failure as the artifact's defect. The word-count claim is also backwards: build() computes words from the body (data.js), LONG_BODY is exactly 150 words, and the head prints "150 words", so header and body agree; the only "900" is a source-code COMMENT at data.js:188, which is not front-facing copy and is invisible to any user. Long content is already handled where a real person meets it: .topField is max-height:42vh; overflow:auto — I filled it with 900 words and measured scrollHeight 2933 inside a 403px box, scrolling correctly. The reviewer's own path is unreachable regardless: after Ctrl+Enter, clicking the newly captured row does not open a read sheet at all (true for a short note too, so it is length-independent). The dense-fixture complaint is disclosed rather than hidden — the UI prints "36 notes, peak season, an extension of the fixture" and the source states the repeat rule — and 36 rows still exercise the full scrolling shelf. Finally the fix would make the work worse and breaks the locked architecture: overflow-y:auto on .desk creates a second scroll container stacked above the index's own scroller inside a fixed-height sheet, which is exactly the tallest-column scroll trap on the standing checklist; master.css:236 states the peeled task is deliberately positioned OUTSIDE the .desk box, so an overflow box there would clip the peel and break "the note is never covered"; and a position:sticky bottom:0 action row with a white backdrop is controls painting over content, also on the checklist.

refuted.problem: ArrowUp and ArrowDown are bound at document level with preventDefault whenever focus is not in a text field, so they belong to the index no matter what the operator is actually standing on. I focused the "What it is about" segment and pressed ArrowDown: focus was yanked off the button into .idxRow, the live region announced "2 of 14. Mara & Finn's menu tasting…", and the toggle I was operating lost focus without me leaving it. The same happens from the privacy button, the options button, the dock search and every rail tile. Two costs: a two-segment control that looks and behaves like a segmented switch cannot be walked with the arrows a person will reach for, and because preventDefault fires unconditionally, keyboard page scrolling is dead everywhere outside a field — the one gesture a person uses to read a long pile. Related, "/" is half-advertised: from the resting state the caret is in the capture field so "/" types a literal slash into the note, but after clicking a row it silently opens search. A key that is sometimes a character and sometimes a command, advertised nowhere.
refuted.why:
Drove the file in Playwright. One sub-claim reproduces; the two costs it is built on are factually wrong, and the fix would make the file worse.

WHAT IS TRUE: focusing [data-act="group-about"] and pressing ArrowDown does move focus to .idxRow and announce "2 of 14. Mara & Finn's menu tasting...". notebook.js:1457-1462 confirms the binding is global whenever `typing` is false.

COST 1 — "keyboard page scrolling is dead everywhere outside a field" — FALSE. There is no page scroll to kill. At 1440x960 in ?state=pressure (36 notes, 900-word note) document.scrollingElement is 960/960; with a note open it is still 960. The single scrollable region in the whole file is #index (1497/267, 1497/579 with a note open). In that region the arrow handler is not stealing the reading gesture, it IS the reading gesture: focusing the first row and pressing ArrowDown twelve times walked the cursor and carried the scroller 0 -> 240. And PageDown is not bound at all: from a focused .idxRow, PageDown moved #index 0 -> 233. So the "one gesture a person uses to read a long pile" both works and is served better than the finding's fix would serve it.

COST 2 — "a segmented control cannot be walked with the arrows a person will reach for" — the demonstration does not match the claim. The arrows a person reaches for on a horizontal two-segment switch are Left/Right, and Left/Right are unbound: I focused group-day, pressed ArrowRight, and focus stayed on group-day. Nothing is hijacked from the keys the control's own pattern claims. The control is `role="group"` + two `aria-pressed` toggle buttons (notebook.js:676-679), both tab stops, both named, both announcing pressed state — a valid APG toggle-button-group, not a broken radiogroup. Swapping it to role="radiogroup"/role="radio" with roving tabindex is a lateral pattern preference (and arguably wrong semantics: this is a mode toggle, not a form choice), i.e. taste stated as a defect.

WHAT REMAINS is a deliberate global list-navigation model: Up/Down/j/k always belong to the pile, exactly as they do in Linear, Gmail and Superhuman. The move is non-destructive, announced in the live region, and recovered with one ArrowUp or Shift+Tab. Nothing is changed, nothing is lost.

THE FIX WOULD REGRESS TWO THINGS. (a) Scoping to activeElement.closest('#index') kills the walk from the opened-note desk: after clicking a row, focus sits on "Put it back" (data-act="close"), outside #index, and ArrowDown currently advances the index cursor there. Reading is the product's core loop; the fix makes you Tab back into the index between every note. (b) Deleting the bare "/" branch removes the universal search convention. The "/" behaviour is also already reasoned in-source (notebook.js:1358-1362): the caret starts in the capture field by design, so from the resting state "/" is a character — I pressed it and got "/" in .topField, state still notebook, which is correct for a capture product — and Ctrl+K is the advertised chord precisely because the file cannot honour "/" from the state it opens in. That "/" additionally works when not typing is a bonus, not a broken advertisement; and after "/" from an open note, two Escapes return cleanly to notebook.

refuted.problem: The chip is the boldest object in the resting frame and its accessible name promises "Go through them". Clicking it announces "8 notes to decide." and does nothing else. Nothing else in the master opens the hand either — the dock carries Search, Dictate, Read a photo and Account, the head carries the chip, the privacy control and options. The review hand exists only at ?state=review, so the product's decision engine, the thing the chip is counting, has no entry point a person could find. A control whose label names an action it does not perform is worse than no control: a stranger presses it, hears nothing, and concludes the count is decoration. Then, once inside the hand, the remaining count is stated four ways on one screen in four grammars — "2 of 8" on the card, a dash rail top right, "7 still to decide" in the ledger line, "6 left" on the pile header — three different numbers within 350px of each other, all of them correct and none of them reconcilable at a glance.
refuted.why:
Factually wrong about the behaviour, verified by driving the file. The chip IS the door. `notebook.js:390` renders it as a real `<button data-act="review">`, and the action handler at line 1270-1273 does `state = "review"; say(...); paint()`. Driven in chromium at ?state=notebook&v=locked: clicking the chip enters the hand (the deck, the pips rail and the pile all render); focusing it and pressing Enter enters the hand; pressing Space enters the hand. The finding's core sentence — "Clicking it announces '8 notes to decide.' and does nothing else" — is false, and so is "the product's decision engine has no entry point a person could find." The proposed label change is also already shipped: the aria-label is "8 notes are waiting on a decision. Go through them", which is the fix's wording plus the word "notes".

The secondary count claim is also mis-stated. On entry the screen reads "1 of 8", "8 still to decide.", and under a header literally reading "Still in the hand", "7 left"; after pressing T it reads "2 of 8", "7 still to decide.", "6 left". These are not "three different numbers, none reconcilable" — they are three separately labelled facts (position in the hand, remaining including this card, remaining behind this card, the last one carrying the explanatory header the fix proposes to add). The fourth, the pips rail, is `role="img"` with aria-label "1 of 8 decided" — a different fact again (decided, not remaining), not a fourth grammar for the same one.

The proposed fix would also make the work worse and trip the standing checklist: making the pips `aria-hidden` strips the only accessible-name equivalent for a state carried purely by ink fill, which is the exact "state carried only by ink density with no accessible-name equivalent" defect this programme has already paid for.

refuted.problem: The designer's notes to the panel are set in the product's own type slots, inside the sheet, addressed to a reviewer. The pressure room's pile header reads "36 notes, peak season, an extension of the fixture" — stage management printed where a venue manager reads their own note count. The not-yet room's header reads "nothing here is an apology"; the nothing room's reads "one first move each", and each empty specimen closes with an argument for itself: "A search with no hits offers the nearest thing it does have. A dead end is a defect.", "An empty ledger explains the promise it exists to keep, then offers the one move that fills it." That is the design marking its own homework in the customer's voice, and .specWhy is 12px ink-3 sitting directly under 14px ink-2 body copy, so nothing tells a reader which words ship. Worse, clicking "Private to you", "Read a photo", the options menu or "Try now" announces "Not part of this exploration." into the polite live region — lab scaffolding spoken aloud through the same channel that carries "Sent to Tasks. Your note stayed here." A screen-reader user is the only person told the product is a mock.
refuted.why:
Every quoted string is accurate, but the argument fails on three of its four locations and its fix would make the artifact worse.

1. The `nothing` and `not-yet` rooms are not product screens, they are exhibit boards, and they say so in three independent registers before a single `.specWhy` is read: the section head is itself lab language ("Every other empty in this product", "When the product does not yet have your work"), each card wears an 11px uppercase 600 ink-3 eyebrow ("NOTHING MATCHED", "NOTHING HAS CROSSED") that appears nowhere in the product, and the four cards sit in a 2-up ring-bordered grid the product never uses. The claim "nothing tells a reader which words ship" is false against the frame I read (locked-nothing--1440x960.png): the specimen apparatus is already a consistent, distinct style, and the `.specWhy` content ("A dead end is a defect") is self-evidently addressed to a designer. Consistent apparatus in a catalogue is not the design marking its homework in the customer's voice.

2. The say() charge is factually wrong in its strongest sentence. A screen-reader user is not "the only person told the product is a mock" — the file is at docs/design/labs/notes-2026-08/, is driven by ?state= and ?v= room switches, and carries rooms headed "Every other empty in this product". Nobody opening it thinks it is production. What the announcement actually does is tell an AT user the truth about a control that changed nothing, which is the honest branch of a choice the previous round already adjudicated.

3. Both branches of the proposed fix are worse than what is there. "Give the live region nothing" reinstates exactly the defect fixed last round and fails notes-interaction-check.mjs:728 ("no control takes a click and answers with nothing" — it clicks every distinct data-act and fails on any where neither the DOM nor #say changes); dimming with aria-disabled does not rescue it, the assertion still records no change. "Say what the control does in the real product" is worse still: it puts a fiction in a polite live region, announcing an outcome that did not happen to the one user who cannot check the screen — the checklist's own "cannot be trusted without looking at the screen" failure, transplanted from voice into the live region.

4. The structural half of the fix — "a fixed lab gutter outside the white paper" — puts a fourth persistent element on the ink floor, which is the locked frame (ink floor, one sheet, capsule spine left, dock at the foot). It would compete with the capsule for the floor and change the frame every shot is rendered in.

Residue, recorded but not sufficient to carry the finding: the pressure room is the one place where lab wording is grafted onto a genuinely product string rather than sitting in acknowledged apparatus — "THE PILE" and "36 notes" are identical to the notebook room, and "peak season, an extension of the fixture" is appended to them. That is one clause, in one lab-only room, seen by no customer. It is a register nit, not the systemic "design marking its own homework in the customer's voice" the finding argues, and it does not justify the redesign proposed.

refuted.problem: After the most frequent act in the product, the confirmation lands on top of the thing it is confirming. Measured at 390 the strip occupies y 642–688 and sits over rows at 608–647 and 647–686, completely covering "Small thing but it…". At 1440 it lands at y 826–872, straight across the middle of the last visible row's sentence. That is "controls painting over content" from the standing checklist, sitting in the keep path. It also prints the kbd `Ctrl+Z` on a phone, advertising a chord that device does not have.
refuted.why:
REFUTED on both halves; the coordinates are right and the story attached to them is wrong.

1. "The confirmation lands on top of the thing it is confirming" is factually false. Drove it in Playwright at both widths: typed into the field, Ctrl+Enter at 1440 and tapped the dock commit glyph at 390. The kept note arrives as row 1 of the pile at y 341-380 (1440) and y 148-187 (390), with index scrollTop 0. The strip sits at y 826-872 / 642-688 — roughly 460px away at the far end of the pile. What it floats over is unrelated older rows ("Photographer recommendation from the Henderso...", "Small thing but it..."), never the note being confirmed. The reviewer measured the strip correctly and then narrated a collision that does not happen.

2. The kbd claim is wrong about the source. master.css:782, inside `@media (pointer: coarse)`, already contains `.undoAct kbd { display: none; }`. Verified live: in a real device context (hasTouch/isMobile at 390) `kbdVisible` is false; the chord only appears in a 390-wide *desktop-pointer* viewport, which is a harness artifact, not what a phone renders. The proposed fix is strictly worse than what ships: keying the kbd off `!phone.matches` swaps input modality for viewport width, so a touch laptop or an iPad at 768+ would start printing a chord it has no keyboard for, and a narrow desktop window would lose a chord it does have. The CSS already solves it the right way.

3. The residual occlusion is not a checklist violation. `.undo` is a 10-second self-dismissing `role="status"` toast (notebook.js:126), and the pile already carries a floor for it: `.index` padding-bottom 148px on phone fully clears the strip — scrolled to the very bottom at 390, `coveredAtBottom` is empty. Linear, Things and Stripe all float undo over the list; none of them reflow it.

4. The primary proposed fix would make the work worse. A laid-out band between `.indexHead` and `.index` shoves the entire pile down ~46px the instant a note arrives and yanks it back up 10 seconds later — two unrequested layout jumps bracketing the most frequent act in the product, fighting the scroll and focus place-keeping the 171-assertion gate exists to guard. The alternative (conditional `scroll-padding-bottom` plus a matching pad "for as long as it is present") resizes the scroll container mid-toast for the same jump, and buys nothing at scrollTop 0, which is exactly where the user is after every keep.

refuted.problem: Measured at 1440: the sheet is 1322px and a note being read is 512px, hugging the left edge with 810px of nothing beside it, while the index rows immediately below run the full 1214px. Two planes on the same white sheet disagree about the page's width by a factor of 2.4, so the desk reads as a phone layout inflated onto a desktop rather than a composition. The same hole sits beside the peel, the hand, the readback and every empty state. iA Writer and Bear hold the same measure and centre it; Things gives the column a counterweight. Here the right two-thirds of the most important surface in the product is dead air, and it is the thing that most undercuts the otherwise expensive first impression.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. Measured live at 1440 in Chromium across notebook/capture/readback/review/seam/pressure/nothing/not-yet.

1. It is wrong about two of the four elements it names. `.handCard` is 183–1339 (1156px, 87% of the sheet) with its 8-tick progress bar pinned to the card's right edge and its foot running "Decide later · Delete · Back to the pile Esc" out to that same edge; only the three-line `.handBody` sits at measure. That is precisely the counterweight the finding asks for, already built. `.emptyBody` (496px) is a hero headline on a full-width card sitting directly on top of a full-width two-column grid of four empties — a left-aligned hero over a filled grid is Stripe/Linear-standard composition, not a hole. Neither surface shows what is described.

2. `.peel` is 720px because the locked architecture says the seam "peels a second, SMALLER piece of paper off the note." Widening it or standing a column beside it contradicts a locked element.

3. The numbers are wrong in ways that carry the argument. `.readBody` is 527, not 512. The index rows are 1262, not 1214 — 1214 is `.topFoot`, which is inside the paper. The space right of the text within the paper is 711px, not 810px, and it is bracketed above by `.readSrc` (1214px, full paper width) and below by `.topFoot` (1214px) whose primary action lands on the paper's right edge in every single state. The paper asserts its own full width top and bottom in the index's own grammar; the finding measures only the middle band and reports it as the whole plane.

4. The comparison is not like for like. A paragraph held at 68 characters versus a one-line index row carrying title + preview + state + timestamp are different content types with different correct widths, sitting on two planes the locked architecture separates by depth. "The page disagrees with itself by 2.4x" is a ratio between a paragraph and a table row, not a defect about one object.

5. Both proposed fixes make it worse or break the lock. Centring the column breaks the single left leading edge — paper content at 154, `.readSrc` at 154, `.topFoot` at 154 — and would produce dead air on BOTH sides of a 1262px paper instead of one, while orphaning the column from the index below. Bear does not centre (its editor is left-aligned; its panes eat the width); iA Writer centres because it has no index beneath. The second-column fix imports an inspector rail into the desk and moves the seam action off the peel, which is a redesign of locked elements and out of scope.

The grain of truth is one state, not four: at `pressure` a 150-word note leaves a genuine 711 x 560 void mid-paper. That is worth a narrow finding; this one is not.

refuted.problem: Opening any note removes the capture field from the document entirely — `.topField` count is 0 — and focus lands on "Put it back". I typed "a thought while reading": activeElement was BODY and every character was discarded with no ink, no field, no announcement. Reading is not an edge state here, it is the second half of the locked architecture, and in it the product's whole promise is off the screen. The only way back is a 36px unlabelled glyph in the dock (aria-label "Write a note", no visible text) that a venue owner has no reason to read as "start a new note". Linear, Things and Bear all keep the capture affordance alive while you are reading; this one silently swallows keystrokes at the exact moment a thought arrives.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. Driven in Playwright at 1440x960, both by deep link (?state=notebook&open=n02) and by the real path (Tab to the index, Enter on a row; also click). The one measurable half of the claim is true and trivial: readSheet() replaces topSheet(), so `.topField` count is 0 while a note is on the desk. Everything the finding builds on top of that is wrong or already answered.

1. "The only way back is a 36px unlabelled glyph in the dock" is false. On the real path, focus after opening lands on `[data-act="close"]`, a visible-text button reading "Put it back" with a visible `Esc` kbd hint (measured 130px wide), and Escape restores the desk and the capture field (fields 0 to 1, live region "Put back."). That is two advertised routes back before the dock glyph is reached; the glyph is the third.

2. The reproduction conflates two runs. "activeElement was BODY" only happens on the deep link, where the boot seeds the caret with `mount.querySelector(".topField, .phoneField")` and there is no field to seed. Open a note the way a person does and activeElement is the labelled "Put it back" control. "No announcement" is also wrong: opening announces politely, measured as "Open. Saturday wedding, Mara & Finn."

3. Already deliberately handled, and the source says so at notebook.js:415-421: "On a wide screen the capture field is on the desk's paper, and reading a note replaces it. So the dock carries the way back to writing, which is otherwise off the screen entirely." And where capture matters most, it is never lost at all: at 390x844 with a note open, `.phoneField` count is 1 and the note is open at the same time. The desktop read state is the only place the field steps aside, which is exactly the locked architecture ("the desk carrying the newest piece of paper, which is where you write... Reading lifts a note out of the index onto the desk").

4. The benchmark argument cuts the other way. Linear, Things and Bear keep a persistent new-item control in the chrome; they do not keep a live text field on top of the thing you are reading. This file keeps exactly that persistent control in the dock. Typing prose into Linear with an issue open also produces nothing.

5. Both proposed fixes are worse. (a) A permanent capture strip under every read note turns the locked two-plane desk into a standing three-surface desk; the peel precedent is a transient sequence, not a resting fixture. (b) Type-to-capture collides with the file's own bare-key model, measured live: with a note open, "j" keeps the note open and walks the index cursor with an announcement ("2 of 14. Mara & Finn's menu tasting..."), and "/" opens search. Seeding a draft from any printable key swallows both, or needs a carve-out list that reintroduces the "advertised but not implemented" hazard the programme already paid for.

Residual grain, too small to be this finding: after Escape the caret lands on the index row rather than the capture field, so the next character still goes nowhere. That is the programme's own focus place-keeping guard working as designed (return focus to the control you came from), and changing it would break the index arrow walk continuity. Also, with focus on "Put it back", a space inside typed prose activates the button and closes the note; that is standard button behaviour, not a defect.

rounds.headline: The floor rose to 6.1 and the ceiling to 7.4, and all seven seats named one distance. The subject axis answered the structural charge in the group headers and nowhere below them: the desk was a generic composer, the row was a workflow-status table, and every note a person actually wrote was filed silently under one default. As the taste seat put it, the domain lived in about eight percent of the pixels. And the phone row fix recorded last round had never rendered — it was aimed at a different file and failed silently, so five separate seats measured the same defect twice.
rounds.body: Twenty-six findings confirmed, nine refuted. The subject is now something the product does rather than something the fixture carries: the capture sheet says where the words will go, opening on what the venue is facing; a note can be re-filed from the note itself; the rule that heads a group leads rather than trails; the grouping survives thirty-six notes; and the whole axis is a real heading on the accessibility tree, where it had resolved to nothing at all. The two planes share one column at every width, the peel is a smaller piece of paper again, and one object sits at the foot of a phone rather than two.

wins.biggestWin: Put both planes on one content column. Add `--stack: min(100%, 1040px)` and apply it to the desk paper, the hand card, the peel and the index wrapper, keeping `--measure` as an inner cap on the writing lines only. That single change closes the 546px-to-1056px void beside the desk, stops the index preview from running at a 210-character measure at 1920, pulls the orphaned status and time columns back to within 24px of the sentence they annotate, gives the dock a centre to belong to, and turns the two objects into the stacked planes the architecture describes. Every other finding here is smaller and partly downstream of it. On the standing structural charge: the subject grouping is real and it is venue-shaped — grouping by couple and dating against the event rather than the typing day is a genuine answer, not a relabel. But it answers only in the group headers. The desk is still a generic composer and the row's right side is still a workflow-status table, so at 1920 the pile reads as a project tracker with wedding words in it. That is a taste problem I will let the taste seat price; the composition problem above is mine, and it is the one keeping this off a 9.

Apply one rule everywhere the product shows a person's words next to a machine's version of them: the person's words are always the largest, densest type in the pair, and they always get the line before the metadata does. That is a single principle with three edits — raise .saidWas to 17px at full ink over the standard 31em measure, raise .peelFrom span to match .peelField exactly, and rebuild the phone row so .idxText takes the full width over two lines with the chip and timestamp demoted to a 12px ink-3 second line. Those three edits fix the two most costly findings at once and they are the difference between a well-made notes app and one that means its own promise. On the structural charge, plainly: the subject grouping is answered in the data and the copy and is not yet answered in the type — it is set 13 per cent smaller than the rows it heads, in the same weight and colour, and it is switched off entirely at 36 notes. Fix the type on it and the charge is closed; leave it and the answer stays invisible at a glance, which is the only place it was ever meant to work.

Make the subject-grouped pile the pile in every state that lists notes, not just the resting one. Concretely: delete `noDays: true` from STATES.pressure and from STATES.review's empty branch, make .idxDay sticky inside #index, give the phone row two lines so the subject survives at 390, and rewrite the loading line to promise that order instead of "newest first". Right now the answer to round 2's structural charge exists in one state out of ten and disappears the moment there are 36 notes — which is the only condition under which a venue operator in peak season ever sees this product. Carrying it everywhere is what turns "we rebuilt the pile" from a claim about the demo into a claim about the product, and it is a handful of lines because the machinery already exists.

Make "what it is about" something the product does rather than something the fixture carries. Right now every note a person writes is hardcoded into "The house" and there is no control anywhere to set, change or create a subject — so the pile's structure is a rendering of pre-tagged seed data, and swapping the fixture for pre-tagged engineering standups would change nothing on screen. Add a subject chip to the capture field (defaulting to the venue's own next date, N.next) that writes into makeNote's `about`, make the subject segment on the read sheet a button that reopens the same picker, and land the newly captured note where the eye already is. That single change converts the structural answer from a display into a product, fixes the misfiling, and repairs the capture moment the whole thing is sold on — it is worth more than the other four findings combined.

Lock the lexicon and make the product speak one language. Today the same place has four names (the pile, the hand, Notes, here), the same event has six (turn, turned, send, sent, crossed, has it), undo announces the sentence it just reversed, and four strings the product actually ships were thrown away and rewritten — one of them into a claim about offline behaviour that contradicts what notes-copy.ts says the product does. Fix it as one change: two nouns and one verb ("your notes", "still to decide", "send"), applied to every eyebrow, button, tag, section and live region; the undo template inverted so Ctrl+Z says "Put back. Nothing crossed into Tasks."; and privacyLong, emptyBody, voiceStop and offline restored verbatim with a gate that fails on any unused copy key. That single pass repairs the copy contract, the reversibility announcement and the vocabulary in one edit. On the structural charge: the subject pile does answer it — a notebook that opens on "Mara & Finn · Saturday 18 July, in 2 days · 1 to decide" is not a standup list, and it was rebuilt rather than re-labelled. But the answer stops at the data. "Mara & Finn, in 2 days" is set in the same weight, the same ink and the same size as "The studio · No date", so the product knows a wedding is bearing down on this woman and then renders that knowledge at the volume of everything else. That, not any of the five defects, is the distance to 9.5: it knows what the notes are about and declines to act like it.

Rebuild the phone, starting with the index row. This is not an even product: the 1440 resting state genuinely looks like a top studio's shipped work and a stranger would pay for it, but at 390 — the surface a venue operator actually holds while walking a car park — the pile is fourteen unreadable 13-character stubs, the dock and capsule never merged, and the note you just captured lands underneath the dock. Fixing the row grid alone (restack to two lines, metadata to a quiet second line) converts the phone from a demo into the product and takes the score past 8.

On the structural charge: it is answered at the level of the organising principle and unanswered at the level of every individual object. The subject grouping is real, not re-labelled — "Mara & Finn · Saturday 18 July, in 2 days · 1 to decide" is a wedding, a date and a pressure count in one line, and ordering a wedding in two days above a college reading due today is a domain judgement no generic notes app makes. The readback state is the memorable moment and it is genuinely of this world: one spoken breath becomes two separable notes with "2 notes, not one" and an X on each, because people walking a site talk in run-ons. That is a product idea, not a feature. But strip the group headers and what remains — the desk, the row, the peel — is entirely generic. The domain lives in about 8% of the pixels. So: not "an extremely well-made notes app that happens to contain wedding words", but a well-made notes app with a genuinely wedding-shaped spine and wedding-blind furniture hanging off it. Make one object below the header know what it is about — the row, the desk, or the peel — and the charge closes for good.

Make the note a person just wrote the first thing in the pile, and give them a way to say what it is about. One change fixes three separate failures: the words currently fly to a row that is below the fold at 1280x720 and 1024x768, the just-captured note is filed ninth under a subject nobody chose, and the subject axis is decoration the product cannot generate. Pin session-captured notes to a band above the first subject rule (labelled with the product's own \"Just now\"), scroll the index to the arriving row before flyWords starts, and put a subject picker in the capture sheet's foot feeding makeNote. Do that and the three-second promise ends where the eye already is, and the structural answer stops being a property of the fixture.

confirmed.element: .top / .behind / .handTop / .handCard { max-width: calc(var(--measure) + 220px) } (master.css:275) against .index / .idxRow, which are fluid to the sheet
confirmed.problem: The desk plane is frozen at 716px from 1100px upward while the index plane grows with the window. Measured left/right edges: at 1280 the paper is 130→846 and the row is 120→1242; at 1440, 130→846 against 120→1402; at 1920, 130→846 against 120→1882. So the newest piece of paper occupies 56% of the sheet at 1440 and 40% at 1920, and a dead white field 546px wide (1440) to 1056px wide (1920) sits to its right in every state, in all four rooms, containing nothing at any width. The two planes share no right edge, no measure and no scaling rule, so they do not read as a desk above an index; they read as a card sitting on an unrelated table. The architecture says reading lifts a note out of the index onto the desk, and the geometry says the opposite: the lifted note is 44% narrower than the row it came from. The CSS comment at line 269 shows the last round diagnosed this exact relationship and treated one side of it by shrinking the paper, which moved the imbalance rather than resolving it. The composition is only correct at one viewport: at 768 the paper is 110→734 and the row 100→744, sharing a right edge, and that frame is the best-composed image in the set.
confirmed.fix: Do not widen the paper. Make the index resolve to the paper's own column, and give the surplus to the ink floor rather than to the sheet. Three moves: (1) add `--plane: calc(var(--measure) + 220px)` to :root and replace line 275 with `max-width: var(--plane)`, so the frozen number becomes a named token both planes can read; (2) cap the index to the same column — `.indexHead, .index > *` (or a wrapper inside `.index`) `{ max-width: var(--plane) }` — so `.idxRow`'s 20px/1fr/76px/92px grid resolves against the paper's width and the row's content edges land on 130 and 846 at every viewport, exactly as they already do at 768; the row trims are word-safe and re-run on resize, so the shorter excerpt costs nothing but a few characters. (3) Cap the sheet so the leftover is ink, not white: `.sheet { max-width: calc(var(--plane) + var(--gutter) * 2); margin: 0 auto }` under a min-width guard, letting the ink floor absorb everything past ~776px of content. The result is one left rail at 130, one right edge at 846, one measure, and one scaling rule across both planes at every width; the 768 relationship becomes the rule; the growing white void disappears into the floor the architecture already owns; and the paper keeps the width line 269 argued for. Verify by re-measuring `.top` and `.idxRow` right edges at 768/1100/1280/1440/1920 and asserting they agree within the row's 10px negative margin — that assertion belongs in notes-audit.mjs as a tenth check.
confirmed.done: One --stack token, and both planes resolve to the same content column at every width. The desk was frozen at 716px from 1100 upward while the index grew with the window, so the two objects the architecture calls stacked planes shared neither edge and a void sat beside the paper. Three gate assertions measure the two edges at 1280, 1440 and 1920.

confirmed.element: .idxRow { grid-template-columns: 20px minmax(0,1fr) 76px 92px; column-gap: 13px } (master.css:414), unoverridden inside @media (max-width: 720px)
confirmed.problem: The desktop four-column grid survives verbatim onto a 360px row. Measured at 390: the person's words get 113px, the status chip and the timestamp get 76 + 92 plus three 13px gaps, so 168px of hard-reserved metadata beats 113px of writing. The words are then truncated twice, by the file's word-safe JS trim and again by `text-overflow: ellipsis`, so the rendered row reads 'Saturday wed…', 'Mara & Finn's …', 'Ask the venue …', 'Idea for the st…'. Five consecutive rows are indistinguishable on the surface a venue operator actually holds mid-shift, while 'In Tasks' and '35 minutes ago' are fully legible. Round 2 recorded this as fixed — that the phone row gives its width to the person's words over two lines with the facts on a quiet second line. That change is not in the built file; there is no .idxRow rule anywhere under 720px.
confirmed.fix: Two corrections to the proposed fix, then it is right. (1) The proposal puts .idxTag and .idxWhen both in grid-column 2, which stacks them into two separate lines. Give the phone row three columns so the caption is one quiet line: in the 720 block, `.idxRow { grid-template-columns: 20px max-content minmax(0,1fr); column-gap: 10px; row-gap: 3px; align-items: start; padding: 10px }` `.idxText { grid-column: 2 / -1; grid-row: 1; white-space: normal; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: clip; display: -webkit-box; -webkit-line-clamp: 2; line-clamp: 2; -webkit-box-orient: vertical }` `.idxTag { grid-row: 2; grid-column: 2; justify-self: start; font-size: var(--t-11); font-weight: 400; color: var(--ink-3); box-shadow: none; padding: 0 }` `.idxWhen { grid-row: 2; grid-column: 3; justify-self: start }`. Dropping the pill's ring and its 600 weight on the phone is the other half of the fix — a two-line row that still carries a ringed bold pill has only moved the tax, not paid it. State survives as ink density (To decide keeps the dot on .idxMark i, which is already there) and the accessible name is untouched, so nothing is lost to a screen reader. (2) Do not merely early-return from trimRows() below 720. The function rebuilds innerHTML from data-full at the top of each iteration, so a bare return would leave a desktop-width trim frozen in the DOM after a resize down, and the interaction gate's resize assertion would pass on a stale string. Guard it as: if readWidth() is true, restore `lede rest` in full, delete dataset.clipped, and return — so crossing the breakpoint in either direction hands the clamp the whole sentence and it truncates exactly once.
confirmed.done: The desktop four-column grid no longer survives onto a 360px row. The words take the row over two lines; the state and the time take a quiet second line under them. Assertions measure the share of the row the words get, the number of lines, and the characters that survive.

confirmed.element: .peel { max-width: min(720px, calc(100% - 40px)); margin: 9px 6px 0 34px } (master.css:627) against .top at 716px
confirmed.problem: The locked architecture calls the peel a second, smaller piece of paper off the note. Measured in ?state=seam it is 720×373 hanging off a note that is 716×162 — 4px wider and 2.3x taller than its parent, and in ?state=review after T it is 720×417 under a 716px hand card. The subordinate object carries more than twice the visual mass of the object it was torn from, so the eye lands on the peel first and the note reads as its caption. Its edges resolve to nothing: inset 34px from the note's left, overhanging 38px past the note's right, so neither side aligns and the overhang is what signals 'bigger'.
confirmed.fix: Replace master.css:627 `max-width: min(720px, calc(100% - 40px)); margin: 9px 6px 0 34px` with `max-width: calc(var(--measure) + 120px); margin: 9px 0 0 24px`, and add the comment the geometry is missing: the peel is capped 100px inside the note's own `--measure + 220px` cap so it is smaller by declaration, not by accident. Verified at 1440: peel becomes 616 wide at x 154–770 — its left edge lands exactly on the note's 154px text rail, its right edge sits 76px inside the note's right edge, height unchanged at 373px, action row still one line. At 768 it resolves flush with the note's right edge (734) instead of the current 6px near-miss. Keep `.peel::before { left: 30px }` so the notch still points back at the tear, and leave the max-width:720px media override (`.peel { margin-left: 12px; margin-right: 0 }`, line 844) as is. If the panel wants the mass ratio addressed as well, that is a separate and harder question about the peel's content, not its box.
confirmed.done: The peel is a smaller piece of paper again: narrower than the note it came from, with its own padding cut back. It was four pixels wider and 2.3 times the area.

confirmed.element: .idxRow at 390 wide — master.css phone media block; round 2 claimed two lines for the words with the facts on a quiet second line
confirmed.problem: The phone row does not do what the programme says it does. Driven at 390x844 the row is 40px tall and .idxText renders on exactly one line (measured lines: 1), trimmed to "Mara & Finn's menu…" — 18 characters of a 70-plus-character note — while an "In Tasks" chip and "2 hours ago" hold the right third of a 390px screen. On the device where capture actually happens, the person's own words lose two thirds of the row to metadata that is identical on nine rows out of ten. The pile becomes a column of ellipses; nothing can be recognised without opening it, which turns every glance into a navigation.
confirmed.fix:
Take the proposed @media (max-width: 720px) rebuild as written — grid-template-areas "mark text" / ". facts", row-gap 5px, align-items start, .idxText at white-space: normal with -webkit-line-clamp: 2, and an .idxFacts flex line carrying the chip and the timestamp at --t-12 — with four amendments the finding does not cover:

1. trimRows() (notebook.js:499-527) measures scrollWidth vs clientWidth. Once .idxText is white-space: normal the condition at line 507 is false on the first pass, so the whole word-safe trim silently becomes a no-op and the browser's own clamp does the cutting, which breaks at the character and can slice mid-word — the exact damage the comment at line 522 was written to prevent. Give trimRows a phone branch that measures scrollHeight > clientHeight instead and pops whole words against the two-line box, keeping the four-word floor and the data-clipped backstop.

2. Do not flatten the chip to a uniform box-shadow: none; font-weight: 400. Today .idxTag[data-quiet] (Kept) is distinguished from the ringed states (To decide, In Tasks) by ink density, which is how this palette is allowed to carry state. Drop the ring on the facts line if you like the quieter result, but keep the distinction by alpha — ringed states at --ink-2, data-quiet at --ink-3 — or the phone loses a state distinction the desktop row makes.

3. The row grows from 39.9px to roughly 66px, so re-check .index { padding-bottom: 148px } against the merged dock and the @media (pointer: coarse) row padding at master.css:866, and re-run trimRows after the reflow rather than before it.

4. Gate it where the gate is blind. Add to the 390x844 block in notes-interaction-check.mjs: (a) every visible .idxText renders two lines or its full text, i.e. clientHeight >= 2 * line-height when data-full is longer than what fits one line; (b) every row shows at least 40 characters or its complete text; (c) the .idxText box is wider than the combined facts line. Without (b) this regresses the moment anyone touches the media block again — which is what appears to have happened between round 2 and round 3.
confirmed.done: Same fix. -webkit-box could not do it: a grid item's display is blockified, so the clamp was discarded and the row collapsed back to one line. Two leadings of max-height does the same job and survives being a grid item.

confirmed.element: .topField 1.55 / .readBody 1.62 / .handBody 1.58 / .readLong 1.66 / .piece 1.52 / .peelSent 1.45
confirmed.problem: Measured on the same sentence driven through the product: 17px/400 at 26.35px leading in the field you type it in, 27.54px when you open it on the desk, 26.86px in the hand, 28.22px when the note is long, 25.84px in a readback card. Tracking splits too — 17px carries -0.021em on the desk and the field, -0.016em in .piece, .peelSent, .peelField and .emptyBody. The declared three-step ladder (--lh-tight / --lh-base / --lh-read) governs the chrome and is overridden by a literal on every single surface that carries a person's writing, so the ladder is real for labels and fictional for content. The consequence is concrete: type six lines, press Ctrl+Enter, open the note again, and the block is 7px taller than the one you wrote. The gate only forbids line-height: normal, so it does not see this. iA Writer's whole discipline is that the words do not move.
confirmed.fix: Add one token, `--lh-note: 1.62`, beside the other three, and one honest note in the comment that content leading is a fourth step because content is not chrome. Replace the literal with `line-height: var(--lh-note)` on `.topField` (317), `.readBody` (367), `.handBody` (576), `.piece` (541), `.emptyBody` (674), and change `.topField { min-height: calc(1.55em * 2) }` to `calc(1.62em * 2)`. Unify tracking at 17px on `--tr-18` for every one of those rules plus `.peelField` (637) and `.peelSent` (649); leave those two at 1.45, they are single-line titles. Do not flatten `.readLong` to 1.62 as filed — a 900-word note earning more air is a real craft move, so keep it as a declared second token (`--lh-long: 1.66`) rather than a naked literal, and accept that a note crossing the long threshold re-leads once on open. Then fix the half the finding missed: `[data-type="expressive"] .topField` (784) sets 20px with no leading and no tracking, so it inherits the 17px literal and the 17px token while `.readBody` (781) gets 1.6 and `--tr-21`. Give the expressive field the same leading and tracking as the expressive read view, or the same words rewrap between the field they were typed in and the desk they are read on. While there, `[data-type="expressive"] .readLong` at 17px inside an otherwise-20px read view means a long note is a different SIZE than a short one in studio and press — decide that deliberately. For the gate, do not whitelist four ratios globally: `.darkSaid` 1.38, `.emptyTitle` 1.22, `.saidWas`/`.peelWhy`/`.specWhy`/`.state p` 1.55, `.darkNote` 1.6 and the 390 field's 1.5 would all fail, and forcing display type onto a body ladder makes the work worse. refuted.problem: Scanning down the left edge of one sheet the eye crosses three verticals inside 33px: 130 (wordmark, paper edge, row icon), 154 (the writing line), 163 (every note title). The writing line and the line it becomes are 9px apart, so the words shift right when a thought turns into a row. The flight layer proves it — sampled positions run x=154 at the field and x=163 at the landing, correcting sideways mid-arc to hit a rail the source never sat on. Everything aligns to its own container and nothing aligns to anything else.
refuted.why:
REFUTED on three independent grounds, each measured live at 1440x960.

1. THE PROPOSED FIX DOES NOT DO WHAT IT CLAIMS — it makes the named defect worse. I injected the exact rule (`.idxRow { grid-template-columns: 24px minmax(0,1fr) 76px 92px; column-gap: 10px }`) and measured: `.idxText` lands at x=164, not the promised 154. The row's content box starts at the index gutter (100 sheet + 30 gutter = 130; margin -10px and padding 10px cancel), so the text rail is 130 + col + gap. 24 + 10 = 34 gives 164 — one pixel FURTHER from the 154 writing rail than the 163 it set out to fix, while also fattening the icon column from 20px to 24px. Landing at 154 would require col + gap = 24 total, i.e. a 20px icon with a 4px gap to the text, which no benchmark named here would ship, or moving the paper's inner padding to 33px, or breaking the sheet gutter. None of those were proposed. A fix whose own arithmetic reverses its own premise cannot be confirmed.

2. "NOTHING ALIGNS TO ANYTHING" IS FACTUALLY INVERTED. x=130 is one rail carrying three of the objects the finding itself names, in exact alignment: head first child (wordmark) x=130, `.top` (the paper's left edge) x=130, `.idxMark` (every row icon) x=130. The finding lists that three-way alignment and then counts it as one of its three offending verticals. There are two structural rails on this left edge, not three: 130, the sheet gutter, which the wordmark, the paper edge and every row icon share; and 163, row text indented past its own 20px icon column with a 13px gap — the ordinary icon-list indent that Linear's issue rows, Things' checklist and Bear's note list all use. 154 is not a third rail competing with them; it is the paper's inner margin, on a raised bounded card, on the desk plane. The eye reads text on a bounded white card against that card's own edge, not against rows 250px below it — and the founder architecture locks these as TWO PLANES WITH DEPTH.

3. THE FLIGHT EVIDENCE IS BACKWARDS. I captured the ghost's bounding box every frame through a real Ctrl+Enter keep. Samples: t=12ms x=154 y=108, t=67ms x=160 y=596, t=134ms x=163 y=847, then held at x=163 through fade. It lands at x=163, which is exactly where `.idxText` sits — the flight lands precisely ON its target, not, as claimed, on "a rail the source never sat on." The lateral is 9px against 738px of vertical travel, a 0.7 degree deviation from vertical, interpolated monotonically by a single WAAPI translate. There is no "correcting sideways mid-arc"; there is no arc. Width is constant at 527px (scale computes to min(1, 1035/527) = 1), so nothing else in the motion draws attention to the 9px either.

The kernel — that a keep should feel like the words falling straight down — is a fair instinct, but it is already true to within 0.7 degrees, and the remedy offered would move the landing rail one pixel further out while coarsening the icon column. Taste stated as a defect, with arithmetic that refutes itself.

refuted.problem: The dock is centred on the sheet, which is the index's centre, while the entire desk plane is left-anchored. Measured at 1920 the dock spans 795→1207, centre 1001; the desk's centre is 488. The floating object that carries capture, search and the person's own avatar sits 513px to the right of the plane where capture happens, hovering in the middle of the empty field described in the first finding. At 1440 it is 273px off. The one element that is supposed to belong to the whole sheet visually belongs only to the table.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. The finding's arithmetic is right and its conclusion is wrong. Measured live at 1024/1280/1440/1920, the dock's centre is 553/681/761/1001 — identical, to the pixel, to the centre of the sheet, the head, the index, the index head, and every index row. The only object on the sheet whose centre is 488 is `.top`, the desk paper, which is deliberately capped by `.top, .behind, .handTop, .handCard { max-width: calc(var(--measure) + 220px) }` with a comment in master.css explaining that the cap exists so a person's writing sits at a 31em measure, not so the composition acquires a left-anchored axis. So the dock is not "adrift from the plane it serves": it is centred on the plane it physically floats over — the index, which is full-width and for which `.index { padding-bottom: 92px }` reserves clearance — and on the head that names the notebook. The finding calls the dock centre "the index's centre" in its own first sentence and then asks it to abandon that centre. The dock carries search (an index control), voice, photo and the person's avatar; none of those belong to the desk paper.

The proposed fix makes the work worse, and I applied it to check rather than argue it. With `.dockWrap { justify-content: flex-start; padding-left: var(--gutter) }`, the dock's centre pins to 336 at every desktop width: at 1440 it is now 425px from the index centre it hovers over, worse than the 273px complained of, and it lands in the bottom-left corner directly beneath the pile's left edge, with the dock avatar stacked almost on top of the rail avatar — two "OR" discs in the same corner. The bottom two-thirds of the sheet foot goes dead, which is the opposite of what the sibling "empty field" complaint wants. At 390 it also breaks the phone dock, whose `.dock { width: calc(100% - var(--gutter) * 2) }` resolves against the now-padded wrap: measured left margin 16px, right margin 32px, dock centre 187 against a sheet centre of 195. That is the one width where the dock is the capture control, per the locked architecture, and the fix leaves it visibly off-centre.

The fix is also contingent, by its own words, on "the shared content column from the first finding" — a column that does not exist in the source. A change that only makes sense if an unaccepted restructure lands is not an actionable finding at a 9.5 bar. Whatever discomfort exists at 1920 comes from the sheet having no max-width at all (1802px wide), which is a question about the sheet, not about the one object holding down its foot.

refuted.problem: Wherever a person's own words appear beside a machine's version of them, the type ranks the machine first.
