In the seam the picked words `.peelFrom span` are 15px/400 and the derived task wording `.peelField` is 17px/600. A product whose stated promise is that only the exact words a person picks ever cross sets those exact words as a caption and the derivation as the headline, twice, in the two flows that exist to prove the promise. This is the deepest defect on the sheet and it is a taste failure, not an oversight.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. The CSS values quoted are real, but the premise built on them — "wherever a person's own words appear beside a machine's version, the type ranks the machine first" — is false in both flows once you drive them instead of diffing two rules.

READBACK. `.saidWas` and `.darkSaid` print the SAME string (`N.speech.transcript`, notebook.js:1017 and :1033). One state earlier, in ?state=voice, those exact words are set at `--t-34` — 34px, the largest type anywhere in the product, alone on the ink floor (master.css:507). The person's words are given the biggest type in the file; the derived pieces get 17px. The 13px `.saidWas` is the third appearance of that text, a held receipt labelled "What you said, once", not the first ranking of it. The measurement is also off: driven at 1440x960, box-sizing is border-box, so the content box is 449px and the widest rendered line is 75 characters, not 82 — and `.piece` (595px) and `.top` (527px) are both physically wider boxes.

SEAM. `.peelFrom span` is not the only place the picked words appear. At the moment the peel is open, the note is uncovered by architecture and the picked range renders in it as `.pick` at 17px / weight 400 / rgb(17,17,17), indigo-washed, 503px wide — measured. That is the same size as `.peelField` and heavier ink than nothing. The picked words are on screen at full reading type at the same instant as the derivation; `.peelFrom` is a second, smaller quotation of them inside the panel so the two can be compared without scrolling. "The derivation is the headline and the source is a caption" is not what is on the screen.

THE FIX WOULD MAKE IT WORSE, TWICE. (1) `.saidWas` at 17px/ink-1/measure inside a wash chip becomes near-identical to a `.piece` (white, 17px, ink-1) — two blocks of the same 174 characters at the same size and ink, stacked, one editable and one not, with only a 3.5% tint separating them. That is an invisible-affordance regression of exactly the kind the standing checklist names, and it grows the receipt from 111px to roughly 170px, pushing both pieces and the "Put both on the pile" commit down a 960px viewport. (2) `.peelFrom span` at 17px/600 becomes byte-identical in type to `.peelField`, so the static quote and the textarea a venue owner must find and edit read as the same object inside a 720px panel.

CONSTRAINT. The fix explicitly proposes to "let the tint carry the difference". The locked constraint is that state is ink DENSITY and FILL, never colour — density is the sanctioned mechanism and it is what is carrying the distinction today. The fix removes it and leans on background tint alone.

The closing law — "nothing derived may be larger or denser than the words it came from" — is already violated by the file's own correct behaviour: `.pick` (source, 17/400) and `.peelField` (derived, 17/600) sit at the same size, and that is right, because one is a quotation and one is an editable field. This is taste asserted as law, with the strongest counter-evidence (34px `.darkSaid`, 17px `.pick`) unlooked-at.

refuted.problem: Four uppercase 11px/0.075em labels of three different structural ranks are rendered identically in one view: a card title (TURN THIS INTO A TASK), two field labels (THE WORDS YOU PICKED, THE TASK WORDING) and a sheet section header (WHAT HAS CROSSED INTO TASKS). Caps stop signalling rank once they answer every labelling problem, and the seam is the flow where rank matters most. In the same card 13px runs at three trackings and two leadings — .act and .picker at -0.156px, .peelBoundary at -0.13px, .peelWhy at -0.078px, at 1.45 and 1.55 — because `--tr-13` is never declared and three rules silently fall back to a literal `-0.01em`. The stated "one tracking curve, by size, declared once" is not true of the file. And .peelBoundary, the boundary promise that opens the peel, is the one paragraph in the product without `text-wrap: pretty`, so it breaks as "the exact words you / pick and check below".
refuted.why:
REFUTED. The observations are partly true but every operative part of the fix fails measurement, and two of its factual premises are wrong.

TRUE: --tr-13 is undeclared (master.css:95-97), three rules use var(--tr-13, -0.01em) (392, 597, 605), and line 93 claims every letter-spacing is a token. Seam does render four identical 11px/0.825px/600/ink-3 caps labels.

1) THE TRACKING HALF IS A NO-OP. Declaring --tr-13: -0.010em and replacing the three call sites changes zero rendered pixels; the fallback already resolves to exactly that. Measured trackings at 13px in seam: .act/.picker -0.156px, .peelBoundary -0.13px, .peelWhy -0.078px. The widest gap is 0.078px per character, ~4.7px over a 60-char line, ~0.026px between the two the fix actually touches. Sub-pixel per glyph. This is a comment that overclaims, not a design defect at 9.5.

2) .topMeta IS 12px, NOT 13px. Computed in all four rooms: 12px / -0.072px. The fix instructs "change .peelWhy and .topMeta from var(--tr-12) to var(--tr-13) so 13px has one tracking" — that puts a 12px element on a 13px tracking and breaks the exact "one curve, by size" rule the finding invokes.

3) text-wrap: pretty ON .peelBoundary IS DEMONSTRABLY INERT. Applied live and re-measured line rects via Range.getClientRects(): before [384,128], with pretty [384,128]. Identical. The fix does not fix the break it names. (balance yields [264,249], but balance was not proposed.) The break is also not a defect: 384/128 of a 403px measure is a 32% second line, not a runt.

4) "THE ONE PARAGRAPH WITHOUT text-wrap: pretty" IS FALSE. .stays ("Your note is still here, still private, still yours") wraps to two lines in the same card with no pretty. Multiple other prose runs likewise.

5) THE CAPS FIX CONTRADICTS ITSELF AND MAKES THE WORK WORSE. It leaves .indexHead ("WHAT HAS CROSSED INTO TASKS") untouched, so the seam still shows two caps labels, not "the only caps label in the seam" as claimed. And the proposed replacement register — 12px / 400 / --ink-3 / no caps — is already the file's register for quiet facts (.topMeta, .pickCount, .stays, .idxDayTail, .indexHead .cnt). Demoting a field label into it removes the one cue separating a label from the 15px ink-1 content directly beneath it, trading a rank collision among labels for a rank collision between label and fact. Caps census across all ten states also shows seam is not the densest: ?state=nothing renders five (4x .specName + .indexHead), unaddressed.

Residue worth one line, not a finding: .peelBoundary (lh 1.45) and .peelWhy (lh 1.55) are two 13px paragraphs in one card at two leadings.

refuted.problem: The product's whole promise is the three seconds between a thought and it being safe, and the moment ends badly. Ctrl+Enter empties the field, and the flying-words layer carries the sentence 670px down the sheet to row 10 of 15, at the very bottom edge of the visible index, under a heading called "The house" that has nothing to do with what was written. At the resting 1440x960 it is on the last visible line; at any longer pile it is below the fold and the animation flies the words off the bottom of the screen. The head count ticks 14→15 and the chip ticks 8→9, so the only reliable confirmation of capture is two numbers changing in the header — not the words themselves.
refuted.why:
Driven in Playwright at 1440x960 against notebook.html, the finding's two load-bearing claims are false and its fix would break a tested contract.

(1) "At any longer pile it is below the fold and the animation flies the words off the bottom of the screen." Measured the opposite. Eight successive Ctrl+Enter captures, pile growing 15 -> 22 rows: the arriving row's position is i=9 on the first keep, then i=4 (top:594, bottom:634) on every keep after, never clipped by #index, never off viewport, always ~250px clear of the dock. The reason is in the source I read: groupsOf() breaks ties between no-date groups with `bag.get(b).length - bag.get(a).length`, so as "The house" accumulates the new notes that group climbs the order. Growth makes the landing more visible, not less. The escalation the finding rests on does not exist.

(2) "The only reliable confirmation of capture is two numbers changing in the header." False on four counts, all measured: #say announces "Kept. 15 notes, 9 waiting on a decision."; the undo strip reads "Kept on the pile. / Undo Ctrl+Z"; the row carries data-arriving with a 620ms arrive animation; and the flying words land on a row that IS on screen — rowT 837.5, rowB 877.4, dock top 878, elementFromPoint at the landing point returns .idxRow, unobstructed. The words are the confirmation, and they are visible.

The one accurate observation — the first keep lands the row on the last line above the dock — is a one-off caused by initial group sizes and self-corrects on the very next capture.

(3) The fix would make it worse. `scrollIntoView({block:"center"})` after every keep moves the pile under the reader on every single capture. Place-keeping across repaint is an explicit contract here: paint() captures and restores #index.scrollTop by design, with the rule stated in the source comment ("Nothing here may cost the operator their place"), and notes-interaction-check.mjs asserts it at lines 93-121. Yanking the pile to centre on each keep is the opposite posture from Things or Bear, where capture never disturbs where you are reading. The pinned "Just now" duplicate row is worse still: it prints a row under a heading that contradicts the grouping the round-3 charge is being judged on.

Residual worth noting but not this finding: if the reader has scrolled the pile down first, the restored scrollTop leaves the arriving row ABOVE the visible index (measured rowT 43 against idxT 303) and the ghost flies up into the desk. That is real, narrow, and the exact inverse of what this finding describes, so it cannot be confirmed as written.

refuted.problem: Four notes-copy.ts strings are never rendered and have been replaced by strings this master wrote: voiceStop ("Stop listening" → "Stop and read it back"), emptyBody ("The capture field is ready above." → "Nobody else can read what you write here…"), privacyLong ("Yours until you send something on" → "Nobody else can read this"), and offline. The offline substitution is not a rewrite, it is a different product: notes-copy says "Reconnect and try again" (the person retries) and the card says "Notes will put it on the pile the moment you reconnect" (it happens by itself). One of those two sentences is a lie to a venue manager whose note is sitting on a phone in a field. Grep confirms copy.privacyLong, copy.emptyBody, copy.voiceStop and copy.offline each have zero call sites.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. The grep is right and the argument built on it is wrong; three of the four sub-claims are factually mistaken about which slot the notes-copy string belongs to, and the proposed fix would put two false sentences on screen.

1. OFFLINE — the headline claim, and it is wrong. `offline: "You are offline. Nothing has left Notes. Reconnect and try again."` lives in notes-copy.ts `errors` (notes-copy.ts:218), the hand-off error set, documented alongside `tasksUnavailable`, `replyLost`, `retryPending`, `sourceChanged`. It is the error for trying to SEND A NOTE TO TASKS while offline. notes-copy.ts has a separate `destination.offline` ("You are offline. Your note stays private here.") and no key at all for a note captured offline. notebook.js:1216 is not that fact: the card is headed "Held on this device", the desk above it reads "Written while the connection was down", and the state describes a note that was WRITTEN offline and is waiting to sync. Two different facts, not two grammars for one. There is no lie and no contradiction. Applying the fix would print "Nothing has left Notes. Reconnect and try again" on a card about a locally held note, i.e. it would tell the venue manager in the field to retry a Tasks send she never started, and would delete the one sentence that answers her actual question (does it sync by itself). The fix makes the product less honest, not more.

2. EMPTYBODY — the fix would state something false about the screen. I drove ?state=nothing at 1440x960: STATES.nothing replaces the top sheet's textarea entirely (notebook.js:1145-1155, no `topField`), so the rendered page is title, body, then two first-move buttons — there is no capture field above the body. On a phone capture is in the dock, below. Rendering "The capture field is ready above." verbatim would point at a field that is not there, and would trade two working first moves ("Write the first one", "Or say it") for a pointer, which is the standing checklist's own "empty states that repeat themselves instead of offering one first move".

3. PRIVACYLONG — no such key exists in notes-copy.ts. data.js invented the name for `capture.headerAssurance` ("Yours until you send something on"), a HEADER string. notebook.js:658 is the capture foot, whose notes-copy counterpart is `capture.privacyAssurance` ("Private until you send it on"). The finding is asking for a header string to be rendered in the capture slot, which is itself the placement change the fixture's own comment permits ("a direction may only decide where a string lives"). Also note data.js's `privacy: "Private to you"` is already not verbatim from notes-copy either, so the "verbatim fixture" premise the finding rests on does not hold at the source it cites.

4. VOICESTOP — the only sub-claim with force: "Stop listening" became "Stop and read it back" at :1024. It is a real deviation and it is two words. On a full-floor takeover the primary action naming its own consequence, where the next state is literally "What you said, once", is what Things and Linear do. The finding itself offers to withdraw it ("put 'and read it back' nowhere"), which is taste conceded as taste. Not a defect at 9.5.

5. THE GATE IS WRONG. data.js is a shared fixture read by render-a.js, render-b.js, render-c.js and notebook.js. I checked all four: none of them render voiceStop, emptyBody, privacyLong or offline. The fixture is a menu of the product's strings, not a manifest of one direction's screen. A gate that fails on any unused key would force copy into slots whose fact it does not state — exactly the three errors above — and would break the three sibling directions too.

refuted.problem: Every undo announces the past-tense sentence for the action it just reversed. Driven live: Ctrl+Z after a keep says "Undone. Kept on the pile."; after a send it says "Undone. Sent to Tasks." A person who is not looking at the screen hears the product confirm the exact thing they just cancelled. Reversibility is this product's safety claim and its announcement states the opposite of what happened.
refuted.why:
The quoted behaviour is accurate — I drove it and got `say="Undone. Kept on the pile."` after Ctrl+Z on a keep and `say="Undone. Kept in Notes."` after undoing K in the hand (notebook.js:144). But the reading of it is wrong and the proposed fix would make the product worse.

WRONG ABOUT THE BEHAVIOUR. "Reversibility ... its announcement states the opposite of what happened" mis-parses the sentence. The head of the utterance is "Undone."; the label is its object. A polite live region is spoken start to finish in order, so there is no moment at which "Kept on the pile" stands alone in the ear. Naming the reversed act is information, not contradiction: it identifies WHICH of several stacked acts came back, which is precisely what an eyes-off operator needs after the ten-second strip has timed out. This is the standard undo grammar shipped by every benchmark named in the brief and by the OS itself ("Undo Typing", "Undo Move"). It is not a defect that undo names its object.

THE FIX WOULD MAKE IT WORSE — three ways, all verifiable in the file:
1. "Put back." is ALREADY the verbatim announcement for closing an open note (notebook.js:468). Reusing it as the undo stem gives one sentence two meanings, breaking the "one noun for one fact" rule this programme just paid to establish.
2. "Nothing was kept." is ALREADY the verbatim announcement for discarding dictation (lines 1448, 1494, 1590, 1596). Saying it after undoing a keep is worse than ambiguous: I confirmed that undo restores the words live into the capture field (`field="Ring the florist about the arch"`, caret returned). Telling a venue owner "Nothing was kept" at the exact instant her words are sitting safe in the field reads as loss. That is the one failure this product cannot afford, and the fix introduces it.
3. "Tasks did not receive it." asserts a fact about another product's internal state that Notes cannot observe. The sealed one-way edge means Notes knows only that it did not send; claiming Tasks did not receive is an unverifiable outward promise.

ALREADY-CONSIDERED. The label string is shared deliberately between the pre-undo strip and the post-undo announcement, and the code comments at notebook.js:186 and :417 record that a previous round shipped the post-undo phrasing on the pre-undo strip and had to reverse it because it told the operator their note had gone back to the sheet while it was safely on the pile. The finding proposes re-splitting that seam with the strings that caused the earlier failure.

refuted.problem: Computed over every element in the resting 1440 view, indigo appears exactly twice: the wordmark dot and an 8% tint on whichever row the cursor is on. The one fact only this product has — that this note's words have already crossed a sealed one-way edge — is rendered in the same greyscale pill as "To decide" and "Kept". The accent is being spent on a browser state and withheld from the product's second promise, which is obeying three colours rather than spending them.
refuted.why:
REFUTED — the count is wrong, and the element it missed is the one that kills the argument. Computed over every element in the resting locked 1440 view, indigo appears three times, not twice: the rail mark dot (5x5 at 58,57), the cursor row's 8% tint, and — by far the largest indigo object on the page — a solid rgb(79,70,229) 1px ring around the entire 716x151 capture sheet (master.css:287, `.top:has(.topField:focus-visible)`), plainly visible in locked-notebook--1440x960.png. The accent is not "spent on a browser state"; it is spent on the product's first promise, drawn around the place a thought goes in three seconds. master.css:20 states that rule explicitly: "the one indigo — the live edge of whatever you are doing right now."

The pill claim is also wrong. "Kept" is not the same pill: it renders `data-quiet` (master.css:443) with no outline, ink-3, weight 400, and reads as unpilled in the frame. "In Tasks" and "To decide" share the outline, but pending rows carry the filled ink dot on their own mark (notebook.js:794, `.idxMark i`), which master.css:19 declares as the "waiting on you" signal and master.css:20 pairs with "in Tasks — an outlined chip, ink at full strength". Both states also differ in the accessible name (notebook.js:779). The selector cited, `.idxRow[aria-current]`, does not exist; it is `[data-cursor]`.

The crossing is already indigo, exactly where it is live: `.pick` on the picked words, `.pickBar` hairline, `.peelFrom` on the words printed above the wording they became, and `.readBody::selection` (master.css:587–625). Indigo means the crossing as it happens. The fix asks it to also mean a settled historical fact on every past row, which is the opposite reading of the same colour on the same screen.

The fix would make it worse twice over. At rest 3 of 14 rows carry "In Tasks", so three indigo pills would sit in the pile competing with the desk ring and the cursor; in the "What has crossed into Tasks" ledger every row is crossed and its tag is the lane name (notebook.js:781), so the proposed rule would not even reach the one surface the finding cares about. And taking the cursor row to "ink 4%" lands it on `--wash` (rgba(17,17,17,0.035)), which already carries both `.idxRow:hover` and `.idxRow[data-open]` — collapsing three distinct states onto one fill and regressing the gated single-tab-stop arrow walk so a keyboard cursor becomes indistinguishable from a hovered row.

refuted.problem: The desk column runs 130 to 846 (716px). The index rows directly beneath it run 120 to 1402 (1282px). That leaves 556px — 43% of the sheet — of permanently empty white to the right of every desk object, in every state and in all four finished rooms. The capture field, the opened note, the hand card and the peel all stop at the same ragged edge while the rows below go to the sheet wall. The two planes do not read as depth, they read as an unfinished right half with a full-bleed list under it. A discerning stranger looking at a 1440 screenshot sees a layout that ran out.
refuted.why:
The geometry is right and everything else about the finding is wrong. Measured at 1440x960: `.top` 130–846 (716px), `.paperStack` 130–1392, `.idxRow` 120–1402 (1282px). So the 556px band exists. But:

1. THE FIX RE-CREATES THE DEFECT ROUND 2 REMOVED, AND I PROVED IT. I applied the exact proposed fix in Playwright (`.top,.behind,.handTop,.handCard{max-width:980px}` + `margin-inline:auto` on `.paperStack`) and re-measured. `.top` becomes 980px (130–1110) — and the content does not move: `.topField` stays 154–681 (527px) and the 900-word `.readBody` in ?state=pressure stays 154–681. Every text-bearing rule on the desk is capped at `--measure` (31em) independently of the paper. So the fix does not remove 264px of white, it relocates it INSIDE the paper, framed by a border and a shadow, and drags "Put it back / Esc" 264px away from the column it belongs to while the foot rule spans 400px of nothing. Screenshot comparison at ?state=pressure is unambiguous: the current paper reads as a sheet on a desk, the "fixed" one reads as a mis-sized card with a paragraph in its left third. master.css line 269 names this exact failure as the thing that was fixed: "A 1262px card holding a 527px column is not a piece of paper on a desk, it is a big empty rectangle with a paragraph in the corner." The brief also lists "The desk paper is capped to its own content" as already landed. This finding proposes undoing a documented round-2 fix.

2. THE SECOND HALF OF THE FIX IS A NO-OP. `margin-inline: auto` on `.paperStack` changes nothing — `.paperStack` is already the full 1262px of the desk column; the paper is left-aligned inside it. Measured after applying it: `.top` still starts at l:130. The fix cannot "centre the desk over the index column" as written.

3. FACTUALLY WRONG ABOUT THE FRAMES. "The capture field, the opened note, the hand card and the peel all stop at the same ragged edge" is false. Measured right edges at 1440: capture field 681, paper 846, hand card 816 inside a 846 hand top, peel 884 — the peel deliberately juts 38px past the paper's right edge, which is the whole visual gesture of a second sheet peeled off the note. Four different edges, staged.

4. "43% OF THE SHEET" IS INFLATED. The band is 43% of the desk row's WIDTH, not of the sheet. In the resting state the desk is 187px tall inside a 924px sheet, so the empty region is ~556x187 = 8.5% of the sheet, and the head above it and the pile below it both run the full width. The reader's eye crosses one short band, not an unfinished right half.

5. IT IS ALSO NOT "PERMANENTLY EMPTY IN EVERY STATE". In ?state=seam the 373px-tall peel occupies that vertical zone and overhangs the paper; in ?state=review the desk carries the hand; in ?state=voice the floor is ink.

The genuinely open question the finding brushes past is the opposite one: at 1920 the index rows stretch to 1882px while the paper holds at 716, so it is the INDEX that has no measure of its own, not the paper that is too narrow. That is a different finding with a different fix, and it is not what was filed.

rounds.headline: Every seat rose, the spread closed to 0.4, and every seat answered the question that was put to them: the structural charge is answered, nothing holding this back is structural, and 9.5 is reachable inside the locked architecture and the three-colour lock. What is left, in the UI seat's words, is that the resting state is composed to about 8.5 and the transitional, secondary and phone states are composed to about 6 — the resting frame plus reflow, rather than every state designed as a frame.
rounds.body: Twenty-five findings confirmed, ten refuted. The desk became a two-column plane with the note's own facts in a margin beside the writing, and the peel opens into that margin. A phone can finally read a note and act on it. The index heading takes the step above the rows it heads. And one Ctrl+Z gives back a whole burst again: nothing is written to the DOM inside the input event, because Chromium ends the browser's typing history the moment the document is mutated during input.

wins.biggestWin: Make the desk a two-column plane and stop treating 45% of the top plane as margin. Right now the upper plane is 1000px wide doing 527px of work in every state, while the index directly beneath it is inked edge to edge — so the plane the architecture calls the desk optically recedes behind the plane it is meant to lift off. Put the note's own facts (kind, age, filing, word count, the In Tasks trail) in a 300px right column at x=937, and open the peel into that same column instead of floating it below the paper. That one change fixes four things at once: the void on the desk, the seam state's empty lower third, the peel's arbitrary left edge, and the density inversion between the two planes — and it gives the hand card somewhere to put meta so its height can be fixed and the review loop stops bobbing. On the standing charge: this is not an extremely well-made notes app with wedding words in it. The subject is load-bearing — filing by house and couple, still-to-decide as the unit of state, the sealed one-way seam, the ledger of what crossed — and that charge is answered. What is holding it below 9.5 is not concept and not the three-colour lock; it is that the resting state is composed to about 8.5 and the transitional, secondary and phone states are composed to about 6. Nothing in my five findings needs a colour, a weight or an architecture change. 9.5 is reachable inside the locks; it needs one composition pass that treats every state as a designed frame rather than the resting frame plus reflow.

Give the index its typographic spine back. The group rule and the first sentence of every row under it are currently identical type — 15px/600/#111 both, measured — so the surface a venue owner spends almost her whole session in has no rank at all, only indentation and a hairline, and the gate's `rule >= row` assertion lets it sit exactly on the floor. Raise `.idxDay` to `--t-17` with `--tr-18`, leave the row lede at 15/600, and change the gate to `>`. That one change lifts every frame at every width in every room, and it is the change that turns a list into an index. I do not think this direction is an extremely well-made notes app with wedding words in it — the lede-plus-tail row (600 first sentence, ink-3 continuation), the subject rules that carry what the house is facing, and the per-group \"1 still to decide\" are a genuine point of view about setting somebody's own sentences, and they are better than Bear's. But this is not yet a type system, it is an excellent eight-step ramp sitting on ladders that are declared in prose and enforced nowhere, which is why four of my five findings exist and why the hero moment ships at browser-default 16px/normal without a single gate noticing. 9.5 is reachable inside the lock — nothing above needs a fourth colour, a third weight, or a change to the architecture — but only if the ladders become assertions rather than comments. Fix the fly first (it is a proven bug, not a taste call), the index rank second, then close the gate holes so round 5 cannot re-open them.

The failure-mode charge does not land: the subject axis ordered by what the house is facing, the ledger that reprints only what crossed, and the honesty states are product ideas a generic notes app does not have, so this is not an extremely well-made notes app with wedding words in it. What is holding it below 9.5 is that the keyboard model stops at the happy path, and the single change that would move the score most is making the pick reachable and discoverable without a pointer: a roving sentence walker inside the note body (arrows move, Space picks, the same offerPick path downstream), with the primary control stating its precondition at rest — "Pick the words, then send" with a Space hint — instead of refusing after the press with an instruction only a mouse can obey. That one change turns the sealed edge from a mouse gesture into a model, removes the only place in the file where a labelled primary answers a person with something they cannot do, and teaches the gesture to a venue owner before they fail at it. None of my five findings need a colour, a weight or a change to the architecture, and none of them are structural: 9.5 is reachable inside the lock, and the honest distance is about a week of keyboard-and-repaint work, not a redirection.

Build the phone's read-and-decide surface. On desktop this is genuinely close to the bar — the subject axis, the grouping by what the house is facing, the seam ceremony, the empties and the not-yets are real design, not a notes app wearing wedding words, and the round-4 charge is answered there. On a phone it collapses to exactly that charge: a well-made list of wedding sentences you can add to and never act on, because .desk is display:none and nothing replaced it. A venue operator's phone is where the thought arrives and where the ten minutes between a ceremony and a dinner service actually is; a capture product that cannot read or decide on that device is missing a third of itself for its primary user. Nothing else on this list moves the score as far — fix the four smaller findings and it is an 8.4; ship the phone read/decide sheet with the same peel and this direction can reach 9.5 inside the locked architecture, which I believe it can.

Lock the vocabulary, then spend indigo on the edge. One editorial pass fixing findings 1 and 2 raises five surfaces at once, because the defect is not in any single string — it is that nobody owns the words. The state has five names, the verb \"keep\" has two opposite meanings, and the live announcements speak a sixth grammar nobody has ever proofread as a set ("Kept.", "Undone. Kept.", "Kept in Notes. 7 left.", "Open.", plus a 200-character legal sentence per keystroke). Print every rendered string and every accessible name and every announcement in one column, in the order a person meets them, and edit them as one document rather than as forty template literals. On the standing charge: this is not an extremely well-made notes app wearing wedding words. The subject grouping is genuinely what a venue is facing, the seam is a real product idea, and the honesty states are better than most shipped work — though six of the fourteen fixture notes are a software founder's notes (studio newsletter, teacher onboarding, student launch pricing, a cash-flow lecture) and two of the five headline groups exist only to hold them, so the pile a venue manager opens leads with a wedding and then a college assignment. Swap those for a venue's own standing work. And to answer the distance question plainly: 9.5 is reachable inside the locked architecture and the three-colour lock. Nothing holding this back is structural. What is holding it back is that the words were written surface by surface and the accent was never assigned a meaning.

Retime the arrival so the thought visibly travels and the row takes the words over on contact. Everything else here is craft debt; this is the only 1.5 seconds a stranger will carry away, and right now it is a fast blur followed by the same sentence printed on itself. On the standing charge, plainly: this is not an extremely well-made notes app with wedding words pasted on. The sealed edge is a real idea, well built and honestly stated once ("Your note stays here. Tasks only ever receives the exact words you pick"), the decision queue has a posture rather than a feature, and the offline and conflict states are the best-written English in the whole programme. What keeps it at 7.6 rather than 9.5 is not concept, it is that the product's own promises are kept everywhere except where they are most watched: the moment does not read, the keyboard walk chases a different list from the one on screen, and the sheet stops accepting a thought the moment you look something up. Fix those three and the remaining distance is small and cosmetic. One thing worth naming beyond my five: nothing on screen behaves differently because Mara and Finn are in two days. The heading says it, the product never acts on it, and that is the difference between a beautiful notebook for a venue and the notebook a venue could not work without.

It can reach 9.5 inside the locked architecture and the three-colour lock — not one of my five findings needs a colour, a weight, or a structural change, and the charge this direction was chosen to avoid does not stick: the subject axis ordered by what the house is facing, the group rule carrying "Saturday 18 July, in 2 days · 1 still to decide", and the sealed seam printing the picked words above the wording they became are venue ideas, not a generic notes app wearing wedding words. The distance is execution, not concept. (2) Stop the rule wrapping at 390 so height is not what the design depends on: lay .idxDay out as grid-template-columns: 1fr auto with the subject and the still-to-decide count on the first line and the date on a quiet second line inside the rule, matching the row treatment the phone already uses. Then add one gate assertion at 390, 768, 1024 and 1440: after scrolling the index, no idxDay box may extend below the top of any later idxDay that is stuck, and all idxDay heights must be equal.

confirmed.element: 390px · .desk { display:none } · tapping .idxRow · ?state=review at 390
confirmed.problem: On a phone the product is capture-only. Tapping a note row tints it and does nothing else: the desk is display:none, so a note can never be opened, read in full, or crossed into Tasks. ?state=review at 390 renders the index alone — no card, no question, no Send to Tasks / Just keep it / Decide later / Delete — and its head still reads "7 left" while eight are pending, because the card that is not drawn is not counted. The header chip is a button whose accessible name is "Go through the notes waiting on a decision"; on a phone it lands you on a list. The primary persona is a venue operator holding a phone on a Saturday, and for them the product is a list they can add to and never act on. The gate does not catch this: its entire 390 coverage is capture (.phoneField fill, one commit, no sideways scroll). "The desk stands down" is the locked architecture; reading ceasing to exist is not the same instruction.

In notebook.js tag the section it emits with what it is (`data-plane="write" | "read" | "hand"`), and in master.css change the ≤720 rule from `.desk { display: none }` to `.desk[data-plane="write"] { display: none }`. Give read and hand a phone home as a sheet over the index: `position: fixed; inset: 9px 9px 112px; z-index: 5` so the dock stays live and uncovered, carrying the source/time line, the full body, and a verb row pinned directly above the dock. In notebook state that row is Send to Tasks (full-width, ink, routing through the same startPeel), Just keep it, and the product's existing "Back to your notes" as the dismiss. In review it is Send to Tasks / Just keep it / Decide later / Delete with the pips under the title, fed by the same .handTop markup so there is no second implementation. Render the peel as a second, smaller sheet inset further from the top so the note's source line and first line stay visible behind it — the lock says the note is never covered, and a full-bleed peel would break that. Fix the number in one place rather than two: on the phone the review index head must carry the same count the chip promises (`${left} left`, including the card on screen), so "8 still to decide" and its destination state one fact. And do not `say("Open. …")` until the plane it refers to is actually painted. Add three gate assertions at 390 so this cannot regress: open a row and assert `.readBody` is visible; load ?state=review and assert all four `[data-act^="d-"]` controls are visible; assert the review head's number equals the notebook chip's number.
confirmed.done: A phone can read a note and act on it. Tapping a row opens a sheet over the pile carrying the whole note, what it is about as a control, picking, the peel, sending, a receipt and a way back — with the pile behind it inert. The product was capture-only on the device the thought actually arrives on.

confirmed.element: .handFoot [data-act="d-task"] and .peel [data-act="peel-send"], both visible at ?state=review after T
confirmed.problem: With the peel open, two black filled primary buttons reading "Send to Tasks" sit on screen 700px apart. The upper one — on the card, the one the person just pressed — is now a silent no-op: clicking it changes nothing, announces nothing, and leaves the peel exactly as it was. The lower one commits. Same word, same weight, same icon, two different consequences, and the one a stranger already trusts is the dead one with no feedback. The same duplication appears on the read desk. This is the single moment the whole product is sold on and it is the moment with the ambiguous button.

In STATES.review (notebook.js:~1075), while `peeling === note.id`, do not paint `.handFoot` at all — the same treatment readSheet already gives `.topFoot` at notebook.js:793-805 — so exactly one black primary exists on screen and it is the one that commits. This is safe for the keyboard model: Escape routes to cancelPeel, which clears `peeling` before paint and then refocuses '[data-act="d-task"]', so the button is back by the time focus is restored; and T cannot re-fire while the peel is open because focus sits in .peelField and the handler returns early on `typing`. Do NOT take the finding's first branch — opacity .35 + pointer-events:none + aria-hidden leaves Just keep it, Decide later, Delete and Back to your notes focusable inside an aria-hidden subtree, which is the standing checklist's own invisible-but-focusable defect. Separately, in the same code path, make decide("task") idempotent — only seed pickedWords/taskWording when `peeling !== note.id`, so re-entering the peel can never overwrite wording the person has already edited.
confirmed.done: While the peel is open the note's own action row stands down and says what is happening instead of offering a second identical primary that does nothing.

confirmed.element: .handBody and .peelLabel "THE WORDS YOU PICKED" on the T route, ?state=review
confirmed.problem: Pressing T in the hand auto-seeds the first sentence of the note, labels it "The words you picked", and announces "The words you picked: ...". Nobody picked anything. On this route .handBody is plain text with no mark, so the note above gives no visual account of which half crosses and which half stays — the selection route on the desk does mark it, so the two routes contradict each other on the one claim the product is sold on. In the note driven, the second sentence ("If not we lose the whole morning setup and the florist has to come back twice") is dropped silently, and the person is told they chose that.
confirmed.fix:
Three parts, in priority order.

1. Close the refusal gap first — it is the bigger defect. In `decide("task")` (notebook.js ~line 288), drop the `|| note.title` fallback and route through the same guard `startPeel` uses: with no pick available, say `N.copy.nothingSelected` and do not open the peel. That requires the hand to give a person a way to pick, which today it cannot — `pickedRange()` scopes the selection to `.readBody` and returns null anywhere else. Widen it to accept a range inside `.handBody` as well, and render `.pickBar` above `.handFoot` on the hand card the way `readSheet` renders it, so T on a card is either the confirmation of a real selection or a refusal, never an invention.

2. Mark the seeded range in place. The class is `.pick`, not `.mark` — reuse the exact `bodyHtml` construction from `readSheet` for `.handBody` when `peeling === note.id`, so the note above the peel shows which half crosses and which half stays. This is a substring replace on already-escaped text, identical to the existing code path, and inherits `.pick`'s existing indigo-wash so no new hue enters.

3. Do not author the label copy — the reviewer does not own it. State the constraint and let notes-copy.ts hold whichever string the founder picks: the label and the announcement must not assert an act the person did not perform. If step 1 lands, "The words you picked" becomes true on both routes and no new string is needed at all — which is the cheaper and better answer than adding a second noun for the same object. Only if the hand keeps a seeded-without-selection path does a second label become necessary, and then both strings live in notes-copy.ts.

Gate it in notes-interaction-check.mjs, in the hand block: after pressing T, assert `.hand .pick` count === 1; assert the marked text equals the `.peelFrom` value; and assert that T on a card with no selection and no pick opens no peel and announces `nothingSelected`. Also extend the existing four-state "a person's own words are set identically" check (line 971) to confirm the `.pick` span inside `.handBody` does not change the type ramp.
confirmed.done: The hand's peel opens empty and asks. It was auto-seeding the note's first sentence and labelling it the words you picked, on a route where nobody had picked anything.

confirmed.element: flyWords() ghost .fly (notebook.js ~245-270) and @keyframes arrive (master.css:323) — state=notebook, after Ctrl+Enter
confirmed.problem: Sampled every frame in a live browser: the ghost covers the whole distance from field to row in 138ms of a 460ms animation (top 108 -> 363 by t=138, left 285 -> 294) and then hangs motionless for another 320ms fading 0.84 -> 0, printed directly on top of a row that renders the identical words at full ink from frame one (@keyframes arrive only washes the row background, never its text). So 30% of the signature moment is travel and 70% is a stationary duplicate of the sentence dissolving over itself. The one thing a stranger would remember about this product reads as a smudge, not as a thought landing. The intention is written beautifully in the source comment and is not on the screen.
confirmed.fix:
Fix the ghost first, because that alone kills the double-print with zero risk. In flyWords: duration 400, easing "cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1)"; keyframes {transform: translate(0,0) scale(1), opacity: 1} / {opacity: 1, offset: 0.68} / {transform: translate(dx,dy) scale(s), opacity: 0}. Travel then occupies the whole duration and the ghost fades out across its last ~130px of motion, so there is never a frame where a static duplicate sits over the row. Also replace the dead scale term: s should be the type ratio, parseFloat(rowFontSize) / parseFloat(fieldFontSize) (15/16 here), not to.width / from.width, which clamps to 1 at every desktop width and is the reason the words never become the row's words. Keep transform-origin 0 0 and set the ghost's -webkit-line-clamp to 1 so a two-line ghost cannot land as a two-line stamp on a one-line row.

Do NOT ship the proposed ".idxRow[data-arriving] .idxText { animation: takeOver 120ms var(--curve) 290ms both }" as written. `arriving` is held for 620ms, and the input handler at notebook.js:1456 calls paint() the instant the draft crosses empty->live — the first character of the next thought, which is exactly the flow the caret-return exists to serve. The row remounts with data-arriving still set, takeOver restarts from its backwards fill, and the person's just-saved sentence blanks for 290ms after the ghost has already gone. Today that same remount only restarts a background wash.

If the hand-off is still wanted after the ghost fix, make it one-shot and repaint-proof by driving it from flyWords rather than from a selector that re-fires on every paint: pass the destination node in, and on the ghost animation's own timeline run row.animate([{opacity:0},{opacity:1}], {duration:120, delay:270, easing:"var-curve equivalent", fill:"backwards"}), cancelling it in the existing done() handler so a cut animation restores the text immediately. A WAAPI animation on the live node dies with the node and cannot be resurrected by a remount, which is the whole failure the [data-arriving] selector walks into. Leave the reduced-motion path untouched — `arriving` is never set there, so neither change reaches it.
confirmed.done: The travel is the moment, so the travel takes the time. It was covering the whole distance in 138ms of a 460ms animation and then hanging motionless for 320ms, which reads as a blur followed by the same sentence printed twice. The row also holds its breath until the words land on it.

confirmed.element: .idxRow arrow handling (notebook.js walk/cursor code) — state=notebook, focus a row and hold ArrowDown
confirmed.problem: Driven live: from the first row, ArrowDown walks rows 1, 2, 3, then jumps to the 5th row on screen ("Idea for the studio newsletter"), then the 6th, then back UP the page to the 4th ("Course reading for Thursday"), then to the 13th, 10th, 14th, 11th, 8th, 9th, 12th. Keep refocus = { kind: "row", id: cursorId } as is. Delete the `listed` variable and its assignment in indexOf once nothing reads it — a second ordering of the same list is what caused this. Add Home/End on the same rendered array while you are in the handler. Then harden the gate so it cannot pass a scrambled walk again: in notes-interaction-check.mjs, capture the aria-labels in document order, walk the whole index with ArrowDown collecting the active element's label at each step, and assert the two arrays are identical in order; repeat with ArrowUp from the last row against the reversed array, and run both under group=about, group=day, and with a search query active, since each of those paints a different order.

confirmed.element: .undo (master.css:525, position:absolute; bottom:70px) — visible on every keep
confirmed.problem: The "Kept. Undo Ctrl+Z" pill lands on top of the last visible index row and covers its words mid-sentence. Captured at 1440x960 sitting across "Follow up with the motion designer about the venue film ... sic choice before she can lock". It is a control painting over content, and it does it on the exact frame the product is proudest of, obscuring the pile it exists to report on for the full ten seconds it is on screen.

Put the room on the scroll container and make it unconditional: growing a scroller's floor only adds reachable emptiness below the last row, so it moves nothing, needs no flag, and has no expiry. .index { padding: 0 var(--gutter) 132px } (was 92px; the pill top sits 116px above the sheet foot, leaving the same >8px clearance the dock assertion demands); the tablet block 128/148px goes to 168px; the phone block goes from 22px to 142px (.undo bottom 88 + 46px height). Then widen the existing gate rather than bolting on a parallel one: in the ?state=pressure block, capture a note first so the strip is live, and assert clearance against every floating object in the sheet, Math.min(dock.top, undo.top) - last.bottom > 8, so the next thing that floats at the foot cannot silently re-open this.

confirmed.element: .idxText at 390 (computed overflow:hidden, text-overflow:clip, 44px box) and .idxDay at 390 (h3, flex, 71px tall)

At 390 the CSS has not solved it: the box clips with text-overflow:clip and no ellipsis, so phone rows simply stop — "drinks on the terrace if it", "Confirm the final", "If not", "Bring the worked" — while the same component on desktop trims on a word boundary and prints an ellipsis. One product, two grammars for the same trim, and the smaller screen is the one that looks like it lost the sentence. Beside it the group heading collapses to three ragged wrapped columns 71px tall ("Mara & / Finn", "Saturday 18 July, in 2 / days", "1 still to / decide"), which is the first thing on the phone screen.

Applying display:-webkit-box + -webkit-box-orient:vertical + -webkit-line-clamp:2 to .idxText with max-height:none collapsed the box from 87px to 43.5px and painted a real ellipsis ("drinks on the terrace if it…") beside an untouched row still reading "Confirm the final". No JS, therefore no added reflow on the capture path — the proposed loop would force roughly 10-40 synchronous layouts per row across up to 36 rows inside paint(), which runs on keep and on the empty/live crossing, against a product whose first promise is the three seconds between thought and ink. (2) Fix the stale comment at notebook.js:522-524 so the next reader is not told the CSS solved something it clips. (3) .idxDay at max-width:430 becomes display:block with the subject on line one and .idxDayNote plus .idxDayTail on one quiet second line, as the finding proposes — that drops 71px to about 44 and puts the heading in the same two-line grammar as the rows under it. (4) Add the missing assertion to the phone block of notes-interaction-check.mjs measuring scrollHeight against clientHeight, and asserting that any row whose shown text is shorter than data-full ends in the ellipsis — the existing scrollWidth check cannot see this failure.
confirmed.done: Same fix.

confirmed.element: notebook.js:1006-1030 STATES.pressure — the hard-coded `.top` block, its [data-act="peel"] and [data-act="close"]; ?state=pressure at 1440
confirmed.problem: The 900-word note on the pressure desk is not a note, it is a photograph, and its primary action breaks the product's second promise. `openId` is null in that state, so three things are true, all measured in Playwright. (1) `Put it back`, labelled with an `Esc` key hint, takes a click and answers with nothing — closeNote() returns at `if (!openId) return`, the live region stays empty, and Escape does nothing either. (2) `selectionchange` bails at `if (!openId || peeling) return`, so highlighting 70 characters inside the note raises no pick bar — on the one note in the fixture where picking one sentence out of nine hundred words is the entire job, picking is dead. (3) Pressing `Send to Tasks` calls startPeel(null), which falls through `work().find(n => n.id === id) || N.notes[13]` to a note that is not on screen; the live region then announces `The words you picked: Switch on before guests arrive, not when.` — words from a different note, that the person never picked — while `.peel` never renders, so a screen-reader user is told a crossing happened and a looker sees nothing change. The gate's dead-control sweep (notes-interaction-check.mjs:775-793) only runs on the resting notebook, which is why it never saw any of this.

Delete the hard-coded desk block and route the density state through the same reading machinery as every other note, with three details the original fix statement gets slightly wrong:

1. `N.long` is NOT a member of `N.dense` (ids d01–d36). So seed() must be `if (state === "pressure") return [N.long, ...N.dense];` — otherwise defaulting openId to the long note's id resolves to nothing and the fallback bug just moves. The head count string can stay `${counts().total} notes, peak season, an extension of the fixture`; it becomes 37 automatically and head/index agreement stays gated.

2. STATES.pressure becomes `notebook()` with openId initialised to `N.long.id` on first entry only (guard it the way STATES.seam guards `seamTouched`, so closing the note does not immediately re-open it). That restores Escape, `Put it back`, selectionchange, the pick bar, refile, `Send to Timeline`, and a correctly-seeded peel in one move.

3. Carry the long-measure over: `.readLong` currently exists only in the deleted block, so readSheet must add it when the body exceeds a word threshold (or when note.id === "long"), or the 900-word measure regresses to the short-note measure and the state stops testing what it exists to test.

Then move the dead-control sweep out of the single resting-state block: loop it over all ten states, and add one assertion that after pressing the primary peel control the announced picked words are a substring of the body actually on the desk — that assertion alone would have caught (3) and would catch any future state that seeds a peel from a note that is not on screen.
confirmed.done: The long note on that desk is a real open note, so its primary action reaches for the note on screen rather than whatever happened to be first in the list.

confirmed.element: master.css `.pickBar` / `.nudge` (position:absolute; left:24px; right:24px; bottom:12px) sitting on `.topFoot`; notebook.js:readSheet() `bodyHtml`

All four stay in the tab order — focusable, invisible, unclickable, the exact standing-checklist defect — and Escape becomes the only exit from a note whose exit is a labelled button. (b) At that same moment the note's own typography re-sets: readSheet swaps the `<span class="lede">` build for the marked-body build, so the 600-weight opening sentence of the person's own writing drops to 400 (measured: `.lede` present at 600 before the peel, absent after; the same in ?state=seam as shipped). The promise is that the note is never touched, and it visibly changes under their hand.

Keep the bar inside the paper and give it its own band instead of the footer's. In master.css, reserve the room on the reading sheet at rest so raising the bar is still an overlay and still causes no layout event: `.top:has(.topFoot) { padding-bottom: 62px; }` (or a `data-reading` variant of `.top` if `:has` is not wanted), with `.topFoot { position: absolute; left: 24px; right: 24px; bottom: 62px; margin-top: 0; }` — the footer keeps its hairline and its place, and the 50px band beneath it is empty white paper at rest. Leave `.pickBar` and `.nudge` exactly where they are (`bottom: 12px`), so they now land in that reserved band with clear air above the action row and nothing covered. Re-measure: `.pickBar` top must sit below `.topFoot` bottom, and elementFromPoint at the centre of each of the four controls must return that control. Add that to notes-interaction-check.mjs as four assertions taken while a selection is live, plus one that the bar's own button and the four footer controls are all hit-testable at once — the existing no-layout-shift assertion still passes because nothing moves on raise.

For the typography, build the body once in readSheet so a note is set identically peeled and unpeeled. Always emit the `<span class="lede">` run and the rest run, then insert the `.pick` span inside whichever run contains the picked range, splitting it across both runs when the pick straddles the sentence boundary — the picked words keep the weight of the run they came from rather than flattening the note to 400. In the same pass, handle the case the current branch silently drops: when `pickedWords` is not a verbatim substring of `note.body`, the note today renders with no mark at all while the peel claims those are the words that will cross. Normalise whitespace and match on the trimmed range before falling back, and if it still cannot be located, do not open the peel from words the note cannot show — the picking promise is that what crosses can be checked against where it came from, and an unmarked source is the one state where it cannot. Gate it: for both the seam state and a live peel, assert `.readBody .lede` is present at 600 and `.readBody .pick` is present and its text equals the words printed in `.peelFrom`.
confirmed.done: The pick control has a reserved slot beneath the writing, so it lands beside the words rather than on the row that acts on them, and raising it costs no layout.

confirmed.element: notebook.js:idxRow() `<button class="idxRow" type="button" role="listitem">`; locked in by notes-interaction-check.mjs:926

confirmed.element: `.idxDay` at 360-390px — the `@media (max-width: 720px)` block has no `.idxDay` rule; locked-notebook--390x844.png
confirmed.problem: The rule that heads each group, described in the source as the one line on this surface that could not belong to any other product, is a three-column flex row with no phone treatment at all. Measured at 390 and at 360, all three parts break onto a second line simultaneously: the couple's name splits across lines ("Mara &" / "Finn"), "Saturday 18 July, in 2 days" wraps at 160px, "1 still to decide" wraps at 79px. A single 22px line becomes a 71px block of three ragged competing columns. It resolves to one line only at 430 and above, so it is broken at every common iPhone width, including the width in the reviewed frame. In the same frame `.indexHead::after` collapses to a 14px stub floating after the "When" toggle (130px at 360) — a decorative hairline with no consistent length.
confirmed.fix: Real, but do NOT apply the proposed fix as written. I tested it: the proposed grid restack sits in the 720px block, so it applies at every width up to 720 and forces the rule from 49px to 70px at 414-720 (tablet portrait, where the line already fits with room to spare) while saving exactly 1px at 390 — a regression bought for nothing. It also fights the bare text node: the label is not wrapped in an element, so it lands as an anonymous grid item and cannot be styled or spanned. Use flex-wrap instead, which stacks only where the line actually runs out. In the same 720 block: `.idxDay { flex-wrap: wrap; column-gap: 10px; row-gap: 1px; white-space: nowrap; } .idxDayNote { flex: none; }` plus `.indexHead::after { display: none; }`. Measured across ?state=notebook and ?state=pressure at 320/360/375/390/414/430/600/720: the subject label stays one whole line at every width (1 client rect, no more "Mara &" / "Finn"), the date stays beside it, only "1 still to decide" drops to a quiet right-aligned second line and only below 414; 414-720 stays untouched at 49px; no horizontal overflow in `.index` at any width. `white-space: nowrap` is what keeps each fact whole, and it is worth adding a gate assertion that `.idxDay` first-child text resolves to one client rect at 320, 360 and 390 so this cannot silently regress the way it did.
confirmed.done: Same fix.

confirmed.element: notebook.js:paint() `mount.innerHTML = …` followed by trimRows()
confirmed.problem: Every act rebuilds the whole tree with innerHTML and then runs trimRows(), which writes innerHTML and reads scrollWidth inside a while loop — one forced synchronous layout per word removed, unconditionally rewriting every row's markup before it even checks whether the row overflows. Measured at 4x CPU throttle (a mid-range phone, or a laptop under load): one repaint costs 81-90ms at 14 notes and 224-287ms at 36 notes. moveCursor calls paint() per row, so at a season's density the arrow walk the product advertises runs at roughly 4fps; filing changes, note open, note close and the undo strip's own 10-second expiry all pay the same. It is also why scroll, caret, focus and the trim have to be hand-stitched back afterwards — and why `.readBody`'s own scroll, which is not in the restore list, is not preserved at all. Nothing at the Linear or Things bar rebuilds the document to move a selection.
confirmed.fix:
Three changes, with one correction to the fix as proposed.

(a) moveCursor must not repaint. Verified safe: cursorId reaches the DOM only via data-cursor (notebook.js:877) and tabindex (882), and CSS keys off it only through [data-cursor] selectors (master.css:468, 469, 476) — including the `+ .idxRow::before` sibling rule, which re-resolves on attribute change with no JS help. So: remove data-cursor and set tabindex="-1" on the outgoing row, set data-cursor and tabindex="0" on the incoming one, focus it, scrollIntoView({block:"nearest"}), call say(`${n} of ${total}. ${title}`), and return without touching paint(). This alone takes the arrow walk from ~47ms to sub-millisecond.

(b) CORRECTION to the proposed trimRows guard. "Check scrollWidth <= clientWidth against the already-rendered markup before writing anything" is wrong on the resize path. trimRows also runs on resize and fonts.ready (notebook.js:1814-1819), where the rendered markup is the PREVIOUS trimmed markup. After a widening resize that markup already fits, so the guard would skip the row and leave it permanently over-trimmed — content silently withheld, which is a worse defect than the one being fixed. The reset write is only redundant on the paint() path, where idxRow (line 885) has just emitted identical full markup. So make it explicit: trimRows(fresh). paint() calls trimRows(true) and skips the reset entirely; the resize and fonts.ready handlers call trimRows(false) and keep it. And restructure the reset as two passes rather than an interleave — write every row's reset first, then measure every row — so the whole reset costs 1 layout flush instead of N.

(c) Replace the word-by-word `while (words.pop())` with a binary search over word count (the fit predicate is monotone in word count, so this is exact, not approximate): ~log2(22) ≈ 5 layouts for a typical row instead of 22, and the same for the lede loop at 540-543 with its floor of four words preserved. Combined with (b), a full trim pass drops from ~364 layouts to roughly 40.

(d) Add .readBody scrollTop to the pair of values paint() captures and restores (notebook.js:1361-1363), keyed by the same open-note id so a restore never lands on a different note's body. Then extend notes-interaction-check.mjs: assert .readBody scroll survives a repaint at 1280x720 in pressure (the reachable case), and add a budget assertion — one cursor move performs zero innerHTML writes, and a full paint at 36 notes stays under a stated layout-read ceiling — so this cannot regress silently the way it did here.
confirmed.done: Typing no longer rebuilds anything at all, and the trim skips rows that wrap rather than measuring the wrong axis on them.

refuted.problem: The desk paper is 1000px wide with a 952px content box, and every piece of content ever placed on it is capped at --measure 527px. Measured: .top 261→1261, .topField and .readBody 285→812. That leaves 425px — 45% of the upper plane — permanently blank on the right, at all three widths, in every state. Directly beneath it the index row runs the full 1020 and is inked edge to edge: title at 294, preview to 1067, tag at 1080, time flush right at 1261. So the two locked planes have opposite densities. The plane the architecture says sits on top is half-drawn, the plane meant to sit beneath it is full, and the index optically out-weighs the desk — which is the exact failure the master.css comment at line 121 claims to have retired. It only moved the void from beside the paper to inside it. In pressure and seam this is unmissable: a 385px-tall column of prose hugging the left of a 952px sheet with an empty rectangle the size of a second note beside it.
refuted.why: REFUTED on measurement. Driven at 1280/1440/1920 in all seven states: the rightmost inked pixel inside .top is 1237 at 1440 — the paper's right padding edge — in notebook (.topMeta), capture (Keep it + count), readback (Keep both), pressure (Put it back Esc), nothing and not-yet. The index row's right edge is 1271, so the two planes land 34px apart (the paper's 24px padding plus the row's 10px inset). That is the shared edge the prior round bought, not "opposite densities", and the desk is not "half-drawn": .topFoot and .readSrc are both 952 wide and inked flush right, framing the measure-capped prose band above and below. Seam is the ONLY state where ink stops at 812, and there the plane is 120px tall. Two of the five elements cited are measured wrong: readback contains no .readBody at all (it renders .saidWas 285→914 and two .pieceField rows 303→801, with a right-hand cluster at 950→1237 carrying "2 notes, not one", Discard and Keep both in the same band), and .handBody is not on the 1000px paper — the hand is a 768px card (377→1145) whose action row runs 403→1119, so the "952px sheet with 425 blank" framing never applied to it. The fix would also make the work worse: a 300px kind/age/filing/word-count ladder is a task-tool properties rail bolted to a piece of paper, aimed at venue operators who need none of it — the exact "well-made kanban with wedding words" failure; docking .peel into it destroys the locked object (width:min(560px,100% - 72px) with a ::before tab arrow at x=30 pointing up at the note it tore from) and squeezes the task-wording field to roughly fourteen characters a line, immediately after a prior round fixed the peel for being too big; "removes 420px of dead sheet under it" is factually wrong since .peel sits outside .paperStack in .pile, over the ink floor, not the sheet; and a focus-only rule at x=937 declares an edge 125px past where the text actually wraps while adding an appearing element to the most protected moment in the product. Whitespace beside a held measure is the discipline --measure exists to enforce, and it is how iA Writer, Bear and Linear's issue body all set a person's own prose.

refuted.problem: One measure, four left edges. The same 527px column of a person's own writing is set at x=285 on the desk, x=294 in the index row, x=334 in the seam peel, x=403 in the review hand and x=433 in the review peel. So the sentence a person wrote slides 9px left the moment it is lifted from the index onto the desk — the exact transition the architecture is built on — and 118px right when the same note comes up in the hand. Round three gated that the words are set identically in size, leading and tracking; nothing gated where the column starts, and it starts in a different place in every room. This is the mathematically-aligned, optically-wrong class: each object is correctly centred or padded within itself, and no two of them share a reading spine.
refuted.why:
Numbers verified in Playwright at 1440 (locked): .readBody x=285, .idxText x=294, .peelField x=334 (seam) / 450 (review, measured after pressing T; the finding says 433, which is the .peel card edge, not the field), .handBody x=403.3. The measurements are right; the reading of them is wrong on every load-bearing point.

There IS one declared spine and the surfaces do share it. master.css line 127 defines --stack: min(100%, 1060px) with the comment "--stack is what the two planes agree on", and --gutter: 30px. Measured: .indexHead and .index are both x=231 w=1060; .index content edge = 231+30 = 261; .idxRow content edge = 251+10 = 261; the desk's .paperStack/.top = x=261 w=1000. The desk paper's left edge and the index row's left edge are the same pixel, 261, in every state. The claim "no two of them share a reading spine" is false — all five surfaces are derived from 261 by one documented rule each.

Each rule is consistent, not ad hoc. Desk paper: 261 + 24px paper padding = 285, and .topField, .readBody, .pickBar (left:24) and .nudge (left:24) all sit on it — the desk agrees with itself. Index row: 261 + 20px .idxMark + 13px gap = 294; that is an icon gutter, and the leftmost ink of the row (the mark) sits exactly on 261, i.e. on the paper edge. Text inset past a leading icon is the convention in every named benchmark — Things, Bear, Linear and Notion all set list-row text inboard of detail-body text. Nine pixels behind an icon that itself lands on the spine is not "optically wrong", it is the gutter.

The peel's two x values are one rule, not drift. Seam: peel 317, parent paper 261 → +56. Review: peel 433, parent handTop 377 → +56. Identical offset from the paper it peeled off, matching `.peel { margin: 9px 0 0 56px }` and the torn corner at left:30px. The peel is anchored to its parent because the locked architecture says it is a second piece of paper peeled off THAT note. Measuring it against a global spine measures the wrong thing.

The hand is centred in the same column, deliberately: hand 377 w=767 → centre 760.5; desk column 261 w=1000 → centre 761. A narrower focus deck centred in the plane it belongs to, with the fanned back-cards (410/399/388) peeking symmetrically — the frame shows this reads as one coherent floating object, not as a stray left edge.

The transition the finding is built on does not show the 9px. Lifting a row is openNote() → paint(), a plane change: the sentence moves ~440px vertically, goes 15px→17px at a different leading, and sheds its icon, tag and timestamp. Nine pixels of x is not perceptible inside that. In the one place the words genuinely travel — flyWords(), notebook.js:241 — the ghost interpolates field(285)→.idxText(294) with dx, dy and scale in one 460ms curve, so the delta is animated through, never a jump.

The proposed fix is also wrong in its own arithmetic and harmful in its other half. From the row content edge at 261, .idxMark at 24px plus a gap of 8 gives 293, not 285; reaching 285 needs mark+gap = 24 total, i.e. a 4px gap between a 15px glyph and the text, which cramps the icon. And left-anchoring .handCard and both .peel instances would de-centre the review deck and delete the 56px derivation indent that makes the peel read as hanging off the note — trading a consistent relational rule for a global one, at the cost of the architecture's own "peeled off the note" reading. Gating "the left edge of the person's own words is identical in notebook, readback, review, seam and pressure" would freeze that regression in place.

This is a real measurement with the wrong conclusion attached: mathematically different x, structurally one column.

refuted.problem: The takeover carries no <kbd> at all (measured: 0 kbd nodes in .dark), while every comparable primary in the product prints its chord — Ctrl+Enter on Keep, Esc on Put it back, T and K in the hand. So in the one flow a person uses without looking at the screen, standing in a room with their hands full, there is no key that keeps what they said. The only key the state binds is Escape, and Escape discards: it drops the transcript, says "Nothing was kept", and offers no undo (measured: .undo count 0 after it), which makes the single keyboard affordance in the flow the irreversible one. Cancel behaves the same by pointer. Every other destructive act in this file is reversible for ten seconds; the one that destroys spoken words is not.
refuted.why:
Driven, not read. Entering the takeover the real way (click the dock mic or the "Dictate" verb at ?state=notebook) sets refocus = {kind:"act", sel:'[data-act="voice-stop"]'} (notebook.js L1620), and I measured document.activeElement === the "Stop and read it back" button on entry. Pressing Enter from there lands on readback with the live region reading "Two notes came back from that."; Space does the same. So the central claim — "the only key the state binds is Escape", "there is no key that keeps what they said" — is factually false in behaviour. The finding counted kbd nodes in .dark and read the keydown switch, and missed that the state places focus on the primary, which is exactly how Linear, Stripe and Things arm a modal: primary focused, Enter commits, Escape leaves. The 0-kbd measurement is right and irrelevant; a printed legend is invisible to the person the finding describes (hands full, not looking), and the affordance that serves that person — focus on a control whose accessible name is "Stop and read it back" — is already there. Half the proposed fix ("bind Enter to voice-stop") is a no-op on code that already does it.

The other half makes the work worse. Escape in this file has one meaning across six branches: picker cancel, peel cancel, review to notebook, readback discard, voice discard, note close, search clear. Making Escape in voice mean "stop and read it back" would make Escape mean advance/commit in exactly one state, and would produce a two-Escape discard (Esc to readback, Esc to discard) that is strictly harder to hold than the current grammar. That is a regression against the checklist item this programme already paid for.

The undo residue is real but weakly grounded and its fix is worse. The finding's premise "every other destructive act in this file is reversible for ten seconds" does not survive checking: Escape from readback also discards spoken words with no undo (measured: undo count 0, live region "Discarded. Nothing was kept."), and Ctrl+Z is deliberately kept off a live capture draft (L1677 comment). offerUndo is used only where the notebook's data changed — kept (L197), refiled (L1521), sent (L446/455), dropped piece (L1569), kept-from-speech (L1659). Cancelling a recording changes nothing in the notebook, so an undo bar there would be the only one in the file offering to revert a transient UI state, and because that bar advertises Ctrl+Z, undo would silently re-arm a microphone. A keyboard shortcut that reopens a live mic takeover is a worse outcome than the thing being fixed.

refuted.problem: The hand advertises T, K and Esc and answers exactly those, so the two remaining decisions are mouse-only — including "Decide later", the most-reached-for act in any triage queue. Worse, the same keypair means two things on one screen: k decides the card, while j and the arrows walk the index below it. Measured, ArrowDown in the hand leaves the card at "1 of 8" and announces "2 of 7" from a different list. One screen states the same queue four ways: "1 of 8" on the card, "8 still to decide" in the deck note under it, "7 left" in the index head, and "2 of 7" in the ear. Two adjacent keys, two objects, three denominators, in the state that exists to be driven blind at speed.
refuted.why: Driven live at ?state=review, 1440x960. (1) The central claim is factually wrong: "Decide later" and "Delete" are not mouse-only. They are real buttons at tab stops #10 and #11 in the review state; tabbing to #10 and pressing Enter produced "Left for later. 7 left.", advanced .handOf from "1 of 8" to "2 of 9" and raised the undo strip. No advertised key is unimplemented — T, K and Esc all answer, and the gate proves it. The accurate residue is "no single-letter shortcut for two of four verbs", a shortcut-density preference, not a broken keyboard model. (2) The proposed fix breaks the file's one consistent navigation rule. Arrows walk the second plane in every state and that is gated (notes-interaction-check.mjs L133-155: single tab stop, arrow walk, 60-press clamp, Enter opens the walked row). In review the second plane is a live list of the remaining queue with focusable rows; returning before moveCursor would leave those rows Tab-reachable but arrow-dead, an inconsistency worse than the one reported. (3) "Up re-opens the last decided card through decided[]" duplicates a reversal model that already exists and is gated: every decision raises an undo strip and answers Ctrl+Z (verified: "Kept in Notes." -> "Undone. Kept in Notes.", .handOf and stack depth restored). Two grammars for undo on one screen is a regression. (4) The "three denominators" is not a contradiction: "1 of 8" is position in the run, "8 still to decide" is the queue including the card in hand, "Still to decide / 7 left" is the count of the rows that head actually heads (the same rule every list head in the file follows), and 1 + 7 = 8. The ear is not a bare "2 of 7" either — measured, it reads "2 of 7. Teacher onboarding, three things they kept asking for...", naming the note, so it cannot be mistaken for the card. Only the j/k mnemonic adjacency survives, and it is announced, reversible and small — not a 9.5-bar defect, and it arrives bundled with three claims that are wrong.

refuted.problem: The affordance is inverted. The read-only quotation "The words you picked" is painted as a tinted, bordered, rounded box — the shape of an input. The one editable control in the seam, the textarea that decides the exact words crossing the sealed edge, computes to border:0px none, background:transparent, 17px/600 — pixel-identical to a heading, and legible as a field only while it holds focus, which it loses the moment anyone touches the destination picker. Worse, the two boxes print the same sentence twice, differing by one trailing full stop, so a stranger reads the pair as a rendering bug rather than as provenance-then-editable and never discovers they can change what crosses.
refuted.why:
REFUTED on the source, on the driven behaviour, and on the fix.

WRONG ABOUT THE SOURCE. There is no `.peelPicked`. The element is `.peelFrom` (notebook.js:767, master.css:696). Two of the fix's prescriptions are already the shipped state: `.peelFrom span` is already `font-weight: 400` (inherited, measured 400), and `.peelField` already carries the global 2px indigo focus ring at 3px offset (master.css:172-173 — measured `outline: rgb(79,70,229) solid 2px`, offset 3px).

THE "SHAPE OF AN INPUT" PREMISE IS FALSE AS A SYSTEM READING. `.peelFrom` is not painted like a field; it is painted as the highlight, echoed. Measured, `.readBody .pick` = bg rgba(79,70,229,0.08), ring rgba(79,70,229,0.32) 1px, weight 400; `.peelFrom` = bg rgba(79,70,229,0.08), ring rgba(79,70,229,0.32) 1px inset, weight 400. Identical tokens, and the mark is on screen two inches above at the same moment. The washed rounded box under an 11px uppercase label is this product's read-only-echo pattern, used identically by `.saidWas` in readback (master.css:577-581) — the words that came back from speech, also read-only, also washed, also with a `b` caption. In this file a wash box means "these are words being quoted back to you". Nothing in the file uses a wash box for an input.

WRONG ABOUT THE BEHAVIOUR. I drove the real flow (open a note, select a range, "Use these words"): the peel opens with `document.activeElement === .peelField`, focus ring lit. "Legible as a field only while it holds focus" describes the one instant a person is not looking at anything else. The duplication charge also fails in the real flow — picked span, `.pick` mark and field value came back character-identical, not "differing by one trailing full stop". That artefact exists only in the `?state=seam` fixture, where the seed pick ends in a period and a task title correctly does not.

THE FIX WOULD MAKE IT WORSE, TWICE. (1) Collapsing the duplication until the person edits deletes the proof of the product's central promise at the exact moment it is made. The two blocks starting identical IS the promise — only the exact words you picked cross — and the boundary line directly above says so. A stranger who sees one field has taken the sealed edge on faith; a stranger who sees the quote and the wording agree has watched it work. It also reverses behaviour the brief lists as settled ("prints the picked words above the wording they became") and that the gate walks at notes-interaction-check.mjs:618-622. (2) A 1px border, white fill and 10px 12px padding would make `.peelField` the only bordered writing surface in the product: `.topField` (:330), `.pieceField` (:593), `.phoneField` (:1018) and `.peelField` (:726) all share `border: 0; outline: 0; background: none` — the paper is the field, which is the locked architecture.
