Then add an assertion to notes-interaction-check.mjs: after walking the index to its last row at 1440, 768 and 390, the focused row's bounding box must sit entirely above the dock's top.

refuted.problem: The desk resolves to a 1000px paper but only becomes two real columns in seam and pressure. In the four states without an aside, the writing column is 527px (285->812) and the remaining 449px is empty white, while .topFoot is stretched across the whole 1000px so that .topMeta ("Yours until you send something on") is parked at 1052->1237, 240px to the right of the longest line anyone will ever type, and in readback the primary "Keep both" sits 335px right of the last field. This is the exact defect master.css says it fixed ("a big empty rectangle with a paragraph in the corner") surviving in the resting frame, which is the frame this product is judged on. The paper reads as an empty box, not as a piece of paper with something on it.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. The numbers are mostly right and the reading of them is wrong, and one of the four named states does not contain the mechanism at all.

Measured live at 1440 (Playwright, ?v=locked): notebook .top 261–1261 (1000), .topField 285–812 (527), .topFoot 285–1237, .topMeta 1052–1237. So far the finding matches. But in ?state=nothing there is no .topFoot and no .topMeta (both measured null): the empty state is a headline at 285–1237, a body at 285–812 and two left-aligned first-move buttons ending at 848. The finding names it as one of the four states where "topFoot is stretched across the whole 1000px so that .topMeta is parked at 1052", and that is simply not what is in the DOM. Its fix is also inapplicable there — the margin is supposed to carry "the filing chip, the privacy line, and Dictate / Read a photo", and ?state=nothing has no filing chip, no verbs, and already prints the privacy line inside the 527 column. One quarter of the finding is fiction, and the fix has nothing to put in the column it wants to open. ?state=not-yet, for the same reason, puts .topMeta at 285–474, left-aligned.

The reading of the remaining numbers is wrong in a more important way. .topMeta at 1052–1237 is not "parked 240px right of the longest line"; it is right-aligned against the paper's right edge, and in ?state=capture the same slot carries the counter (1004–1065) and the "Save it" primary (1071–1237). Those right-anchored objects are the only thing currently holding the paper's right edge. The proposed fix explicitly shrinks .topFoot to the writing column, which deletes them from that edge — so it would manufacture the empty rectangle it claims to cure unless the new margin is well filled, and at rest the margin would hold nothing but chrome.

The master.css quotation is misapplied. The comment condemns "a 1262px card holding a 527px column" — a card 2.4x its only content. The resting card is 1000px, 153px tall, with four objects distributed across the full 1000 in its foot. The area the finding calls dead is the top-right of an empty two-line text field, i.e. the paper a person's own sentence grows into. Judging that as dead white proves too much: it condemns the resting capture surface of Bear, iA Writer, Things and Linear's create sheet equally. The capture frame confirms it optically — placeholder or two lines of ink top-left, verb cluster bottom-left, counter and primary bottom-right, balanced.

The fix would also make the work worse on the direction's own terms. The margin's stated rule in master.css is "everything that is true ABOUT the writing goes in a margin beside it"; before anything is written nothing is true about it, so a resting margin is a category error, and Dictate / Read a photo are capture entrances, not facts, which would give one region two grammars. Stacked (chip 34 + privacy 2 lines + two 34px verbs + gaps) the margin runs ~165px against a 55px field, so the resting desk's height would be set by its chrome column rather than by the writing — the exact "taller column plus an arbitrary remainder" failure the same CSS block records as already paid for. And --stack caps the paper at 1060, so the band does not grow with the window: at 1920 the paper is still 1000 and .topMeta still sits on its right edge (1292–1477).

refuted.problem: The two planes agree on a column (--stack) and on the paper's outer edge (261 = the index's mark column), but not on the axis the actual words sit on. The paper's 24px padding puts a person's writing at 285; the row's 20px mark plus 13px gap puts the same words at 294 once they land. So the signature moment of the whole direction — the words flying from the field into the row they became — ends with a 9px lateral snap, and lifting a note back onto the desk snaps it 9px the other way. It is small enough to read as sloppiness rather than as intent, which is the worst size for it to be.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. The measurement is right and everything built on it is wrong.

Measured (Playwright, ?v=locked, .top padding-left 24px): 1440 → .top 261, .topField 285, .readBody 285, .idxText 294. Same 9px at 1280 (181/205/214) and 1920 (501/525/534) and at 768 (110/134/143). So the 9px exists.

1. The behavioural argument is false. notebook.js flyWords() is handed `to = rowEl.querySelector(".idxText").getBoundingClientRect()` and animates `translate(dx…)` where `dx = to.left - from.left`. The words land ON the row's own text axis, exactly, because the destination is read live from that element. The 9px is not a snap at the end of the flight, it IS part of the flight — 9px of lateral travel inside a 520ms cubic-bezier over a ~300px vertical drop, invisible as a discrete event. The row is even held at opacity 0 until 470ms so the handoff is single-printed. The one real discontinuity is 2px, not 9: the ghost is placed at the field's box left (285) while the textarea's UA 2px padding put the glyphs at 287 — and the field is emptied in the same frame, so there is nothing left on screen to compare it against.

2. The second half is fiction. "Lifting a note back onto the desk snaps it 9px the other way" — openNote() sets openId and calls paint(). There is no shared-element travel on the lift at all, no ghost, no transform. Nothing moves laterally, so nothing can snap. A claim about a motion that does not exist.

3. The fix breaks two of the four finished rooms. .idxRow's column-gap is 13px in locked and studio but 11px in quiet and press, so the index's text axis is 294 in two rooms and 292 in the other two. A literal 33px paper padding aligns in locked/studio and misaligns by 2px in quiet/press — it trades one consistent, explicable 9px offset for a room-dependent 0/2px wobble, and hard-couples the paper's margin to the row's mark geometry so any future change to the mark silently de-aligns the desk. The proposed assertion is also wrong on its own terms: it tests computed left of .topField, which carries the textarea's 2px UA padding, so it would go green with the field's actual glyphs sitting 2px off .readBody and .idxText — false precision in exactly the state the finding calls the signature moment.

4. What is left is taste with no argument. Both planes already share --stack, and the paper's edge sits on the mark column (261 = 261). The desk's text is inset because paper has a margin; the row's text is inset because the row has a mark. Those are different reasons to inset, not a broken law, and the build has already chosen the stronger of the two available alignments. "Small enough to read as sloppiness" is an assertion, not evidence.

If a later round still wants the two text axes to coincide, it cannot be 33px: it would have to be derived (calc of the mark width plus the row's gap token) so it holds in all four rooms, and it would have to be asserted on glyph position, not on .topField's box.

refuted.problem: The group heading is separated from the sentences under it by two pixels and nothing else: same weight, same ink, same case, same family. On the phone even that goes — .idxDay steps to --t-15 while .idxText b is already 15/600, so "Mara & Finn" the heading and "…Mara & Finn." the lede 40px below it are typographically identical, and the same words appear three times in the top 330px in three roles at nearly one setting. Bear and Things both separate a list heading from a list item by category, never by a size step. The phone step-down also changes size without stepping tracking, so .idxDay carries --tr-18 (-0.021em) at 15px, off its own curve.
refuted.why:
REFUTED on the measured file, on three counts.

1) The central premise is factually false. "Separated by two pixels and nothing else: same weight, same ink, same case, same family" ignores everything the heading actually carries. Measured live at 1440 and at 390, .idxDay and only .idxDay carries: a sticky white band (position: sticky, top 0, z-index 2, background var(--white)); a 1px hairline rule at its foot (::after, rgba(17,17,17,0.055)); a 15px lead-out gradient below that rule (::before, white to transparent) so a row dissolves into it rather than being sliced; 20px of lead-in (16px on phone); an inline companion at 13px/ink-3 sentence case (.idxDayNote, measured 13px 600 rgba(.72) desktop, 12px phone); and a right-aligned 12px/400/ink-3 tail count. And the rows it heads are indented from it: heading left 261 vs lede left 294 desktop (33px), 25 vs 57 on the phone (32px). That is separation by category — band, rule, indent, companion metadata — which is precisely the Bear/Things pattern the finding cites as the standard being missed. It is already the standard being met.

2) The proposed fix reverts a fix a previous round already paid for, and lands worse than the pre-fix state. master.css carries the note in the file: "The subject rule … was set thirteen percent SMALLER than the rows beneath it, in the same weight and the same ink. It leads now." Setting .idxDay to --t-13/ink-3 puts the group heading two steps SMALLER and one ink level LIGHTER than the 15/600/ink-1 lede it heads — a stronger version of exactly the defect that was corrected. It also collides with .indexHead directly above it, which is already 11/600/--tr-cap/uppercase/ink-3: two uppercase micro-labels 30px apart differing by 2px is a worse register collision than the one alleged. And it uppercases user content — the group heading in the default "What it is about" mode is a couple's name, so the fix renders MARA & FINN on a wedding product whose copy rule is sentence case. It further breaks the heading's ink-density state model (.idxDay[data-soon] ink-1 / [data-undated] ink-2, measured rgb(17,17,17) vs rgba(.72)), which is how this surface says which date the house is facing without a second hue.

3) The supporting claims are overstated. Desktop: the three "Mara & Finn" occurrences in the top 330px measure at 15/600/ink-1 (head), 13/400/ink-2 (desk source line) and 17/600/ink-1 (heading) — three distinct settings, not "nearly one". The heading-to-lede gap is 62px, not 40. The tracking sub-claim is real but trivial and off no enforced curve: master.css already sets 15px at --tr-16 (.headNext b, .topField) and at --tr-14 (.idxText), so there is no 1:1 size-to-tracking mapping in the file, the measured gate accepts any declared step, and the delta at 15px is 0.135px per character.

Underneath it, the request that "600/ink-1 mean one thing in the plane" cannot be met under the locked constraint of two weights only: with 400 and 600 the only registers available, 600 must serve both the earned lede and the group heading, and the file separates them by size, band, rule, indent and companion instead. The one grain worth naming — on the phone the head's "Mara & Finn" (.headNext b, 15/600/ink-1) and the group heading are identical type 70px apart — is a different element the proposed fix does not touch, and they sit in different planes across an uppercase "YOUR NOTES" head and the group control.

refuted.problem: "Yours until you send something on" is printed while the sheet is empty and removed the moment there is something private on it. In its place appears "16 / 4000" — a limit stated from the sixteenth character, machine-facing, of no use to a person writing a thought. On the phone it degrades to a bare "40" floating in the dock with no unit and no context. The product's second promise is shown only when it has nothing to promise about, and the pixel it is traded for is engineering furniture.
refuted.why: The central claim is factually wrong. The privacy promise is not evicted: notebook.js:898 renders a permanent head control in every state and at every width, visible text "Private to you" with accessible name "Private to you. Yours until you send something on." I confirmed it live at 1440 in idle, in the live/count state, and past 4000 characters, and at 390 on the phone (visible at 202,18); both the locked-notebook and locked-capture frames show it top-right, ~25px above the foot slot in dispute. What the count replaces is a second, longer printing of a promise that never leaves the sheet, shown at idle where it does first-contact reassurance before the first word and retired once the row is needed for the act. The proposed fix is also worse on two counts: (1) it makes the doubling permanent, stating one fact in two grammars in the same right-hand column 25px apart, which is a named item on the standing checklist; (2) it does not fit. Measured .topFoot in the live state, the spacer slack is 175px at 1440 and 1180 but 77px at 1080, while a nowrap .topMeta carrying "Yours until you send something on" measures 185px, so a permanent fixed right-hand slot alongside the count and "Save it Ctrl+Enter" overflows the foot at the gated 1080 fold width. On the phone, .dockCount is aria-hidden="true", so "no unit and no context" never reaches assistive tech; it is a decorative 11px tint beside the field being typed into.

refuted.problem: The same string is printed twice inside one viewport, 380 pixels apart, in the same words and the same order, and both are inert text. Nothing tells a stranger that one is what the house is facing and the other is a pile of notes; nothing connects them. Two days before the wedding the notebook states the wedding in its largest type and offers no way to act on it — the venue owner cannot ask the product the only question she has, which is "show me Saturday".
refuted.why:
REFUTED. Driven live at 1440 (?state=notebook&v=locked) and at ?state=pressure, plus master.css and notebook.js read. The only true part is the bare duplication; every claim the finding builds on it is wrong, and the fix would break a gated assertion and delete the better of the two instances.

1. The hierarchy claim is inverted. Measured: `.headNext b` = 15px/600, `.headNext span` = 13px/400 at y=38. `.idxDay` = 17px/600 at y=305 (gap is 267 CSS px, not 380). The notebook's largest type is 17px — the wordmark and the INDEX group rule. So "the notebook states the wedding in its largest type and offers no way to act on it" is describing the index heading, which is the thing the finding proposes to DELETE, while the instance it proposes to convert into a filter is the smaller, quieter one. The finding wants to keep the 15px echo in the chrome band and drop the 17px rule that also carries the group's own pending count ("1 still to decide", "3" under pressure). That is keeping the weaker copy.

2. "Nothing tells a stranger that one is what the house is facing and the other is a pile of notes; nothing connects them" is false against the rendered DOM. The index instance sits directly under a labelled band — `.indexHead` prints "Your notes · 14 notes" followed by the lit `groupBtn` "What it is about" (aria-pressed=true) beside "When". That band states, in the product's own words, that the rules below are subject groups of the pile. The head instance sits in the chrome row with the wordmark, the workspace name "The Orchard, events", the chip and "Private to you". Two visibly different registers, each framed.

3. "The venue owner cannot ask the product 'show me Saturday'" is false in effect. The default grouping is `group = "about"`, and `groupsOf()` sorts by stake then days, so the couple's notes are already gathered, first in the pile, under one rule carrying their own count. That is the answer to "show me Saturday", delivered with no mode to enter and no mode to leave, and it is why the rules exist (data.js:56-75). Toggling "When" removes the duplicate entirely (verified: index heads become Today/Yesterday/Monday/Sunday/Saturday) — so the "collision" is a consequence of a first-class visible control the product ships, not an unanswered question. The proposed filter adds a third scope mechanism alongside grouping and search.

4. The fix breaks the gate and gets its own number wrong. "Scopes the chip to '3 still to decide about Mara & Finn'": in ?state=notebook the couple-scoped pending count is 1, not 3 (3 is the pressure fixture). More seriously, notes-interaction-check.mjs round 6 asserts "the head does not print the chip's phrase beside the chip" (`!lede.includes("still to decide")`) and "the chip names its own scope … across the whole notebook". Re-scoping the chip to the couple reinstates the exact two-counts-in-one-line stutter round 6 paid to remove, and fails a standing assertion.

5. Residue, for the record, narrower than the finding: "Mara & Finn / Saturday 18 July, in 2 days" does render verbatim twice at rest, and by construction always will while grouping is "about" (N.next is hardcoded to the one stake-1 subject, which always sorts first). If a seat wants to act on it, the edit is on the head — drop or shorten the head's date clause when the first group rule is already printing it — not a new filter mode, and never on the index rule that carries the count. As stated, the finding is a misread of the hierarchy attached to a fix that is a net loss.

refuted.problem: The standing privacy line in the head reads "Private to you". That string does not exist in notes-copy.ts. The product's own word is privacyAssurance: "Private until you send it on" — conditional, because the product is a one-way edge into Tasks and the promise is only true until you use it. The lab replaced the conditional with an absolute and then printed the honest version thirteen hundred pixels away on the desk foot ("Yours until you send something on"), so the same screen carries the promise in two grammars, and the louder, lock-badged one is the one that overclaims. data.js's own header says these strings are "Verbatim from notes-copy.ts… No direction may rewrite them"; four have in fact been rewritten (privacyAssurance, wordingLabel → "What the task will say", destinationLabel → "To", voice.stop → "Stop and read it back"). Three of those four are improvements. This one is a regression on the single sentence the venue offer legally rests on.
refuted.why: REFUTED on the source, on measurement, and as a restatement. 1. "Private to you" is not a lab invention. It is the SHIPPED header string, verbatim: src/modules/notes/app/workspace/NotesWorkspace.tsx:909 renders `Private to you` in the same header slot, with the same lock glyph and the same sibling "Notes options" button as the lab's `.headAct[data-act="privacy"]`. The lab mirrors the product's own header 1:1. It is absent from notes-copy.ts because notes-copy.ts governs the capture and hand-off flow, not the header badge — grep confirms `capture.privacyAssurance` and `capture.headerAssurance` have zero call sites in NotesWorkspace.tsx. The proposed fix would make the lab DIVERGE from the shipped product on the one string the finding says the offer legally rests on. 2. The conditional promise is ALREADY in the accessible name the finding asks for it to be added to. Driven live at 1440x960 in Playwright across ?state=notebook, seam and voice, the chip's aria-label reads, in all three: "Private to you. Yours until you send something on." The finding proposes an aria-label carrying the conditional clause. It is already there, word for word, in the second half. 3. The "thirteen hundred pixels away" measurement is false by an order of magnitude. Measured getBoundingClientRect().top: head chip 32, `.topMeta` "Yours until you send something on" 199. That is 167px, same fold, badge directly above its own expansion — a title and its subclause, not two grammars at opposite ends of a screen. And that foot line IS the product's own conditional, rendered verbatim (notes-copy.ts:172 headerAssurance), so the honest sentence is on screen, adjacent, not exiled. 4. The proposed swap puts a string in the wrong slot. notes-copy.ts documents `capture.privacyAssurance` ("Private until you send it on") as the standing line next to the CAPTURE label, and `capture.headerAssurance` as the header string. The fix asks for the capture string in the header slot while the header string is already rendered in the capture foot — i.e. it would swap two correctly-placed strings into each other's wrong slots. 5. Three of the four "rewritten" keys are factually wrong about data.js, which the finding names as the culprit. data.js:327/335/336 read `voiceStop: "Stop listening"`, `destinationLabel: "Which project"`, `wordingLabel: "The task wording"` — all three verbatim from the generic register. Those were fixed in an earlier round. (The seam does render "What the task will say" and "To", and voice renders "Stop and read it back", from notebook.js at render time — but "What the task will say" is itself verbatim from notes-copy.ts's WEDDING register at :272, and the fixture's own comment permits a direction to decide where a string lives. The finding's account of the mechanism and of the file is wrong regardless.) 6. It is a restatement three times over. log.html:670, :1332 and :1997 each refuse this exact premise against the same NotesWorkspace header citation, and :1332 already refuted a near-identical "every rendered string must equal a copy-module value" gate on the ground that data.js is a shared fixture read by render-a/b/c and notebook.js, so such a gate would force strings into slots whose fact they do not state. The brief's own settled list also carries "No privacy claim stronger than the product's own conditional promise, anywhere" — this finding restates it. The fix would make the work worse: it deletes a string the shipped product uses, moves two correctly-slotted strings into each other's slots, and adds a gate three of whose four premises are false.

refuted.problem: The strongest mark the three-colour lock permits is solid ink at full density, and it is spent on a chore counter. "8 still to decide" is a black pill and it is the loudest object on a white sheet whose entire promise is the three seconds between a thought and safety. It outranks the venue's name, the wedding two days out, and the words the person is actually writing, and it stays lit through the dictation return and through the middle of the seam, where the person is deciding what crosses. The product's own reassurance in the hand — "Nothing is decided until you say so" — is set in ink-3 at 13px; the nag is set in white on full ink. The ink is being obeyed, not spent.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. Driven live at 1440x960 across all ten states, plus master.css:265-275 and notebook.js:886-900.

1. The finding's central proof is a juxtaposition that never renders. It contrasts "the nag set in white on full ink" against "the product's own reassurance in the hand — 'Nothing is decided until you say so' — set in ink-3 at 13px." That sentence is `.deckNote`, and it exists ONLY in the review room. notebook.js:888 reads `state === "review" ? "" : ...` — the chip is already suppressed in exactly the room where the hand and that sentence live. Measured: `?state=review` returns chip `null`. The two objects the finding puts side by side are never on screen together.

2. "It stays lit through the dictation return" is wrong at the takeover. In `?state=voice` the head is covered by `.darkBody` (elementFromPoint at the chip's centre returns `darkBody/DIV`) and `.sheet` carries `inert`. The chip is neither lit nor reachable while she is dictating. It is present in readback, but readback is the sheet, not the takeover — she is back in the notebook.

3. Half the proposed fix is already the build. "Reserve full-ink fill for the one control that commits the person's words" is precisely what `.act[data-ink]` already is, and the only thing it is: Save it, Keep both, Write the first one, Open that one, Delete (inverted to white-on-ink in the destroy room, master.css:964). Every ink fill in the product other than the chip is a commit primary. The finding proposes as a correction the rule the file already obeys.

4. "The loudest object on a white sheet" does not survive measurement at the moment that matters. Mid-thought (`?state=capture`) the Save it primary is 5961px² at 13px against the chip's 2842px² at 12px — more than twice the area, on the paper, at the eye's centre, while the chip is a 26px pill at the top edge of a 62px head. In readback the ink primary is 4123px² against the same 2842px². In the resting notebook the chip is the only fill, but it is 2842px² of a 1440x960 composition whose index carries sixteen rows of bold 15px ink-1 — it is the smallest text in the head, last in its reading order, not first.

5. "It outranks the venue's name and the wedding two days out" misreads a deliberate two-channel head. The head is ordered by importance left to right: wordmark, house (`The Orchard, events`, ink-2/400 by design — it is the label, not the news), then the wedding as the lead fact at 15px/600 ink-1 with its date, then the count. The chip emphasises by fill; the wedding emphasises by size, weight and position. Reading order gives the wedding the lead, and the chip is the last thing before the chrome.

6. The demotion would make the work worse. `chip[data-off]` already exists as exactly the register the finding asks for — no fill, ink-2, hairline inset, weight 400. Moving the live count into it collapses the one route into the decision queue to the same register as the `.headAct` chrome (Private to you, options) and the same drawn treatment as the sixteen "To decide" row markers below it. The only object in the notebook that says something is outstanding would become indistinguishable from a settings button. That is a legible hierarchy traded for an even one.

What is left is a taste position — that fill should mean act, not count — argued with a composite screenshot nobody sees, against a rule already implemented, with a fix that flattens the head. Not a defect at the 9.5 bar.

refuted.problem: The one gesture that makes this Notes and not Bear — a second, smaller piece of paper peeling off the note — is explicitly deleted on the primary surface. In the review hand the peel is real: it has its own edge, its own shadow, and a notch pointing back at the card it came from, and it is the best moment in the build. On the desk, where almost everyone will meet the seam, the same component is stripped of shadow, notch and padding and becomes a flat right-hand column separated by a hairline. It reads as a share sidebar, not as paper. The comment in the stylesheet states the reason outright: "so the sheet's lower third is not left empty." The product traded its signature idea for a layout convenience. The whole file also carries only two @keyframes — `arrive` and `recPulse` — so nothing about paper lifting, peeling or crossing is ever played anywhere; the metaphor is asserted in copy and drawn only once, in the room fewest people open.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. Three of the finding's load-bearing claims are false against the source, and the proposed fix visibly degrades the surface when applied.

1. "Drawn only once, in the room fewest people open" is wrong. master.css:664 is `.phoneSheetBody .peel { width:100%; margin:12px 0 0 }` and :665 kills only the notch — it does NOT reset box-shadow or padding. On the phone, where the couples in this product's audience meet the seam, the peel keeps `border-radius: var(--r-paper)`, `box-shadow: var(--ring), var(--paper)` and `padding: 15px 17px 16px` from :880-883. So the signature gesture is drawn as real paper in the hand AND on the phone; the two-column desk is the only place it folds into the margin.

2. "Only two @keyframes, so nothing about paper lifting, peeling or crossing is ever played anywhere" mistakes an implementation technique for an absence. Paper motion in this build runs on transitions, not keyframes: :378 `.top { transition: box-shadow/transform/opacity var(--dur-settle) }` with :379 `.top[data-settling] { transform: translateY(14px) scale(0.972); opacity: 0 }` — the sheet physically leaves for the pile; :763 `.handTop[data-settling] { transform: translateY(-14px) scale(0.985); opacity: 0 }` — the card lifts off the hand; :750-752 the `.handCard[data-n]` stack transforms. Counting `@keyframes` blocks is not counting motion.

3. The stylesheet comment is quoted selectively. :885-886 reads "Inside the desk's own margin, so the note and the task it is becoming are side by side AND the sheet's lower third is not left empty." The first clause is the architectural reason and it matches :309-312 ("everything that is true ABOUT the writing goes in a margin beside it, which is also where the peel opens"). The finding drops that clause and presents the second as "the reason ... stated outright", then calls a considered composition a "layout convenience".

The measured geometry also contradicts "flat right-hand column" as a size complaint: at 1440 ?state=seam the desk peel is 392px wide against a 496px writing column — already the smaller of the two, inside the note's own paper, and never covering it.

Most decisively, I applied the proposed fix live at 1440 (width: calc(100% - 10px); margin: 0 0 0 10px; ring + paper shadow; r-paper; notch at left:-7px top:34px) and screenshotted before/after. It is worse: (a) the peel becomes a floating white card nested inside the desk's white card, growing 259px to 290px tall and running to within ~10px of the sheet's right and bottom edges, so the sheet's own margin is broken and the panel reads as a popover, not as paper peeled off; (b) `.deskAside` still carries `box-shadow: inset 1px 0 0 var(--line-soft)` (:329), which the fix does not remove, so the column rule is left orphaned 30px to the left of the new card — a doubled frame; (c) the notch, whose shadow is `-1px -1px 0 var(--line)` (lit on top and left, drawn for a downward-pointing tab), at left:-7px lights the wrong two edges and points into an empty 34px gutter rather than at the picked sentence, which sits on line two at the far left of the note.

The added `peel` keyframe is also a hazard, not a gain: startPeel sets `refocus = { kind: "field", sel: ".peelField" }` (notebook.js), so the panel takes the caret on open. Translating a container 10px on the X axis while a textarea inside it receives focus is a scroll-anchor and caret-placement risk on the one surface whose whole job is to let a person check the exact words before they cross.

What is left after the false claims are removed is a bare taste preference — "the widest desk should render the peel as a detached sheet" — with no argument that survives the pixels, against an architecture line the current build already honours ("the note is never covered") and a two-column desk composition the file argues for explicitly.

refuted.problem: At 36 notes the index is a uniform wall. Every row is the same height, the same weight structure and the same tint; a group can hold nine rows spanning 23 minutes to 12 hours with no rule, no thinning, no fold, nothing to navigate by but scrolling. A working venue owner will pass 36 notes in a fortnight and 300 in a season, and this plane has exactly one answer for that: search. That is the point at which the product stops being a notebook that knows its owner and becomes a list. It is also the state where the whole architecture of desk-and-index has to pay off, and it does not — the index below 36 rows feels no different from the index below 5.
refuted.why: Factually wrong about the source, and the fix is inert at the state it targets. (1) All 36 pressure notes have n.day === "Today" — verified by driving ?state=pressure&group=day, which yields ONE group headed "Today". The proposed "hairline day rule whenever n.day changes between consecutive rows" would draw zero rules at pressure. (2) The day axis is not missing: groupControl() (notebook.js:1267) paints a segmented "What it is about" / "When" toggle in the index head, visible in locked-pressure--1440x960.png, announced live, and scroll-preserving (scrollTop 600 held across the repaint). (3) "No rule" is false: master.css:554 .idxRow + .idxRow::before draws a 1px var(--line-soft) hairline between every consecutive pair, and each group head is a sticky var(--t-17)/600 rule a full step above the 15px rows with its own ::after hairline and a 15px lead-out gradient. (4) "Drop the rest text to var(--ink-3)" is already shipped: .idxText span { color: var(--ink-3) } (master.css:582), measured rgba(17,17,17,0.62) on every row. (5) "Same weight structure" is false: 6 of 13 rows in "The studio" are lede-less, one weight end to end; heads vary by data-soon (--ink-1, 600 note) vs data-undated (--ink-2) and carry the facing date plus an "N still to decide" tail; rows carry source glyph, pending dot, tag and time columns. (6) The fold would make it worse: only one group exceeds 12 rows (13), so it hides exactly one row and prints "1 older" — a second count in a plane whose count discipline is gated (head/index agreement, one object owns each count), and it contradicts the locked architecture's "everything older, one line each", which every 40px row already satisfies. What remains is the unargued taste claim that the register does not change between 14 and 36 rows, contradicted by the file's two grouping axes, stake ordering, per-group facing dates and decide-counts, tags, search and the arrow walk.

refuted.problem: The product has two orderings of one pile and the deciding surface uses the weaker one. The index knows the house's clock — it sorts Mara & Finn to the top because stake is 1 and the date is two days out — and the head prints "Saturday 18 July, in 2 days". The hand, which is where the decisions actually get made, deals oldest-first with no reference to stake or days: card 1 is the Saturday ballroom question, card 2 is a no-date idea for the studio newsletter, and the two remaining Saturday decisions sit behind it. So the one fact that makes this Notes-for-a-venue rather than Notes is displayed everywhere and operative nowhere in the room built to act on it. This is precisely the "well-made notes app that happens to contain wedding words" reading, and it is one comparator wide.
refuted.why: Factually wrong about the fixture on two counts, and its central charge is disproved by the artifact. (1) The hand does not deal "oldest-first" — it deals NEWEST-first: driven at ?state=review, cards 1-5 read 3 hours ago, 5 hours ago, 6 hours ago, 9 hours ago, Yesterday. Direction reversed. (2) "the two remaining Saturday decisions sit behind it" is false: n01 and n02 are `sent: true` (already in Tasks, not pending, not in queue()). Exactly ONE Mara & Finn note is pending, and it is card 1 — "Ask the venue whether the ballroom can be accessed from 8am on the Saturday" (about: mara-finn, stake 1, days 2). So the deciding surface already opens on the highest-stake, nearest-dated note; the claim that the venue's clock is "operative nowhere in the room built to act on it" is contradicted by the first card the room deals. Applying the proposed comparator to the shipped fixture moves exactly one card — n06 (the course, stake 2, days 0) from position 4 to position 2 — and leaves card 1 identical. The fix would also make it worse where it bites: stake outranks days in groupsOf, so as a deal order it hands the person a Mara & Finn item two days out ahead of a course deadline due TODAY; that comparator was written to order groups ("the house's business first"), not to rank individual cards against each other. The label half duplicates a fact already printed in the head ("Mara & Finn / Saturday 18 July, in 2 days", verified in the DOM) directly above a sentence that itself says "the Saturday" — the standing "same fact in two grammars" defect — and answers a "why did this come first" question the current order does not raise, since the answer is "it is the newest" and the card already prints "3 hours ago". Newest-first is the same clock as the locked desk ("the newest piece of paper") and the reverse-chronological index rows; re-sorting only the hand would put it on a different clock from both planes.

refuted.problem: Dictation takes the whole floor to ink, marks the sheet and the rail `inert`, and tells a non-looking user none of it. The container is a generic with a label, not a dialog: no role, no aria-modal, so nothing announces that a modal opened. Focus on entry is on BODY, so the way out is an untargeted Tab away and the microphone is live with the keyboard nowhere. The LISTENING state and the 0:07 elapsed timer exist only as painted text. The disclosure — the part that is legally required — is printed at the foot and never spoken. This is the third product-specific item on the checklist: a voice flow that cannot be trusted without looking at the screen.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. The finding's load-bearing evidence was measured on the wrong entry path, two of its three fixes are already shipped or actively harmful, and one of them would break a gated assertion a previous round deliberately established.

1) "document.activeElement is BODY on entry" — measured on the lab deep-link `?state=voice`, not the product path. Driven live: entering via the verb (`.verb[data-act="voice"]`) puts `activeElement` on `BUTTON|voice-stop|darkAct`. notebook.js:2041 already does exactly what the fix proposes: `refocus = { kind: "act", sel: '[data-act="voice-stop"]' }`. Worse, the proposed selector is `'[data-act="stop"]'`, which matches nothing in the file — applying the fix as written would delete the working focus placement and produce the very BODY-focus bug it claims to fix.

2) "the way out is an untargeted Tab away and the microphone is live with the keyboard nowhere" — false. notebook.js:2245 collects the takeover's stops and notes-interaction-check.mjs:740-762 already gates a full round-trip trap: focus lands on voice-stop, six Tabs never leave `.dark`, Shift+Tab stays inside, Escape exits with "Nothing was kept." Restating that is restating the measured baseline.

3) "tells a non-looking user none of it" — false on three counts. `say("Listening. Speak whenever you are ready. Stop when you are done.")` fires into the polite `sr` region on entry (verified live: sr text present via click, gated at check line 304). The sheet and rail get `inert` (notebook.js:1804), which removes the background from the accessibility tree outright — a stronger guarantee than `aria-modal`, which is advisory only. And the container is `<section aria-label="Dictating">`, which maps to a named region, not the "plain div"/"generic" the finding describes.

4) The `.darkSaid` change is the part that would make the work worse. `role="status"` is `aria-live="polite"` — polite regions queue and wait for a pause; they cannot "interrupt the speaker continuously". Turning it to `aria-live="off"` is the single change that would actually create the checklist defect the finding invokes: a voice flow that cannot be trusted without looking, because the words the engine heard would no longer be read back. It also directly violates the gated assertion "the words arrive as a live region, not as decoration" (notes-interaction-check.mjs:311-314), a decision an earlier round paid for.

What survives is thin: the disclosure is not folded into the entry announcement, and `.dark` lacks the `role="dialog" aria-modal="true"` that the sibling `.phoneSheet` (notebook.js:1320) carries. That is a semantic tidy-up, not "a voice flow that cannot be trusted without looking" — and it is not worth a finding at a 9.5 bar when the surrounding claim is wrong about the entry path, wrong about the tab trap, wrong about the announcement, proposes a selector that does not exist, and would regress the transcript live region.

rounds.headline: The bar arrives and the scores fall: five seats find one defect, and the desk stops ending a note on the word and
rounds.body:
Read the numbers before the work: the floor went from 8.2 to 6.4 and the spread from 0.2 to 2.2. That is the bar arriving, not the work regressing. Rounds 1 to 7 held Notes against Things, Bear and iA Writer alongside Linear, Stripe and Vercel; this round held it against Linear, Stripe, Vercel, xAI/Grok and SpaceX, the same five the two sibling surfaces use, and the seats were told to cost the work against those five even if it cost points. It did. Nothing regressed between round 7 and round 8; the same artifact was graded against a harder question and answered it less well.

What the harder question found is one defect, and five of the seven seats found it independently without knowing the others existed. The desk clamped a long note to less room than a short one, cut four lines out of the middle of a person's own writing with no fade, no scrollbar and no count, stopped the visible text mid-sentence on the word and, and then held three lines of blank paper below the lie. It did this in the pressure room, the room that exists to prove long notes survive. From the fourth arrow press onward the keyboard picked sentences that were off screen, so the product's second promise — only the exact words you pick ever cross — was operable blind, with a live Send to Tasks above words nobody could see. UI costed it seven tenths, Typography six, Interaction nine, Taste named it the contradiction of your words are safe here staged in the frame built to prove it.

It is closed. There is one window for every note the desk lifts, sized from the room the desk actually has rather than a fraction of the screen, so the index keeps a named floor and the 150-word debrief now renders whole at 1440 and 1920. Where a screen is genuinely too short the clip says so: a fade that is set only when something is truly hidden and cleared at the end of the scroll, a line that counts what is still below the reader, and the same fact in the accessible name. The picked sentence is scrolled onto the screen before it is announced, and the reading plane's scroll now survives a repaint like the index's always has.

Around it, twenty more findings closed. The card grows when it is refused instead of throwing its buttons onto the grey over the line promising every decision can be put back. Dictation, the one room where a person is not looking at the screen, has the product's own commit chord, keycaps on both its verbs, and a voice that says it is still listening every fifteen seconds. The hand keeps the keyboard while it holds the floor, so one arrow press stops producing two counts of one queue in two grammars. The index answers Home, End and both page keys, and a chord reaches it from the caret. Reading a note lands on the note instead of on the way out of it. The ledger's lane column carries a lane again rather than a project name. The invented verb crossed, which notes-copy.ts never says, is gone from every visible string and every accessible name. The legally required disclosure was the smallest type in the room set as the longest line in it, and now has the product's own measure. And two of the fourteen demo notes had been a software founder's backlog inside a venue product; they are the venue's own.

Both gates grew, and both grew because a seat proved they were blind. The audit gained a measure rule, which immediately found the loading sentence running seventy-seven ems, and a coarse-pointer pass driven with a real touch pointer at three phone widths — the first time that branch has been measured rather than assumed, which immediately found the search field 31px tall on a phone. The behaviour gate went from 425 assertions to 457, including three that replace round-6 and round-7 assertions this round proved were inverted. Both exit zero.

wins.biggestWin:
Make the desk's paper sized by what is on it rather than by the list beneath it. One move — fold the read-mode margin under the note using the `@media (max-width: 1080px)` rule that already exists in the file, then hand the ~150px of freed vertical to `.readLong` and give whatever still overflows a measured bottom fade — closes both the 340px void beside a person's own words and the note that stops mid-sentence on "and". Those are the two most expensive composition defects in the master and they share one cause.

What stands between this artifact and 9.5 is mechanical, not structural, and I will size it. The architecture is right and the resting frame proves the bar is reachable: at 1440 the two planes genuinely read as two planes, the paper shares its left and right edges with the index sections beneath it, the index's fixed metadata columns hold the right-hand verticals dead still, and the dock has a real 132px reserved band so it never eats a row. That is Linear-grade. What fails is the states nobody screenshots for the deck: the foot of the lower plane, read mode, search, and the 721-900px band. Sized: fold the read margin and re-cap `.readLong` with a measured fade, 4-6h including re-shooting pressure and seam; make the dock scrim conditional and `--ground` coloured and give the index a designed foot, 3-4h; anchor the peel and its tail to the picked range with a clamp, 4-6h including the resize and fonts.ready re-runs; collapse the dock's field under `[data-searching]` and freeze the dock's width, 2-3h; fix the head's truncation order at 721-900 so the date and the venue name outrank "Private to you", 2h; re-shoot all ten states and re-run both gates, 2h. Seventeen to twenty-three hours — three focused days for one person. Not one of those needs a new idea.

One thing I will not say of this: it is not an extremely well-made notes app with wedding words in it. The seam, the ledger of what has crossed, "8 still to decide" as a pressable head, and the date register that the whole index groups by are this product's own ideas, and a generic notes app would not have any of them.

Fix the desk's clamp: let .readBody grow into the 78px of blank paper already sitting beneath it, and where it still overflows, add a fade measured after layout plus a "11 of 15 lines shown" line at the cut. Right now the surface tells a reader that a note ends on the word "and" while holding three lines of empty paper below the lie, and that is the one defect here that destroys a person's own content rather than merely mis-setting it. What stands between this and a 9.5 is mechanical, and I will size it: two to three days. Half a day for the clamp, the measured fade and its re-measure on resize and fonts.ready; two hours to fold .peelSent and .peelFrom span into the shared writing rule and settle on one weight for a person's words on the seam; one hour for the two measures (.darkNote off 62ch onto --measure, .specWhy and .emptyTitle given one at all); half a day for the tracking reconciliation plus the notes-audit.mjs assertion that a rule's --t-N and --tr-M tokens must agree, which is the part that keeps it fixed; half a day for the index's two-tone grammar and reseeding data.js so the frames show the index a real capture produces. Everything else in this type layer is genuinely at the bar — one eight-step ramp actually honoured, five declared leadings, an em-based measure landing at 66.6 characters on the writing surfaces, word-safe trims, tabular numerals scoped to columns only, uppercase micro-labels with text-indent compensation. What polish will not close, and I name it rather than size it: at rest this product sets none of a person's writing at reading size. Fourteen notes are fourteen truncated 15px lines and the desk holds an empty field, so the resting frame reads as a capture tool with a list, not as a writing surface — which is the locked architecture, not a defect, and it is the reason this will always be graded a step below iA Writer or Bear on the one thing those two are for. Within the architecture, it is not "a well-made notes app with wedding words": the desk/index density split and the measure work are specific to this job. But the wedding is carried entirely by the copy. The type does nothing a venue owner would recognise as their register.

Make the reading plane grow into the sheet it already owns and make the pick keyboard scroll: replace the 31vh clamp with a measured floor and ceiling, call scrollIntoView on the picked sentence before announcing it, and paint a measured overflow fade. That single change removes the only defect in this file that touches the product's second promise — right now, from the fourth sentence on, a person can pick words for Tasks, be told "Send to Tasks will use exactly these", and never see them.

What stands between this and a 9.5, for this seat, is 2 to 3 days and it is all mechanical: roughly 4 hours for the reading plane and the pick scroll, 3 for the voice keys and a repeating listening announcement, 5 to bind the arrows to the hand and derive its two counts from one accessor, 1 for Home/End/PageUp/PageDown in the rover, 1 for the readback row, and half a day re-driving every state and extending notes-interaction-check.mjs to assert scrollTop moves with the pick, that Ctrl+Enter keeps in voice, and that no key produces two counts of one queue. There is no structural distance. The foundations that are hard to buy are already here and correct: capture is genuinely zero actions from intent to ink (the caret is in the field at rest and blind typing lands), the undo strip states its own 30 seconds and Ctrl+Z honours it, the subject head narrows both planes and puts "All 14 notes" on screen as the way back, Escape restores the exact index cursor, and the dock band is reserved in real layout on both the phone and the desktop. And the charge that this is a well-made notes app wearing wedding words does not hold: a still-to-decide queue, a subject that is a wedding date, and a sealed seam with a ledger of what crossed are venue mechanics, not generic ones. The gap is the second layer of interaction, not the idea.

Fix the long-note edge: make the desk's clipped paper declare what it is hiding — a measured fade only when it overflows, no dead white space beneath the cut, the rail's LENGTH fact naming how many words are below the fold, and one 'Read the rest' line. It is the only place in the product where a person is shown something untrue about her own words, and it lands on the pressure state, at both desktop widths, on the same screen that asks her to pick which words cross. Everything else on my list is smaller than it. What stands between this and a 9.5, from this seat: nothing structural. I looked for it. The two planes read as two planes, the seam is genuinely sealed and genuinely reversible (send updates the ledger 3→4, the head 8→7, adds IN TASKS AS to the fact rail, says 'Your note stayed here', and offers thirty seconds back), the voice floor is properly modal with the sheet inert and Escape returning 'Nothing was kept', the empties each offer one first move, and the wedding is in the information architecture rather than sprinkled on the strings — this is not a well-made notes app with wedding words in it. What remains is mechanical: the overflow work above is roughly half a day including re-measuring on fonts.ready and resize and adding the zero-silent-clip assertion; the lane string, the focus target, and the hint copy are under two hours together; the head-count scope wording is an hour. The one piece that is design rather than patching is the phone read view, where a thirty-word note leaves about 480px — 57 per cent of the sheet — blank and silently drops the three facts the desktop desk carries (How it arrived, What it is about, Length); reflowing those into the void as a footer rail is a day on its own. Call it two to three days of work, plus a gate run and a re-shoot.

Retire the invented verb. Pull every user-visible string, live announcement and accessible name that says "cross" or "crossed" back onto the vocabulary notes-copy.ts already owns, and fix the wedding-register label leaking into a venue surface at the same time. This is the highest-value single change because the sealed one-way edge is the product's second promise, and right now it is told in three competing grammars on three screens — "yours until you send something on" in the header, "nothing has left Notes yet" in the empty, "what has crossed into Tasks" in the ledger — with the ledger using the founder's architecture word rather than a word Orla would say. Fix that and the boundary story becomes one sentence the product repeats, which is what makes a promise legible.

To be plain about the sibling accusation: this is not an extremely well-made notes app that happens to contain wedding words. The head that names Mara & Finn, dates the Saturday, counts the days and narrows both planes when pressed is a venue-shaped object, not decoration, and "still to decide" is a better triage word for a venue manager than any inbox metaphor. The residual domain-thinness is in the fixture project name "The Orchard, events", which reads like taxonomy an engineer invented rather than a name a person typed.

What stands between this and a 9.5 from my seat is mechanical, and I will size it: two days. Half a day for one writer to pass every string in notebook.js against notes-copy.ts and fix the five findings above; half a day of implementation and re-shooting the eleven frames. But there is one structural thing behind that number and it is worth naming rather than sizing away. notes-copy.ts covers capture, voice and hand-off only. Every string this master invented — the index, the head, the hand, the ledger, all ten empties, all five honesty states, every one of the forty-odd live announcements — has no home in the shipped copy module and therefore no banned-word test, no register test, and no gate. That is why "crossed" and a wedding label could get in at round eight and why the round-seven claim that "the words got a gate as strict as the pixels" is not true of most of the words on screen. Add one day of engineering to extend notes-copy.ts to the surfaces this master invented and run notes-copy.test.ts over them, and the drift stops re-opening every round. Three days total.

Build the landing. Make the words you just typed physically travel from the desk into the index — the same text, shrinking to one line over ~260ms — and put the 'Saved. Undo' reassurance inline on the row that arrived instead of on a pill 700px away at the dock. Right now the most important three seconds in the product are expressed as a textarea going blank, and that single absence is why nothing here is memorable. What stands between this artifact and 9.5 is two different distances, and only one of them is work you can schedule. The mechanical half — the long-note guillotine, the review foot escaping its card, the disclosure that cannot be heard, the grid that does not breathe, the orphaned Put it back — is roughly three days of one engineer with the designer alongside, and it takes this to about 7.5. The other half is structural and I will not size it: this product has exactly one original idea, the sealed one-way edge where only the words you pick ever cross, and that idea is currently a popover with a caret and a text input. Everything else on the surface — compose box, grouped one-line index, grey previews, state pills, relative timestamps — is a very well-made notes app wearing the Linear house style, and the wedding is carried by the strings and one head control rather than by the structure. Until the seam is the thing a stranger remembers about this product the way the command menu is the thing you remember about Linear, polish cannot close the gap. That is a re-authoring problem with the founder, not a backlog.

Make the phone a measured surface rather than an assumed one: rewrite the @media (pointer: coarse) block as a 44x44 union-target rule covering the merged dock's suite tiles, the account disc, the index head's grouping control, the undo strip's button and the read sheet's filing chip, and then run notes-audit.mjs's target pass with hasTouch:true at 360/390/430 against a 44px floor so that branch can never rot again. Right now a whole responsive branch — the one the locked architecture singles out, on the device where a thought actually arrives — is invisible to both gates, and every control in it is undersized.

The remaining distance to 9.5 is not structural. The architecture is real, not decorative: two planes with a ground of their own, a peel that is a second sheet, a merged dock, a keyboard model that is advertised and implemented and reversible, place-keeping that survives every repaint I could throw at it. What is missing is one unmeasured branch, one unspoken flow, one sticky element undoing last round's fix, and a fixture that belongs to a different business. I size it at five days: one day for the coarse-pointer targets and their gate; one day to give the dictation floor a spoken model (live clock at intervals, transcript into the existing #say region, destructive tab stop moved last, the disclosure onto --measure); half a day to put the day rule on the plane's own ground at the rows' width; one day to rewrite the three off-world notes and add the vocabulary assertion to the copy gate; one day to close the compositional holes I measured but did not spend findings on — the readback's 392x290px void beside the two transcript pieces, the desk margin running 422px against a 496px writing column at every width above 1080, and the 159-615px of empty ground under the seam, review and search planes; half a day for the resting cursor mark and aria-current. None of that requires a new idea, only the same discipline already spent on the ten static states spent on the interactive and touch ones.

confirmed.element: .readBody.readLong in ?state=pressure and ?state=seam (master.css:485-495)
confirmed.problem: The state built to prove a long note survives is the state where it does not. At 1440x960 `.readLong` is `max-height:31vh; overflow:auto` = 298px against a 413px body, so 28% of the note is hidden. There is no measured fade, no visible scrollbar in the shipped frame, and no count of what is not shown. The words stop mid-sentence on the word "and" ("...label the supplier crate for the extraordinarily long North Coast Botanical Installations and") and then 130px of EMPTY paper runs to the divider. The blank space actively reads as "this is the end, there was room to spare". A venue owner reading back her own post-event debrief is shown a note that appears to terminate in a conjunction. This is the guillotine class the library already paid for, on the one state that exists to catch it.
confirmed.fix:
Scope to ?state=pressure and any `.readBody.readLong` — ?state=seam is unaffected and should be struck from the finding.

1. Measure, then decorate. On every desk repaint, after layout (and on fonts.ready and resize, matching the existing trim discipline), compute `scrollHeight - clientHeight` on `.readBody`. Only when it is positive, set `data-more` and a `--hidden` custom property. Gate the fade on that attribute: `.readBody[data-more] { mask-image: linear-gradient(to bottom, #000 calc(100% - 56px), transparent) }`, mirrored at the top once scrollTop > 0. Never an always-on decoration — a fade must mean something is actually hidden.

2. Delete the air at its real source, not at readBody. `.readBody` is completely full; the 78px of blank paper is the empty `.pickSlot` (54px) plus its gaps. Collapse `.pickSlot` to zero when it holds nothing, or give it its band only once a pick exists. Do not touch `.readLong`'s max-height and do not hardcode 413px.

3. Scroll the pick into view. Arrow-picking currently lands the marked sentence below the fold at scrollTop 0. After each arrow move, scrollIntoView({block:"nearest"}) on the `.pick` span. This is the library's "focus that leaves the screen" and it is the same edge.

4. Put the truth in the accessible name, not in rewritten copy. Leave "LENGTH 150 words" alone. Extend the existing sr-only channel on the note's group label so that when data-more is set it reads "...more of this note is below, scroll or press Page Down" — the fact exists in words without inventing a new aside grammar or touching notes-copy.ts.

5. Assert it. Add one line to notes-interaction-check.mjs: at ?state=pressure and at 1280 as well as 1440, `.readBody` either does not overflow or carries data-more. That is the property that stops this recurring.
confirmed.done: round 8

Two search entries on one screen, one of them holding "marquee" and the other claiming nothing has been searched. Beneath that, the found set is stranded: one 39px result row sits at the top of 735px of ground, so 62% of the sheet is unassigned, and the no-hit variant is worse — a heading, a line and two buttons occupying the top 27% with 800px of empty ground below and nothing to close it. Separately, the dock is the product's one constant object and it does not hold still: it measures 413px wide at rest and 464px in ?state=pressure and in review-after-T, where it grows a fifth compartment, so the eye has to re-find it between screens.

Replace it in place with the dock's own 36px search glyph carrying the current state (`data-ink` or `aria-current="true"`, accessible name "Search, open") so the dock still says which mode it is in and its remaining compartments — voice, photo, avatar — keep their order. Drop the two riders: no optical-third re-centring of the found set (it would move rows under the reader on every keystroke and the proposed clamp cannot be written in CSS), and no visibility:hidden reservation for the fifth compartment (it appears only when the way back to writing genuinely exists; reserving it leaves a dead 51px gap and a dead rule in the resting dock). confirmed.element: .readBody / .readLong on the desk, ?state=pressure at 1440x960
confirmed.problem: The 150-word note is clamped to max-height:31vh. Measured live: clientHeight 298px, scrollHeight 413px, so 115px (4.2 lines at lh-read) of the person's own writing is hidden. There is no fade, no visible scrollbar and no cue of any kind; the last rendered line ends on the word "and", and directly beneath the clamp sits 78px of blank white paper before .topFoot's rule. The composition positively asserts that the note ends mid-sentence: four lines are cut away while nearly three lines of empty paper are held below them. The one fact that would contradict it, "LENGTH 150 words", is parked 500px away in the right rail. This is the product's primary content and the exact guillotine class the paid-for library names.

Keep the second half of the proposed fix; drop the first half as written and replace it. "flex:1; min-height:0 on the writing column" is underspecified against this DOM: master.css:487 records that the desk is capped to its content and that the 31vh exists because a long note once squeezed the index to three rows. Removing the vh without first giving .desk a bounded share re-opens the defect the clamp was bought to close.

1. Kill the inversion first, and it costs nothing: one clamp for every read note, not 46vh for short and 31vh for long. A 150-word note must never get a smaller window than a 149-word one. Take the single value from the desk's share so the index keeps its documented floor.
2. Spend the 54px that is already there. .pickSlot sits empty under the cut at rest; either let the text occupy it until a pick exists, or put the overflow statement in it — the honest line then lands exactly in the space the composition is currently wasting, and the layout does not move when the pick bar arrives.

confirmed.element: .darkNote, ?state=voice; and .specWhy, ?state=nothing
confirmed.problem: The legally required voice disclosure is simultaneously the smallest type in the room (12px), the lowest-contrast text in the room (on-ink-2, 62% white), and the longest line in the room: measured live at 493px wide, which is 87–91 characters per line. Three lines above it the said text runs 27px at 68 characters. The disclosure is capped with max-width:62ch, the one measure in the file declared in ch — the exact unit master.css:127 argues against by name ("Geist's average glyph is about 0.45em, so 31em lands near 68 characters"), and 62ch duly resolves to about 90. The same fault repeats in the nothing room, where .specWhy carries no max-width at all and runs 82–86cpl at 12px in all four cards, giving each card a longer line at 12px than the 15px body directly above it.
confirmed.fix:
Keep the measure half of the fix, drop the colour half and drop the .emptyTitle clause.

DO: set `.darkNote { max-width: var(--measure); }` in place of `62ch` (master.css:760) — verified live: 372px, 64/72/71/36 characters, foot grows 19px with no collision. Add `max-width: var(--measure);` to `.specWhy` (master.css:1022) — 372px at 12px, taking all four cards from 81–84cpl to ~68 and restoring the rule that the caption's measure is never longer than the body's above it. Then assert it: extend scripts/design/notes-audit.mjs with a measure rule (it currently has a leading rule and no measure rule at all) — every element carrying a sentence of prose computes a width no greater than 32em at its own font-size. That rule would have caught 62ch as 41em.

DO NOT raise .darkNote to --on-ink-1. It is already at --on-ink-2 (7.7:1) and the CSS comment at master.css:757-759 records that it was deliberately raised from --on-ink-3 (4.1:1, failed AA) for exactly this reason. Pure white would put the third party's legal boilerplate at the same tint as the person's own dictated words three lines above, against the defect library's "a person's words outrank the machine's". 90 characters per line, not 62% white, is what makes it unread; fixing the measure is the whole fix.

DO NOT add max-width to .emptyTitle. I drove ?state=search and typed a 64-character query: the title rendered "No note says "zzzzqqqq wobbleflange marquee sideskirts for the ballroom terraceorchard"." across two balanced lines of ~578px and ~525px (~47 and ~43 characters), because `.emptyTitle` already carries `text-wrap: balance`. The 101cpl figure is the container's capacity, not anything that renders. That clause is refuted.

confirmed.element: .readBody.readLong (?state=pressure and any note over 31vh) — ArrowDown/ArrowUp/Home/End on the note body
confirmed.problem: The note body is clamped to max-height:31vh (298px at 960, 279px at 1280 and at 1000) with overflow:auto, no scrollbar (offsetWidth === clientWidth), no fade, no mask, no data-over. The sentence-pick keyboard captures ArrowUp/ArrowDown/Home/End/Space and never scrolls the container: driving from the fourth ArrowDown onward the .pick element sits at offset 195px, then 332px, inside a 298px box while scrollTop stays pinned at 0, and End announces "28 words picked. Use these words to make them a task." with all 28 words below the cut. The screen then reads "28 words picked. Send to Tasks will use exactly these" above a live primary Send to Tasks, and none of those words are visible. The product's second promise — only the exact words you pick ever cross — is operable blind from the keyboard. Meanwhile the same sheet is half empty: the right column ends at 150px of a 504px sheet and there is clear white below the button row, so the person's own words are the only thing on the desk being rationed. Four changes, all in notebook.js and master.css, desktop only (the phone already sets max-height:none).

2. Put the picked sentence on screen before announcing it. After the refocus block in paint(), `mount.querySelector('.readBody .pick, .handBody .pick')?.scrollIntoView({ block: 'nearest' })`. This is one line and it is what makes moveSentence()/jumpSentence() honest — the announcement and the ink then agree.

3. Measure the overflow and say so. After layout (and on the body's own scroll, on resize, and on fonts.ready), if scrollHeight > clientHeight set data-over="top" | "bottom" | "both" on the body and paint a 24px linear-gradient mask on the overflowing edge only — never an always-on decoration, so a fade means something is genuinely hidden. Pair it with the accessible name so the fact is not carried by ink alone.

4. Give .readLong a real floor and ceiling instead of the flat 31vh. It currently clips 115px at 1440x960 and 165px at 1280x800 while ~80px of blank white sits between the clipped text and the button divider. Set min-height to 12 lines and max-height from the space the desk actually has (pile height minus the meta column and the action row), so the 150-word pressure note renders whole and only a genuinely longer note scrolls — the index keeps its share, which is what the 31vh comment was protecting.

Also let PageUp/PageDown fall through the .readBody/.handBody key handler untouched, so the two scroll keys stay scroll keys now that Space is a pick key. Leave Space bound as it is; with (1)-(3) in place its behaviour is at least visible.

confirmed.element: ?state=voice — the dark floor, [data-act="voice-stop"] and the global keydown handler
confirmed.problem: Dictating is the one flow where the person is by definition not looking at the screen, and it is the only room with no key that keeps. Escape leaves and says "Nothing was kept" — the only universal key on the floor throws the words away. Ctrl+Enter, this product's own commit chord (it saves a note in capture, and Ctrl+Z reverses everywhere), does nothing here: driven live it left the dark floor up and produced zero readback pieces. "Stop and read it back" carries no keycap while T, K, Esc and Ctrl+Enter are keycapped everywhere else in the product, so Enter only works by the accident that focus happens to land on the primary; one Tab moves it to Cancel, where Enter discards. And the floor speaks once ("Listening. Speak whenever you are ready.") and then never again — the running clock and the wave are visual only, so with your eyes off the screen there is no way to know it is still listening or how long it has heard you.
confirmed.fix:
Three changes, all inside the existing keydown handler and STATES.voice.

1. Make the takeover own the commit chord. In the `(e.metaKey || e.ctrlKey) && e.key === "Enter"` block at notebook.js:2504, before the `editing` and `draft.trim()` branches, add: if (state === "voice") { e.preventDefault(); act("voice-stop"); return; } and if (state === "readback") { e.preventDefault(); act("keep-both"); return; }. This does double duty — it gives the spoken chain the same chord as capture, and it closes the live bug where Ctrl+Enter over the ink floor silently saves the draft hidden behind it and announces "Saved. 15 notes" to a person who thinks they are dictating.

2. Print the keycap. In STATES.voice (1807) render `Stop and read it back<kbd>${MOD}+Enter</kbd>`, and in the readback footer render `<kbd>${MOD}+Enter</kbd>` inside Keep both — same kbd span as capture, no new type or hue. Add `<kbd>Esc</kbd>` to Cancel so the floor stops being the one room that advertises nothing.

3. Make the floor audible. In the startListening tick (806), every 15 seconds call say() with the clock in words: "Still listening. Twenty seconds so far." Route it through the existing polite `.sr` region and only on the 15s multiples, so it never speaks over a person mid-sentence. Also call it once on entering ?state=voice directly, since that path currently announces nothing at all.

Drop the Escape-undo. Instead make Escape in voice consistent with the button beside it — it should behave exactly as voice-cancel does today — and separately fix the real inconsistency this exposed: Escape in state==="readback" (2565-2573) discards without the 30-second undo that the Discard button earns at 2351-2352. Route readback's Escape through the same discard-speech handler so one grammar covers both ways out of that room.
confirmed.done: round 8

confirmed.element: ?state=review — global keydown falls through to moveCursor() while .hand has the floor
confirmed.problem: With the hand of cards up, the most obvious key in a queue drives the wrong plane. Driven live: the card reads "1 of 8"; one ArrowDown leaves the card untouched and moves the cursor in the STILL TO DECIDE index behind it, announcing "3 of 7. Teacher onboarding, three things they kept asking for...". A second press (j) says "4 of 7". So one keystroke produces two counts of the same queue in two grammars — the card counting the current card in eight, the list behind counting seven without it — and names a note that is not the note on screen. Focus at load in this room is on BODY, so nothing anchors the keyboard user to the object that owns the floor; T and K work only because the handler is on document. refuted.problem: The lower plane's only identity is its 2.7% ink ground, and an unconditional 96px `linear-gradient(to top, #fff 66%, transparent)` bleaches the bottom of it to pure white in every state. Two failures at once. First it is always on: in ?state=review, ?state=seam and ?state=search the index reports `scrollHeight - clientHeight = 0` — nothing is under the dock — yet the band still paints, promising content that continues when none does. Second it is the wrong colour: it is white, not `--ground`, so across the bottom 96px the index stops being a plane and becomes the sheet. In ?state=seam the index ground is 336px tall and 96 of it (29%) is white, and the 66% stop renders as a visible horizontal edge rather than a fade. The index therefore has no designed foot anywhere in the product: last row, ~200px of ground, a white band, dock.
refuted.why:
REFUTED on three grounds, the third fatal.

1. The perceptual claim is measurably false. I sampled the rendered column at 1440x960 through the foot of the index (x=140, dsf=1). The ground reads 248,248,248; the band reads 255,255,255; the ramp is 248 -> 255 monotone across ~27px (y=848 -> y=875) with no discontinuity anywhere, because a stop of white at 66% into transparent-white is continuous by construction. "The 66% stop renders as a visible horizontal edge rather than a fade" is wrong: it renders as a soft vignette, confirmed in a 2x crop of the seam foot (_rf_crop_seam.png). The total delta is 7/255, about dL* 2.3. That same magnitude cannot simultaneously be too weak to see and strong enough to "promise content that continues" — and nothing on the surface reads a 2.7% whitening under a white pill as a scroll cue. The element is .dockWrap::before, anchored to the dock and sized to it (96px vs a 64px pill), not to the scroller's clipping edge. It is the dock's bed, not an overflow indicator, so the library's "always-on decoration where a fade should be measured" class does not attach to it.

2. The proposed colour is a provable regression, and of the worst class in the library. I applied the fix literally — `linear-gradient(to top, rgba(17,17,17,0.026) 62%, transparent)`, height 72px — to ?state=notebook at mid-scroll (scrollTop 167, where I measured two rows at 896-936 and 936-976 travelling into the 846px band). Render: _rf_crop_fixapplied.png. Full-ink rows run straight into the dock; the pill cuts through "Walk-in couple this morning, June 2027, ... dweek rate...", and the section head "The enquiries / No date / 1 still to decide" sits at full ink behind the dock. That is controls painting over content. The current white band (_rf_crop_current_mid.png) does exactly the job it exists for: the row and the group rule dissolve before they reach the pill. The gating on data-more does not save the fix — data-more would be present precisely in the overflow states, so opacity 1 plus a transparent-ink gradient is that crop. Worse, --ground is translucent (rgba(17,17,17,0.026)) and .indexWrap is already painted --ground underneath, so the proposed gradient composites to ~5.2% ink: not a plane-preserving band, a visibly darker one. White is not an arbitrary choice here; it is the only value that erases ink under a white pill, and it is the dock's own colour.

3. The closing device duplicates a fact already stated. .indexHead already carries the count ("14 notes", notebook.js:1595), and the interaction check asserts head/index count agreement. "That is all 14" at the foot is a second grammar for one fact, is not in the product's copy source, and is a Bear/Things device, not a Linear, Stripe, Vercel, xAI or SpaceX one — the bar this round is the five, and none of them close a list with a sentence.

The only residue is that overflow is 0 in review, seam and search (verified: 0/0/0 against 333/337/216/1601/42/234 elsewhere), so the bed measures nothing in three states. Gating it there costs more than it buys: in ?state=search the bed would fade out and back in as each keystroke crosses the overflow threshold, pulsing 96px of chrome under a floating object while somebody types. The team has already designed this foot once — .index reserves 132px so the last row never rests under the dock (the comment at master.css:507-509 records that fix) — and a soft white bed under a white dock at 7/255 is a deliberate, correctly executed seat for it.
