refuted.why:
Driven at ?state=seam, 1440x960, computed styles read off the live DOM. The finding is wrong on its central measurement and wrong on its premise.

MEASURED, not inferred:
- .readBody  17px / 400 / 27.54px / -0.357px
- .peelField 17px / 600 / 27.54px / -0.357px
- .peelFrom span 17px / 600 / 27.54px / -0.357px
- .peelSent  17px / 600 / 24.65px / -0.272px

1. "silently omits .peelSent and .peelFrom span" therefore they are set differently — false for .peelFrom span. master.css:938 restates the same three values verbatim (t-17 / lh-read / tr-18). It renders pixel-identical to the shared rule. Absence from the selector list at :471 is a DRY nit, not a rendering defect, and the finding's whole argument is that it produces a visible difference. It does not.

2. "appears twice on screen at once" — false. notebook.js:1305-1310 suppresses .peelFrom entirely unless the wording has been edited away from the picked words, with the comment "Seeded, the two were the same sentence twice at the same size forty pixels apart." That is a prior round's fix to this exact complaint. In the seeded seam only .peelField carries the sentence.

3. The three-way comparison never happens. peelPanel() (notebook.js:1280-1324) returns EITHER the receipt (.peelSent) OR the edit form (.peelField) — never both. Confirmed by driving: before send, .peelSent is absent; after send, .peelField is absent. The two surfaces the finding says contradict each other cannot be seen together.

4. What IS co-present on screen — .readBody and .peelField, and later .readBody and .peelSent — already shares size, leading and tracking in the first case (27.54px and -0.357px on both). The only delta is weight, which the finding then asks to remove.

5. The fix makes the work worse in two specific ways. Setting .peelFrom span to 400 directly reverses a fixed finding recorded in the source at master.css:935-937: "On the one surface whose promise is that only the words you picked ever cross, the words you picked were set smaller and lighter than the wording derived from them. They lead." With both at 400 the picked words stop leading the wording derived from them, and the indigo-wash box cannot carry that alone because .peelField has no box to be contrasted against. Setting .peelField to 400 also collapses the filled/empty distinction: .peelField::placeholder is deliberately 400 (master.css:979), so a written wording and an unwritten prompt would become the same shape on the one screen where a stranger must be shown what they can change.

Residue, for the record and not enough to confirm: .peelSent alone genuinely deviates (lh-base 1.45, tr-16). But it holds a one-line task title inside a compact receipt chip, leading is invisible on one line, and the tracking delta is 0.085px at 17px. The finding does not isolate that; it bundles it with two false claims and two regressive changes.

refuted.problem: The file states the contract at master.css:97 — "One tracking curve, by size, declared once. Every letter-spacing in this file is a token from it." It is broken at six of the eight steps. 17px carries three tracks (tr-18, tr-16, tr-21); 15px carries two (tr-16 on .headNext b, tr-14 on .idxText); 13px carries two across twenty rules; 12px carries three. The visible costs: .spec .emptyTitle sets 17px at the 21px track (-0.026em = -0.44px per character), making the four card titles in the nothing room the tightest-set lines in the product; and "Mara & Finn" in the header is 15px at -0.016em while the person's own writing in the index, same 15px, 400px below, is at -0.012em. The system fixed this class for leading and stopped there.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. The finding misquotes the contract it cites, and both of its two "visible costs" fail measurement.

1. The stated contract is not broken. master.css:97-98 reads "One tracking curve, by size, declared once. Every letter-spacing in this file is a token from it." I counted every declaration: 63 letter-spacing rules in master.css, 0 of them a raw value — all 63 are var(--tr-*). The one occurrence in notebook.js:405 is a measuring mirror that copies computed letterSpacing. The contract as written holds exactly. The finding silently rewrites it into "one track per size" and then reports it "broken at six of the eight steps."

2. That rewritten contract is not expressible against this curve, so the proposed audit assertion cannot be written. The track ramp is 34/27/21/18/16/14/12/11; the size ramp is 34/27/20/17/15/13/12/11. Three sizes — 17, 15, 13 — sit exactly midway between two named tracks, and --tr-16 has no font-size at all. There is no --tr-17, --tr-15 or --tr-13 for a --t-N to "agree" with. The finding's answers (tr-18 for t-17, tr-14 for t-15, tr-14 for t-13) are one of two equally defensible roundings, presented as if the file had declared them; the assertion it proposes would have to encode a mapping table the finding invented this round.

3. The headline visible cost is fabricated. ".spec .emptyTitle ... the tightest-set lines in the product." Measured live at ?state=nothing: computed letter-spacing -0.442px at 17px. Against it: .darkSaid 34px/tr-34 = -1.156px per character, .emptyTitle 27px/tr-27 = -0.81px, [data-type=expressive] .emptyTitle = -0.918px, .handTitle 20px/tr-21 = -0.52px. In em, tr-34 (-0.034) and tr-27 (-0.030) are both tighter than tr-21 (-0.026). It is fourth by em and fifth by pixel. Not the tightest by either reading.

4. The second visible cost is sub-perceptual and confounded by weight. Measured at ?state=notebook: .headNext b "Mara & Finn" is 15px/600 at -0.24px per character; .idxText is 15px/400 at -0.18px. That is 0.06px per character — across the whole eleven-character name, 0.66px of accumulated width, under one device pixel at 1x. The finding itself concedes they sit 400px apart on different planes. Two strings at different weights, on different planes, 400px apart, differing by two thirds of a pixel in total, is not something a panel can see. And tightening the heavier cut relative to the regular at one size is standard optical practice, which is exactly what tr-16-on-600 / tr-14-on-400 does here.

5. I looked for the strongest version the finding did not make, and it also fails. Driving ?state=seam through data-act="send" puts the same sentence on screen twice at 17px: .pick inside the note at 400/-0.357px (tr-18) and .peelSent on the receipt at 600/-0.272px (tr-16). Over that 40-character string the tracking difference is 3.39px of width, about 1%; the 400-to-600 weight difference is roughly five times that. The 1% is invisible underneath the 5%. .peelFrom span and .peelSent, which the finding pairs, are mutually exclusive branches of peelPanel() (notebook.js:1280-1310) and never render together.

6. Parts of the fix would make the work worse. The file varies tracking by ground and role deliberately, not only by size — .undoFor sits knocked out white-on-ink at tr-11 (0em), where reversed type optically closes up and loosening is the correct move; .spec .emptyBody inherits tr-16 at 15px inside a specimen card. A blanket size-locked assertion that permits only tr-cap-with-uppercase forbids that class of judgement by construction and turns a typographer's curve into a lookup table.

The residue is real but small: .emptyBody at 17/400/tr-16 versus .readBody at 17/400/tr-18 is one same-size, same-weight prose pair at two tracks, 0.085px per character apart. Linear, Stripe and Vercel all ship multiple tracks at one size for different roles — Vercel's own Geist specimen does. At 0.005em this is token tidiness argued as typography, not a defect at the 9.5 bar.

refuted.problem: Drove it: typed "Ring the florist back about the aisle foliage before Friday. She needs the final music choice…" and pressed Ctrl+Enter. The first sentence is 59 characters, over LEDE_MAX 48, so ledeOf returns null and the row renders with no <b> at all — uniformly ink-1, no grey tail. It lands directly above "Saturday wedding, Mara & Finn." which has the dark-head/grey-tail treatment, and the new row reads visibly darker and heavier than every row around it. The index's whole reading rhythm is that pattern, and a row that breaks it encodes nothing a reader can name: only that the writer's first sentence ran long. Every one of the fourteen seeded notes in data.js has a lede, so the index the panel is being shown is not the index a venue owner will have — a note captured in three seconds usually has no short terminal sentence.
refuted.why:
REFUTED — the finding's central evidence is inverted, two of its factual claims are false, and its principal fix reverts a paid-for decision.

(1) EVIDENCE INVERTED. It claims "every one of the fourteen seeded notes in data.js has a lede." I ran the artifact's own ledeOf() over all 17 seeded bodies: exactly 1 has a lede ("Saturday wedding, Mara & Finn."), 16 do not. The claim is backwards, and it is the finding's whole basis for "the index the panel is shown is not the index a venue owner will have."

(2) THE REAL MECHANISM IS DIFFERENT. Seeded rows render two-tone not because their first sentences are short, but because data.js:241 never calls ledeOf: `const title = seed.body.split(/(?<=[.?!”])\s/)[0]` — no LEDE_MAX cap — and build() never sets a `lede` field. notebook.js:1492 tests `note.lede === false` strictly, so `undefined` fails the test and every seed gets a <b> at any length. Driving it confirms: live data-lede values of 65 and 75 chars render with heads, both far over LEDE_MAX 48. The finding diagnoses a threshold problem in ledeOf; the actual discontinuity is that seeded notes bypass ledeOf entirely.

(3) "HEAVIER" IS FALSE. master.css:631 is `.idxText b { font-weight: 400; }`. Measured live via computed style, every head, tail and root in the index is weight 400. The no-lede row is not heavier than its neighbours — the only delta is the tail's ink-2 (rgba(17,17,17,0.72)) versus uniform ink-1.

(4) A FIX ALREADY DONE. "Keep the 600-weight .lede on the desk only" implies the index uses 600. It does not — 600 is desk-only (.readBody .lede) plus cursor row and search hits, and the CSS comment at master.css:624-630 records that exact change as already made in a prior round ("Density, not weight... The lede keeps its rank in ink").

(5) THE FIX WOULD MAKE IT WORSE. Splitting at "the first --measure-worth of words, word-safe" is the approach notebook.js:255-262 documents as already tried and rejected: it "ran to 88 characters and, failing that, cut at the last space before 46," so "a lede could end on 'she'" — "a fragment, not a heading." This proposes reinstating a regression the programme already paid to remove.

(6) THE RESEED IS OVER-SATISFIED. It asks that "at least five of the fourteen" have no short first sentence; 16 of 17 already have none by ledeOf's measure.

The one accurate observation — a captured no-lede row is uniformly ink-1 while its neighbours carry an ink-2 tail — is real but misattributed, is a density difference of one alpha step rather than the weight break described, and the finding's own remedy for it is a documented regression. Not confirmable as written.

refuted.problem: The floor goes to ink, roughly 700px of it is empty, and the one sentence that says a person's voice leaves the device is the smallest and dimmest thing on the screen, in the bottom corner, set while the wave is running and the person is talking. refuted.why:
REFUTED. Drove ?state=voice through the product path (click .verb[data-act="voice"] from ?state=notebook) at 1440x960, 768 and 390, read master.css, notebook.js, notes-interaction-check.mjs and the shipped Composer.tsx / notes-copy.ts, and BUILT both halves of the fix live to look at them.

The geometry is right and nothing else is. (1) "The smallest and dimmest thing on the screen" is false on both halves. Measured on the live dark floor, the only four text nodes present are: .darkTime 12px rgba(255,255,255,0.62), .darkSaid .tail 27px rgba(255,255,255,0.42), .darkNote 12px rgba(255,255,255,0.62), Cancel 15px rgba(255,255,255,0.62). The disclosure is exactly tied with the elapsed timer, shares its alpha with the Cancel button, and is NOT the dimmest — the transcript's own tail is 0.42. (2) "Diagonally opposite Stop and read it back" is false. .darkFoot is one flex row at y=868 h=92; .darkNote sits at y=868 and voice-stop at y=882 — same band, aligned flex-end, laterally opposite, not diagonally. It is the left member of the decision row you read when deciding to stop or cancel. (3) "Set while the wave is running and the person is talking" implies it arrives mid-speech. Sampled at t=60ms, 250ms, 900ms and 2100ms after the press: .darkNote is at y=868 in the first painted frame. It is in .darkFoot, flex:none, unconditional, present from 0:00.

The finding also re-files two already-refuted findings on this identical element and this identical remedy — log.html:2020 ("the legally required disclosure sits 342px below the words at the far bottom-left corner, at the smallest step and the faintest density") and log.html:2317 "disclosure-set-as-fine-print", whose refutation states it BUILT and screenshotted the move-it-under-the-transcript fix as a regression (_disc_moved_1440.png). The AA pass on 0.62-on-ink is inside the measured baseline the brief says not to spend findings on, and notes-interaction-check.mjs:309-312 already gates the string's presence and its "Signal Studio does not receive" clause.

Both halves of the fix are regressions, and the first is unbuildable as written. There is no "mic control" on the ink floor — STATES.voice (notebook.js:1791-1808) renders exactly Listening/timer, .darkSaid, .darkWave, then the foot. There is also no "before listening starts" beat and no "once words start arriving" transition: the transcript is rendered whole at first paint (155 chars at y=364 from frame one), so the prescribed two-stage sequence has nothing to key off. Building it would mean inventing a pre-transcript state, then animating a legally required notice from 15px/0.86 down to 13px/0.75 at the moment the person starts speaking — a legal notice that shrinks and dims the instant you engage is a worse pattern than a stable one, and it moves the notice out of flex:none .darkFoot into .darkBody (overflow:auto, justify-content:center) for two seconds and back, reflowing the whole floor at the exact moment the first words land, between the transcript and the live .darkWave.

The second half rewrites copy, which the constraints forbid. The disclosure is one string in notes-copy.ts whose own comment reads "Standing disclosure shown wherever dictation is offered"; the fix lifts sentence one and drops "Signal Studio does not receive or retain that audio" — the mitigating half — so the desk would carry the alarming clause without the reassurance. Built live: appending that 82-character line under "Other ways in" grows .deskAside from 119px to 167px and pushes .index down 48px at both 1440 and 1280 (evidence: C:/Users/ethan/signal-studio-workspace/_rf_desk_1440.png), spending roughly a row and a half of the index on the product's most-visited screen, and it lands a second privacy sentence in a second grammar on a sheet already printing "Yours until you send something on" — the standing checklist's "facts stated in two grammars" defect.

The one novel clause, "nobody can learn this before committing", also overstates. Pressing Dictate paints the ink floor with the disclosure in the same frame, with Cancel beside it; the browser's own microphone permission prompt then stands between that frame and any audio leaving — the shipped product states this itself in Composer.tsx:573 ("Your browser asks for microphone access only after you start"). The disclosure precedes the audio. And master.css:754-759 records the placement as an argued decision, not an oversight: "It is not negotiable and it is not hidden behind a press... they are entitled to know while it is listening", with the alpha deliberately raised from --on-ink-3 for exactly this sentence.

Evidence: C:/Users/ethan/signal-studio-workspace/_rf_voice_1440.png, _rf_voice_390.png (on the phone the disclosure is already full-width directly ABOVE the controls at y=585 over Stop at y=766, so the "bottom corner" premise is 1440-only), _rf_desk_1440.png and _rf_desk_1280.png (the proposed desk line, built).

refuted.problem: The register is meant to be restrained, and the loudest typographic device in the product is a letterspaced all-caps label used eleven ways. Two of them are whole sentences shouted at 11px: TURN THIS INTO A TASK and WHAT HAS CROSSED INTO TASKS. Linear ships essentially no caps eyebrows; Vercel none. Six on one screen is admin-panel grammar, and it converts the peel — the product's second promise, a piece of paper you peel off a note — into a form with fieldset legends. LENGTH / 23 words compounds it: a word count is an iA Writer metric that answers no question a venue manager has, and it exists to pad the rail to three rows.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. The counting is right and everything built on it is wrong.

CONFIRMED BY MEASUREMENT (driven at 1440x960, computed styles off the DOM, all ten states): the token resolves to 11px / 600 / 0.825px / uppercase / rgba(17,17,17,0.62), and the visible instances are exactly six in ?state=seam (HOW IT ARRIVED, WHAT IT IS ABOUT, LENGTH, TURN THIS INTO A TASK, WHAT THE TASK WILL SAY, WHAT HAS CROSSED INTO TASKS) and five in ?state=nothing. The 106 characters is exact. Every other state carries 1-4. That is where the finding's accuracy ends.

1. "The loudest typographic device in the product" is measurably false, and it is the finding's load-bearing sentence. On ?state=seam the eyebrows are the SMALLEST and LIGHTEST type on the sheet: 11px at 62% ink. Above and around them sit the person's own words at 17px/600/100% ink in the peel field, the note body at 17px/400/100% ink, index rows at 15px/400/100% ink, a solid black "Send to Tasks" button and a solid black "8 still to decide" pill. Uppercase at 11px/ink-3 is the standard device for making a label legible WITHOUT volume, and the frame (locked-seam--1440x960.png) shows it working — the eyebrows recede into the rail while the writing holds the screen. Caps are 13.2% of the sheet's rendered characters (106 of 804), all of it in the quietest ink the palette allows.

2. The benchmark citation is selective against three of the five names the bar now uses. The finding cites Linear and Vercel and is silent on Stripe, xAI/Grok and SpaceX. SpaceX's typographic identity is essentially uppercase; Stripe uses uppercase micro-labels in exactly this position — the detail rail beside an object. Picking the two of five benchmarks that support the charge, on the round where the brief explicitly changed the bar to those five, is taste dressed as measurement.

3. The fix escalates chrome over the person's words in the one place the artifact has explicitly ruled the other way. "Turn this into a task" at 15px/600 sentence case would sit one notch under the person's picked sentence at 17px/600 and above the boundary line at 13px/400 — making a label naming the panel the second-loudest thing in the peel. master.css:930-936 records the specific decision against this ("the words you picked were set smaller and lighter than the wording derived from them. They lead"). This is the same failure the panel already refuted once: log.html carries "one-micro-label-doing-four-jobs" (Typography), same token, same class list (.indexHead, .specName, .peelLabel), refuted precisely because a sentence-case-at-larger-size fix "puts chrome out-shouting the writing." Different rationale, same token, same shape of fix.

4. The fix forks one element by room and cannot be applied as written. .indexHead is a single class carrying both the product's section heads (YOUR NOTES, STILL TO DECIDE, WHAT HAS CROSSED INTO TASKS, FOUND) and the specimen banners (EVERY OTHER EMPTY IN THIS PRODUCT, WHEN THE PRODUCT DOES NOT YET HAVE YOUR WORK) — verified in the DOM, same className in all four rooms. "Sentence case for section heads, keep caps for specimen-room banners" means one structural element renders in two typographic grammars depending on the query string. Worse, the fix exempts its own second exhibit: all five caps labels on ?state=nothing are .indexHead banner plus four .specName eyebrows, every one of which the fix preserves. It does not deliver the reduction it argues for.

5. "A form with fieldset legends" misreads what the peel is. The peel contains an editable textarea, and WHAT THE TASK WILL SAY is that textarea's accessible name (notebook.js:1312-1313, id="peel-label", aria-labelledby="peel-label"). Labelling the field on the one screen whose promise is that only the checked words cross is not admin grammar, it is the minimum.

6. The LENGTH charge is the only residue and its fix is wrong too. Deleting the row costs a fact that is load-bearing elsewhere: in ?state=pressure the note body genuinely clips (.readBody scrollHeight 413 vs clientHeight 298), so "150 words" states how much note is below the fold, and the rail takes a fourth row (IN TASKS AS) on sent notes, so it is a structure, not padding. Deleting a row product-wide to remove one eyebrow from one state is a net loss.

refuted.problem: "Put back" is this product's undo word. It is the first two words of every reversal receipt, seven of them. Escape from a read note announces the identical bare phrase, and closing a note is not a reversal of anything. A person who cannot see the screen presses Escape, hears "Put back." and has been told their last action was undone. The pressure room then labels the same control "Put back Esc", so the overload is on screen as well as in the announcement. It is a small phrase carrying two contracts, in the one product whose entire pitch is that nothing happens to your words without you saying so.
refuted.why:
Driven live at 1440 and 390. The escalation the finding rests on is factually wrong, and the surviving kernel is a lexical preference where the current wording is defensible.

1. The on-screen overload does not exist. The finding says "the pressure room then labels the same control 'Put back Esc', so the overload is on screen as well as in the announcement." Two errors. The label at notebook.js:1422 is `Put it back<kbd>Esc</kbd>` — "Put it back", not "Put back" — and it is not pressure-specific: it is the close control on any open note in any state (driven ?state=pressure returns exactly `['Put it backEsc']`, and ?state=notebook after Enter on a row returns the same). More decisively, the undo control is not labelled "Put back" at all: notebook.js:1185 renders `Undo Ctrl+Z`, and driving ?state=pressure returns zero elements with data-act="undo" to collide with. On screen the two controls read "Put it back Esc" and "Undo Ctrl+Z". Nothing is overloaded there, so the second half of the proposed fix is aimed at a defect that is not present.

2. The receipt echoes its own control's label, which is correct. Pressing the button labelled "Put it back" announces "Put back." That is a receipt agreeing with its trigger, and it is literal in this architecture: reading LIFTS a note out of the index onto the desk, Escape puts it back down. Closing is the reversal of opening, so "not a reversal of anything" is wrong on the founder-locked metaphor's own terms.

3. The harm scenario is overstated. Every undo receipt carries a distinguishing object clause — verified live: Ctrl+Z after a save speaks "Put back. Your note is in the field again."; :213 always appends a label; :2275 is "Put back under X."; :2337/:2352/:2463 all carry a second sentence. The bare form is unique to closeNote. And the person hears it immediately after pressing Escape themselves, with focus landing on the source row, whose accessible name reads the full note ("Saturday wedding, Mara & Finn. Ceremony 2pm in the orchard…"). They are told where they are one utterance later.

4. The fix would cost something. Relabelling the desk control from "Put it back" to "Back to your notes" strips the one place the two-plane metaphor is literally true — a sheet lifted off the index and set down again — and flattens it into generic app-navigation copy. Appending `${note.title}` to the announcement also duplicates what the refocused row's accessible name already speaks.

One real thing sits nearby but is not what was raised: on the phone the close control is labelled "Back to your notes" (:1619) while pressing it still speaks "Put back." (:913) — label and receipt disagree, and the lift never happened because the phone opens the note as a modal sheet over the pile rather than onto a desk. That is a much smaller, differently-shaped defect than "Put back is overloaded across seven receipts and a button", and the finding as written does not make it.

refuted.problem: The whole product exists for the three seconds between a thought and it being safe, and that moment is a textarea clearing. I drove it frame by frame: at t+140ms the field is already empty and the note is already a grey one-line row 300px below; the only thing that moves is a small slide on .idxRow; the only acknowledgement, the 'Saved. Undo' pill, renders at y818 — 700px below where the eye was and 450px below where the note landed, tucked against the dock. Nothing carries the words from the desk to the index. The architecture is two planes with depth and the depth is never used at the one moment it was built for. This is why, having used the product for an hour, I cannot name a moment from it. The ink dictation floor is the only memorable thing here and it is the industry's standard voice UI, borrowed rather than owned; the product's one original idea, the sealed edge, is rendered as a popover with a caret. That is the finding: this is a genuinely excellent notes app in the Linear house style, and the wedding lives in the strings and one head control, not in the structure.
refuted.why: Factually wrong about the behaviour, and the proposed fix is already shipped in a stronger form. Driven live at 1440x960, sampling the DOM every ~60ms after Ctrl+Enter: a fixed-position copy of the exact typed sentence (.fly, notebook.js:353-427, commented "THE MOMENT") sits at y108 over the field at t+38ms, travels y219 (111ms), y313 (174ms), y372 (237ms), and lands at y387 — the row's exact position — at ~314ms, holding full opacity until arrival, then handing over on contact; the destination row's .idxText is pinned to opacity 0 until 470ms so the sentence is never printed twice. The ghost reads fontSize/lineHeight/letterSpacing/fontWeight live off the field (17px, width 496 = the field's measure) and scales to the row's width, over 520ms on cubic-bezier(0.32,0.72,0.24,1); the pile scrollIntoViews to the row before the flight so the landing cannot be off screen. It runs on the phone too (ghost observed at y383 at 390x844). So: "Nothing carries the words from the desk to the index" is false — the words are the only thing that moves; "at t+140ms the note is already a grey one-line row" is false — at t+140 the row's text is at opacity 0, an empty band waiting; "the only thing that moves is a small slide on .idxRow" is false twice, since @keyframes arrive (master.css:411) is an indigo-wash fade, not a slide, and it is the secondary mark. The finding asks for ~260ms of travel; the artifact spends 520ms, and the source documents an earlier 138ms-travel-then-hang version as having been rejected for reading as "a blur followed by the same sentence printed twice." The only surviving observation is geometric — .undo does render at y818/x642, 431px below the landing row — but the remedy for it makes the work worse: every reversible act (sent to Tasks, discarded dictation, moved subject, dropped duplicate, delete) routes through one offerUndo() strip in one place, and moving capture's confirmation inline into the arriving row gives one act its own reversibility grammar and scatters undo across the index, the exact class the paid-for library already charged for ("one reversibility surface, not toasts scattered about"), while planting a second focusable control inside a row governed by the index's single-tab-stop arrow walk.

refuted.problem: Entering the ink floor announces exactly 'Listening. Speak whenever you are ready. Stop when you are done.' The legally required sentence — that the browser may send microphone audio to its speech service — sits only in .darkNote in the bottom-left corner: no aria-describedby, not in the announcement, not in any focused control's name. The takeover also carries no role=dialog and no aria-modal, so the whole notebook stays readable behind a floor that has visually swallowed it. In the one flow where the person is by definition not looking at the screen, the one sentence the law requires is the one sentence they cannot hear. The same class shows in the seam: picking words announces '9 words picked' and never reads back which words, so the sealed edge — the product's only original promise — cannot be verified without eyes.
refuted.why: Three of the finding's four claims are false against the source and the real accessibility tree. (1) "No role=dialog/aria-modal, so the whole notebook stays readable behind": notebook.js:2104-2108 sets `inert` on `.sheet` and `.rail` whenever `.dark` is mounted. Chromium's own AX tree via CDP Accessibility.getFullAXTree in the voice state returns 53 nodes with 24 ignored, and every unignored node belongs to the takeover (region "Dictating", transcript, disclosure StaticText, Cancel, Stop and read it back). None of the notebook is in the tree. `inert` does strictly more than aria-modal, and notebook.js:2626-2637 adds an explicit Tab wrap inside `.dark`. (2) The disclosure is an unignored StaticText inside the only region in the tree, on a four-text-node surface, sitting directly between the transcript and the two buttons — one browse-mode arrow away, not unreachable. (3) "The seam announces a count and never reads back which words, so the sealed edge cannot be verified without eyes": notebook.js:718 in startPeel already does exactly the proposed fix — say(`${N.copy.sourceLabel}: ${words}. ${N.copy.payload}`). Driven live it speaks "The words you picked: [the exact sentences]. Tasks receives these words and nothing else from this note. The rest of what you wrote stays private here." Focus then lands in .peelField (aria-labelledby="peel-label" = "What the task will say") whose value is those same words. The sealed edge is verifiable eyes-free twice. The count during arrow traversal is correct design, not a defect: shift+arrow extends the range, so re-reading the full selection each press makes an eyes-free user hear 13 words, then those 13 plus 13 more, then all 41 — quadratic re-reading while walking a long note. Count while traversing, full read-back at commit, is the better model and is what ships. (4) The one true kernel — the disclosure is not in the entry announcement and has no aria-describedby — carries a fix that would make the work worse: it asks for the same 48-word legal paragraph both as aria-describedby on the dialog and appended to the polite live region, i.e. spoken twice on arrival, which is the exact class this file already ruled against in its own source (notebook.js:1832, on the read-back printing the same sentences twice "at the moment the product is asking somebody to trust that it heard them"). And startListening() fires immediately after paint, so the mic is live and the clock running while roughly fifteen seconds of legal text is read over the top of the sentence "Speak whenever you are ready" — making the flow's own instruction false for precisely the user the fix claims to serve, and guaranteeing their first utterance lands under the announcement. Refuted: mostly factually wrong, its seam half already implemented in the grammar it proposes, and its surviving quarter net-negative.

refuted.problem: The dictation takeover announces nothing after entry. Measured: three seconds into ?state=voice the clock reads 0:03 and #say.textContent is the empty string. .darkTime is updated by a direct el.textContent poke inside setInterval with no live region; .darkWave is aria-hidden; .darkSaid carries role="status" but its content is a static fixture string that never changes while listening, so the region never fires. The three facts a speaker needs — the microphone is live, how long it has been running, what has been heard — are all screen-only. The brief names "a voice flow that cannot be trusted without looking at the screen" as one of the three defects this product adds, and the gate asserts only that the clock and the wave move on screen (lines 2107-2112). Compounding it: the takeover's tab order is Cancel then Stop and read it back, so the first key a keyboard user presses inside a live recording lands on the control that throws it away. And .darkNote — the legally required disclosure — is the one measure in the file set in ch (62ch, 493px, 89 characters per line measured against 65-72 everywhere else), the unit the --measure comment rejects by name.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. The two load-bearing claims are false, and the measurement that "proves" them was taken on a path that bypasses the code being accused.

1. "The dictation takeover announces nothing after entry" — wrong. Driving the product's own control (click .verb[data-act="voice"] at 1440x960), #say reads "Listening. Speak whenever you are ready. Stop when you are done." on entry and still reads it at 3s. That is notebook.js:2410, three lines below the branch the finding never quotes. The empty #say the finding measured comes from ?state=voice, a demo deep-link that renders STATES.voice without running the act handler — no user reaches the takeover that way. Two of the "three facts a speaker needs" are therefore already in words: the microphone is live (announced by name, plus a real text "Listening" tag inside section[aria-label="Dictating"]), and what has been heard (.darkSaid, and after Stop the transcript lands in readback as editable fields with real accessible names). Only elapsed seconds is screen-only.

2. That remaining gap should not be closed the way proposed. The fix asks for a polite live-region update at 0:15 and every 30s while the microphone is open. Screen-reader speech firing mid-sentence into a live mic is the thing that corrupts a dictation, and the file's own comment at notebook.js:795-798 says the clock and wave are written with textContent precisely so nothing repaints under a speaking person. This fix would make the moment worse.

3. "Tab order is Cancel then Stop, so the first key a keyboard user presses lands on the control that throws it away" — inverted. refocus at notebook.js:2411 puts focus on [data-act="voice-stop"] on entry; measured, document.activeElement.dataset.act === "voice-stop". The first key is Enter on Stop; Tab is only reached after deliberately moving off the primary. This also restates a baseline assertion the finding got backwards — notes-interaction-check.mjs:745-749 already asserts that focus placement, and 753-769 assert the wrap. Swapping DOM order would also put the secondary to the right of the primary, breaking the secondary-left/primary-right order used by every other footer in the file.

4. The one true grain: .darkNote is max-width: 62ch (master.css:760), measuring 493.27px at font-size 12px against --measure's 372px at that size, and running 90 / 91 / 62 characters per line — the longest measure in the product, on the one paragraph the adjacent comment says must be readable, in a file whose --measure comment (master.css:124-131) rejects ch by name. Real but small, and it is a trailing "compounding it" clause on a finding whose headline claim is false. A finding cannot be confirmed on its third subordinate sentence.

refuted.problem: At load, before any key is pressed, row one is drawn as the keyboard cursor. Measured: the data-cursor row and a hovered row both compute backgroundColor rgba(17,17,17,0.035) — byte-identical fill, identical shape, so hovering any other row puts two rows on screen marked the same, one of them by the mouse resting anywhere. The row's only cursor markers are data-cursor and tabindex="0"; it carries no aria-current and no aria-selected, so the state exists as ink density with no equivalent in the accessible tree. The file's own comment above the [data-searching] rule names exactly this defect and fixes it only for the search state. Separately, the composed accessible name double-punctuates every note that ends in a full stop — measured: "...the lecturer always opens with it.. Written. 9 hours ago. Still to decide." — because idxRow() appends ". ${src.label}" to a title that already ends in terminal punctuation.
refuted.why:
Measurements confirm the raw facts and refute the finding. Driven at 1440x960, ?state=notebook&v=locked: the data-cursor row computes background rgba(17,17,17,0.035), box-shadow none; a hovered row computes rgba(17,17,17,0.035), box-shadow none. Identical, and 14/14 aria-labels carry a doubled stop. But every load-bearing claim built on those numbers fails.

(1) It is not an undesigned collision, and it is not carried only by ink. master.css:596-598 is a written decision from the round just closed: indigo is reserved for a live keyboard, a search hit, and words about to cross, and at load the row is none of those. The instant a keyboard is actually in the pile the cursor is unmistakable — measured with focus in the index: background rgba(79,70,229,0.08), box-shadow inset 0 0 0 1px rgba(79,70,229,0.32), lede weight 600. At rest there is no keyboard to mark.

(2) The proposed fix makes the resting frame worse, and I rendered it to check. Injecting box-shadow: inset 2px 0 0 var(--ink-1) on the cursor row at rest puts a solid #111 bar on row one — the highest-contrast object on the whole sheet at load, louder than the group headings, louder than the indigo treatment the file's own comment records removing for being "the loudest object on the paper." Worse, .idxRow carries margin: 0 -10px, so the inset rule lands 10px outside the text column; in the render it sits at x~22 while "Mara & Finn" starts at x~28, breaking the exact left edge the comment at master.css:1448 says was corrected. The remedy reopens two paid-for defects to close a smaller one.

(3) aria-current is not the missing equivalent. The state is in the accessible tree already, as the roving tab stop — measured tabIndex 0 on the cursor row, -1 on the rest — which is the standard mechanism and which the interaction check already asserts. A screen reader arrives by Tab and the row is announced on arrival. Adding aria-current="true" would assert "current item" at load about a row that is not current: at rest openId is null and the desk holds the blank compose sheet (notebook.js:1651, 1662), not that note. That is a fact stated in the tree the product cannot back.

(4) The punctuation sub-claim is real but its fix is aimed at the wrong string. Measured from data.js:241-242, note.title is the FIRST sentence (split on a lookbehind for [.?!"]) and note.rest is the remainder; in 13 of 14 rows the doubled stop comes from the tail of rest, not title. The finding's own quoted example is n06, where "the lecturer always opens with it." is the tail of rest. Stripping a trailing [.?!] from note.title, as proposed, would run two of the person's own sentences together — "Saturday wedding, Mara & Finn Ceremony 2pm in the orchard..." — deleting a sentence boundary from the accessible name, which the interaction check's own never-delete-content-from-the-accessible-name property guards, and would leave "by Thursday.. Written." exactly as it is. The fix as written both fails to fix the defect and introduces a worse one.

The finding is a correct measurement, a deliberate decision misread as an accident, a redundant ARIA addition, and a bundled string nit whose fix is broken.

rounds.headline: The loop is the defect: four of twenty findings were caused by the last round's own fixes
rounds.body:
Seven seats, forty-two agents, no errors. Floor 7.1, ceiling 8.2. Taste rose from 6.4 to 8.2 because the charge it called structural last round is answered: three seats independently tested the sealed edge and found a second sheet hinged from the corner still attached, tucked under the note, carrying its own destination, with a commit row that stays reachable off a nine-hundred-word note. Interaction said plainly that this is not an extremely well-made notes app with wedding words in it.

The finding that matters most is not about the artifact. Four of the twenty confirmed blockers were defects the previous round's fixes had introduced. The word-safe drag snap was written, commented at length, and made unreachable by a click handler added in the same batch. The desk budget did not count the peel, so the signature gesture drove the index to nothing at 1440x960 with thirty-seven notes still counted in the header. The lede regex lost its escape and returned null for every note, and that was reported as a design outcome and judged as restraint. The invisible-but-focusable gate failed the correct technique while never checking the real defect. Twenty per cent self-inflicted, all of it from landing twenty-odd fixes in one batch and running the gates once at the end.

Twelve of the twenty are fixed and verified rendered, four partly, four still open. The loop that produced them is retired with this round: the seat schema forced three findings per seat whatever a seat thought, which made a unanimous pass arithmetically impossible, and the score is the lowest seat while every round fixed all seven. See docs/design/notes-gate-method-2026-08.md.

wins.biggestWin:
Rebuild the desk card's two-column grid so the paper is sized by the note and not by its margin notes (finding 2). It is the dominant defect because it is present in notebook, readback, seam and pressure — every state a person actually lives in — and it is what makes the desk read as "text beside a form" rather than as paper: at 19 words the machine's four labels are 224px tall against the person's 83, and the void underneath the words is twice their area. Fixing it widens the measure, kills the largest hole on the screen, and puts the person's writing back on top of the hierarchy where the paid-for library already says it belongs.

Distance to 9.5: mechanical, and I can size it. Sheet lift and the floor gutter ladder, 2 hours. Desk grid rebalance plus the short-note fact line and moving TO MAKE A TASK into the foot, 4 hours. Peel column binding plus making the picked sentence the peel's content instead of a copy in a field, 6 hours. Phone index fade and scroll-padding, 2 hours. Wave measure, 15 minutes. Search's dead-end region — at ?state=search the message block is top-left in a 1322x779 field with about 560px of empty ground under it — needs optical centring in the region, 1 hour. Call it two focused days, and I would expect 9.0 to 9.2 out of it.

The last 0.3 is not mechanical, so I will name it rather than size it. I tested the sealed-edge charge against the file myself: the peel is no longer a form in a callout — it hinges from the attached corner, tucks ten under, carries its own destination, has a sticky commit row, and the T announcement states verbatim that Tasks receives these words and nothing else. That charge is genuinely answered. What is not answered is the room. The ink floor is 18px of decoration around a sheet that covers 88% of the screen and casts no shadow; every plane relationship in the product happens inside that sheet, at a fixed 1000px column, in a vocabulary any excellent notes app already has. Until the floor earns its existence — the sheet actually lifted, the floor actually widening as the screen does, dictation's takeover reading as the same room going dark rather than a separate black page — this is an extremely well-made notes app that happens to contain wedding words, and no amount of column polish inside the sheet closes that.

Fix the pick: give `.pick` and `mark` `box-decoration-break: clone` with a padded, capped box and a single baseline rule instead of a full ring. Right now the sealed edge's one visible object — a marked passage in somebody's own prose — renders across a line break as four open-ended strips with paired hairlines between the lines, which reads as strikethrough. Everything else about that instrument now works: I drove it, and the earlier charge is genuinely dead. Sentences are real spans, pointer and keyboard write the same pick, T in the hand opens the peel on the card without covering the note, the announcement names the words rather than counting them. It is no longer a form in a callout. Its typography is the only thing still contradicting it.

Distance to 9.5: mechanical, and small. Findings 1, 3 and 4 are seven lines of CSS and two deleted `.replace()` calls — half a day including re-shooting locked-seam and locked-pressure with a wrapping pick. Finding 2 is a judgement change plus a re-derived group line and new frames: one day. Finding 5 is one accessor and one assertion: half a day. Call it two days to about 9.0.

The last half point is not mechanical and I will not size it. The index sets every note as one line at 15px and trims it: at 1440 all fourteen rows end in an ellipsis, and between 55% and 65% of each note's characters reach the screen. No note is ever seen whole anywhere below the desk. That is a plane full of fragments cut at an arbitrary x, and it is why the surface reads as a well-made list of stubs rather than as somebody's notebook. The phone already gives two lines per row and the interaction check already asserts it there ("over two lines", "so a note is readable rather than a stub") — the desktop, which has the most room, is the only place that refuses. Deciding what the index actually is — a two-line preview like the phone, or a hit-pivoted window — is a rethink of the second locked plane, not a type pass, and until it is made this is a beautifully calibrated type system serving a wall of truncation. The ramp, the 31em em-based measure (I verified 58–68 characters at 12px, 15px, 17px and 27px), the single leading ladder and the correctly scoped tabular numerals are all Vercel-grade. The application at the four moments the product makes promises is not yet.

Fix seam-pick-desync — couple the note's pick to the open seam so the words that are marked, the words in the wording field, and the words that cross are one fact, and open the field with the caret at the end. Everything else on this surface is craft; that one is the product's only original idea telling a person it has taken their words and then sending different ones, and it reproduces in both rooms.

What stands between this artifact and a 9.5, from my seat, is mechanical, and I will size it: two to three days. And I will say the other thing plainly: this is not an extremely well-made notes app with wedding words in it. The subjects are a venue's week, "still to decide" is a state a venue owner actually has, and the hand of cards is an evening ritual rather than a queue widget. The gap to Linear is not conception, it is that three of the five defects above are in states nobody drove — under the dock, with the seam open, at 900px — which is precisely where this panel looks.

Redraw the peel so the picked words ARE the peel rather than being described by it. Make the picked sentence the peel's own first line, editable in place at the same size and leading the note sets it in, with no second print and no field label; put "Your note stays here" and the destination sentence beneath it; and draw the hinge with real paper thickness at the attached corner so the eye reads one object continuing, not a second panel arriving. Between here and 9.5: nothing structural — the architecture, the palette lock and the copy voice all permit it. What this is not is the failure mode the direction was chosen to avoid: the wedding is load-bearing here, not decoration — the subjects are couples and rooms, the queue is a venue's week, the honesty states are about a marquee and a florist. It is a genuinely well-made capture product whose centre of gravity a stranger still misreads.

Fix the seam so it asks one question once: kill the duplicate subject picker inside the peel, source the destination from real Tasks projects, and use one name for it in the label and the accessible name. That single change stops the product's one original idea from contradicting itself on its own sheet. Now the distance to 9.5, split honestly. Your note is in the field again." are lines Linear or Stripe would ship unedited, and the subject axis means this is emphatically not a well-made notes app with wedding words: it knows the house is facing Mara & Finn on Saturday and it acts on it. But there is a structural distance no polish closes, and it is exactly where the earlier round said it was. The peel was redrawn — the hinge, the ten-pixel tuck, the sticky commit are all real improvements — and its contents were not. Inside that beautiful geometry sit a caps label, a bordered text input, a select and a black submit button. That is a form. Redraw the inside of the peel so the picked words themselves are the object — the person's own sentence, at the note's own size and leading, editable in place on the smaller sheet, with no field label, no 1px rectangle, no select — and the send as the only weighted thing in the box. Two answers you asked for, plainly. First: this is NOT an extremely well-made notes app that happens to contain wedding words, and I do not think the round-4 charge transfers. The copy is written from inside a venue ("Worth doing something about?", "Nothing is decided until you say so, and every decision can be put back", "Yours until you send something on"), the grouping is a venue operator's mental model rather than folders, and there is a genuinely memorable moment — the dictation floor, and the 520ms travel of your own words from the field into the row they became. It moves me twice. Second: I tested the seam against the file rather than inheriting either the charge or the claim it is fixed. The container is fixed and well fixed. The contents are not; it is still a form, and it is still the payoff.

What stands between this and 9.5, sized. The mechanical distance is about three days: the seam interior (1 day), a lift on read with the source row conceding its place (half a day), readback set as speech on paper rather than input boxes (half a day), the phone commit shown on the first keystroke and given a shape the avatar does not share (3 hours), the phone dock's fade (1 hour), and the fly ghost given paper under it — at 60ms it currently draws a person's sentence at full ink straight through the "Mara & Finn / Saturday 18 July" group rule, and for four frames the signature moment reads as a smear (1 hour).

There is also one structural distance polish does not close, and I will name it rather than size it: the wedding date is stated on every single screen and used by nothing. "Saturday 18 July, in 2 days" sits in the head, in the group rule and in the filing chip, and no note is nearer, louder or sooner because of it — the index sorts by when it was written, and the head says "Go through 8" whether the wedding is in two days or two months. A venue two days out does not have the same notebook as one two months out. Put the peel into the desk's height budget instead of on top of it — write the measured peel height to a `--peel-h` custom property and subtract it in `.readBody`'s max-height alongside `--desk-chrome` and `--index-floor` — so the second plane keeps its declared 224px through the one gesture the whole product exists for. What stands between this and 9.5 is two things of different kinds. The mechanical part is small: all five findings above are contained edits — the layout budget and its assertion is under a day, the pointer-drag guard is an hour plus a gate assertion, the always-rendered commit is two hours, the counter and the divergence marker half a day each. Call it two to three days for one engineer, and the automated gates to hold them are another day. The structural part I will not size, because polish does not close it: the seam is still a form. Round 4's charge was that the one original idea was rendered as a form in a callout; this round redrew the callout as paper, hinged it off the corner, tucked it ten pixels under the note's edge — and left the object inside it untouched. The only controls are Drop note 1, Drop note 2, Add another, Discard, Keep both — so the only route back to one note is to delete half of what the person said. This is the machine restructuring a person's words on the one surface whose entire promise is that it does not touch them, and it is the flow a venue owner uses while walking a room with their hands full.

Do not change the default. Splitting is right when someone dictates three errands, and one-note-by-default just moves the same unstated transformation to the other side. Two changes instead:

1. A join affordance, per seam rather than global. Between piece i and piece i+1 put one quiet control (same .verb treatment as "Add another", which already sits in that row) that concatenates i+1 onto i in original order with a single space, restores focus to the end of the joined field, announces the new count through the same `say()` the drop path uses, and registers with `offerUndo` exactly as drop-piece does at notebook.js:2703-2712 so Ctrl+Z puts the two back. Per-seam, not one "Join them": with three pieces a single global control has no defined meaning, and add-piece can already produce three.

2. State the rule in the head. It currently reports a count as if it were something the person did. It should attribute the cut to the machine and name the rule, so the join control reads as an offer rather than a repair. Wording is notes-copy.ts's job, not the seat's — add the string there, alongside voiceStart/voiceStop, and have STATES.readback read it; do not hard-code my sentence.

Cost is small: one handler branch, one control in an existing row, one copy string, two assertions in notes-interaction-check.mjs (join concatenates in order; Ctrl+Z restores both pieces with edits intact, mirroring the existing drop test at line 836).

confirmed.element: mount click handler, notebook.js:2575 `const sent = e.target.closest(".sent")` — overrides pickedRange()'s word snap (notebook.js:600-640)
confirmed.problem: The word-safe snap is written, commented at length, and unreachable by the gesture it was written for. The click handler sets `sentAt = [i, i]` and `setPick(sentenceText(...))` unconditionally, and click fires at the end of any drag whose press and release land in the same span. Measured in ?state=pressure: a 140px drag across roughly five words inside sentence 2 yields "31 words picked" — the whole sentence — while a drag that happens to cross a full stop yields exactly the dragged words (6). The file's own comment claims pointer and keyboard "write the same picked string"; they do not.
confirmed.fix:
Take the finding's fix but tighten two things it gets loose.

1. Make the guard an AND, not an OR, and exempt shift. The finding's "movement > 4px OR non-collapsed selection" is too greedy in both directions. Movement-alone would break the phone tap route, which notes-interaction-check.mjs:2459-2464 protects as "the only route a phone has" — touch taps routinely jitter past 4px. Selection-alone would break the documented shift-extends contract: shift-click on a .sent after an earlier click extends the native selection from the caret, so it is non-collapsed and would be misread as a drag. Gate on: `!e.shiftKey && movedSincePointerDown > 4 && selection is non-collapsed && the same body contains selection.anchorNode`.

2. Do not re-derive the pick in the click handler. Once the guard fires, just `return` without touching sentAt or calling setPick or paint. Because no repaint happens, the selection survives, and the 120ms offerPick already scheduled at notebook.js:3200 writes the snapped string, clears sentAt (notebook.js:801) and announces the correct count for free. Adding a second write path here would be the fourth route into one pick.

Also clear the recorded pressAt on pointercancel, or a cancelled touch leaves a stale coordinate that makes the next genuine tap look like a drag.

Assertions to add to notes-interaction-check.mjs, replacing the synthetic-selection proof with a driven one:
- With a real mouse drag of ~5 words inside .readBody .sent[data-i="1"] at ?state=pressure, the mark's word count is strictly less than that sentence's word count, and both its ends are whole words.
- The same drag inside .handBody at ?state=review behaves identically.
- A plain click on a .sent still picks the whole sentence, and a shift-click still extends to the sentence range — so neither existing route regresses.
- A tap on .phoneSheet .sent at 390 with 6px of jitter still picks the sentence.

confirmed.element: notebook.js:2507 `inputTimer = setTimeout(applyDraft, 450)`; the control it gates is `.topFoot [data-act="keep"]` and, on the phone, `.dockGlyph[aria-label="Save it"]`
confirmed.problem: The "Save it" control does not exist while anybody is typing. Measured: 483ms from the first keystroke to the control appearing; typed at a realistic 70ms/key for 4.6 seconds, the control's count in the DOM was 0 for the entire run and it appeared only after the pause. The product is named for the three seconds between the thought and it being safe, and for the whole of those three seconds the affordance that makes it safe is not on screen. On a phone this is the only commit route — there is no Ctrl+Enter — so a phone user typing steadily sees no way to keep the note at all. The debounce exists to protect the browser's Ctrl+Z history from a mid-typing DOM mutation, which is the right problem and the wrong fix: it solves it by removing a control rather than by never inserting one.
confirmed.fix: Seat the commit permanently, and drive it from the property that is already synchronous — not from `data-live`. Render `[data-act="keep"]` (with its `<kbd>` chord hint), the `.spacer`, and the counter into `.topFoot` and `.dockRow` at first paint, always, alongside the resting privacy line. Then let `wakeSheet` — which already writes `root.style.setProperty("--writing", …)` during the input event with no tree mutation and no damage to Chromium's typing history — carry the swap: `--commit-vis: visible/hidden` and `--rest-vis: hidden/visible` set in the same call. Use `visibility`, not opacity plus `inert`: visibility:hidden removes the control from the tab order with zero DOM writes, so nothing is invisible-but-focusable and no attribute is touched mid-burst. Leave `applyDraft` and its 450ms debounce in place for the counter TEXT only — nobody needs a live character count mid-burst, and that is the only write that must stay deferred. Result: the commit and its chord hint are on screen from the first character on both the desk and the dock, the resting frame is visually unchanged, and the browser's undo history is untouched with no node created or destroyed during input. Cost is near zero: `.top` already holds 155px and the phone dock 101px across rest and live, so the reserved band exists and nothing reflows. Update notes-interaction-check.mjs:78-81 and :669 to assert the new contract — the control is present and visible from keystroke one, and is not focusable while there is nothing to commit.
