refuted.problem: The architecture's first sentence is an ink floor with one white sheet lifted off it. Measured, .sheet has box-shadow: none, sits at a flat 18px inset on three sides, and covers 88.4% of the viewport area at 1440x960, 90.7% at 1920x1080. There is no lift: the floor is an 18px black border with a 16px radius, which reads as a browser bezel around a screenshot, not as a room. The inversion is the damage — the 1000px desk card inside carries a three-layer --paper-lift (0 2px 3px, 0 8px 16px, 0 26px 52px) and floats convincingly, while the object the architecture says is lifted is the one drawn flat. At 1920 it gets worse, not better: the sheet stretches to 1802px while the content column stays 1000, so 401px of unused white opens on each side and the floor stays a hairline.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. The measurements in the finding are correct (box-shadow: none, --inset 18px, sheet 1322x924 = 88.4% at 1440 and 1802x1044 = 90.7% at 1920, verified live) but every load-bearing claim built on top of them fails.

1. The lead fix is a measured no-op. I applied edit (1) verbatim at 1440 and pixel-diffed the two full frames: mean delta 1.3/255 over the 9.8% of pixels that changed at all, and the change on the floor runs rgb(17,17,17) -> rgb(16,16,16), i.e. one level DARKER. rgba(17,17,17,alpha) over #111111 composites to #111111 for any alpha, which is arithmetic, not opinion. The only delta above noise is maxDelta 12/255 — the rgba(255,255,255,0.06) ring, which resolves to a 1px rgb(31,31,31) hairline sitting immediately against a 255-white edge. Before and after are visually indistinguishable. The finding concedes this in its own parenthetical ("ink alpha reads as nothing on #111111") and then proposes the ink alpha anyway. A fix whose author has already documented that it does nothing cannot carry a finding at a 9.5 bar.

2. Edit (2), measured, makes the composition worse. With --inset:56 and .sheet{max-width:1600px} at 1920 the live geometry is: rail.left 56, rail.right 120, sheet 176..1776, left floor 56, right floor 144. The sheet left-aligns inside the padded floor, so the "room" the fix promises is a 2.6x asymmetric ink gutter, not a floor. Centering it to fix that breaks a second object: .railTile[data-active]::after is a 7px caret at right:-12px whose whole job is to point across the inset gap at the sheet it opened (measured gap today: exactly 18px, matching --inset). At inset 56 with the sheet centered, that caret floats 54px+ short of the sheet and points at nothing.

3. It is factually wrong about the inversion, which is its stated damage. At rest .top carries box-shadow: var(--ring), var(--paper) — max alpha 0.06 at 22px blur, a whisper. The three-layer --paper-lift the finding quotes (0 26px 52px at 0.14) is the writing/focus state only (.top[data-live] and .top:has(.topField:focus-visible), master.css:394,400). The desk card does not "float convincingly" while the sheet is drawn flat; both are restrained, and the one that lifts does so only while a person is writing on it.

4. The premise is a constraint, not an oversight, and the source says so at master.css:236: "White against ink needs no shadow. Contrast is the elevation." The palette lock allows exactly three colours, so a shadow under white on #111111 is physically unavailable — the only tool left is a white bloom, which the same token block rejects on purpose ("a blur is a haze, and paper is not hazy", master.css:150). The sheet edge is a 238-level luminance step from 17 to 255. That is a stronger elevation signal than any 0.14-alpha blur, and Linear, Vercel and Stripe all run this exact figure-on-dark-ground without a halo.

5. The "browser bezel" characterisation ignores the left side. Left floor is 100px (inset 18 + rail 64 + inset 18) and it contains the capsule spine, which is the architecture's own named object. Three sides at 18 and one at 100 with a floating capsule in it is not a uniform bezel.

The one residual observation with life in it — 401px of unused white opens each side at 1920 while --stack holds at 1060 (the finding says 1000; 1000 is .pile after gutters) — is a wide-width column finding, not a lift finding, and it is asserted as damage with no argument. It should be raised on its own terms by someone willing to argue that a full-bleed chrome plane with a centered measure is wrong at 1920, which is the pattern all five named benchmarks ship.

refuted.problem: The desk card's height is max(note, aside) with align-items:start, so whichever column loses leaves the largest void on the screen. Lift a 19-word note: body is 496x83, aside is 422x224, card is 1000x324 — roughly 170x496px of empty paper sits under the person's words, twice the area of the words themselves, and the card's height was set by four grey labels. Invert it at ?state=pressure: body 413 tall, aside 224, and 190x422px of void opens under the rail instead. The aside is a fixed 422px, 42% of the card, and it caps the reading measure at 496px even at 1920 where the sheet is 1802px wide. TO MAKE A TASK is a two-line instruction paragraph inside that rail, so at 19 words the standing help text is physically larger than the note. The CSS comment above this grid says a twenty-word note used to float in a column of dead white; it still does, now vertically.
refuted.why:
Measured live at 1440x960 and 1920x1080 (Playwright, ?state=notebook lifting the 19-word "Course reading for Thursday" note, and ?state=pressure). The raw geometry the finding quotes is real — .top 1000x324.1, .deskWrite 496x82.6, .deskAside 422x224.1; pressure inverts to write 413 / aside 224 — but four of the five load-bearing claims built on it are false, and the fix is broken.

(1) "The standing help text is physically larger than the note" is measurably false. The TO MAKE A TASK block renders 392x56.6 = 22,187px2; the note renders 496x82.6 = 40,970px2. The help text is 55% of the note by area and shorter by 26px. The note's words already outrank it, which is the defect-library rule the finding is trying to invoke. (The void is likewise 1.71x the words, not "twice".)

(2) "The aside is a fixed 422px" is false. master.css:341 is `minmax(0, var(--measure)) minmax(276px, 1fr)` — the rail is 1fr and takes only the remainder.

(3) "It caps the reading measure at 496px even at 1920 where the sheet is 1802px wide" is false twice over. The measure is capped by `--measure: 31em` (master.css:131), documented as a 68-character calibration; deleting the rail entirely would not widen the note by one pixel. And the paper is not 1802 at 1920 — .pile/.top measure 1000 and the index 1060 at both 1440 and 1920, because `--stack: min(100%, 1060px)` (master.css:138) exists precisely so the two planes share edges; the 1802 figure is the outer .sheet, not the paper.

(4) "It is a permanent paragraph in the margin" is false — notebook.js:1579 renders that fact only when `standingPick(note)` is empty. Driving it: clicking one sentence drops the rail 224.1 to 154.5, raises the writing column 82.6 to 146.6 as the pick bar lands in the blank band, shrinks the card 324.1 to 254.5 and hands the index 70px back. The band the finding calls dead white is where the product's next move renders, and the rail is already engineered to stand down for it. At ?state=seam the same short note's desk is 190.5 tall with a 71px band — no void at all in the state that matters most.

The fix would make the work worse. Simulated in the live DOM: `minmax(0,560px) minmax(0,300px)` leaves 58px of paper unallocated to the right of the rail, orphaning its inset edge rule off the sheet's right edge — the exact "void beside the paper" class master.css:133-138 records as already paid for. --measure 560px is 35em, ~78 characters per line, past the top of the measure range on the one surface that is entirely somebody's own sentences. The height-under-180px branch is self-referential: the writing column's height depends on the track width the branch itself changes (496 vs ~952), so notes near the threshold resolve differently depending on which mode they were laid out in first. Collapsing the rail to a text run destroys two real controls — the aria-haspopup="listbox" refile button and the "In Tasks as" receipt link that was just converted from a dead anchor. And moving a 71-character instruction into .topFoot re-wraps the button row that the comment at master.css:346-351 records as a fixed defect, and restores the 54px of desk height that notebook.js:1574-1578 records as already removed for the index's benefit.

What survives is only the un-picked read state's 141px band under a short note, on a card whose margin is by locked intent "everything that is true ABOUT the writing, beside it". That is taste, it is 8px in the picked state, and the proposed remedy costs the measure, two controls, the foot, and the paper's right edge.

refuted.problem: On the index — the plane that carries 14 of the 15 notes — the grouping label the machine assigned ("Mara & Finn", "The studio", "The house") is set two ramp steps larger and one weight heavier than the person's own sentences beneath it. The eye lands on the machine's labels and skims the writing. The file's own paid-for rule is "a person's words outrank the machine's", and its own comment at line 682 defends 400 in the rows on exactly that ground, then spends the size axis in the opposite direction on the line above. It is worse than a rank error: the first group header is the byte-identical string already in the head ("Mara & Finn" + "Saturday 18 July, in 2 days"), so the largest type on the lower plane is the one piece of type that is pure repetition. The phone branch (master.css:1381) already sets .idxDay at t-15 and lets weight alone carry it, which is the right answer sitting in the same file.
refuted.why:
Refuted on four counts, two of them factual against the file.

1. THE MEASUREMENT IS WRONG. The declared ramp is `--t-11/12/13/15/17/20/27/34` (master.css:83-84). 15px → 17px is ONE step, not "two ramp steps". The finding doubles the size of the delta it is indicting. Measured live at 1440: `.idxDay` 17px/600/-0.357px, `.idxText` 15px/400/-0.18px. A 13% step for a section heading over list body is the most orthodox move in typography, not a rank error.

2. THE HEADER IS NOT "THE MACHINE'S LABEL". The group label is the subject the PERSON filed the note under — `note.aboutKey`, set through the "Filing under" picker that is visible in the resting frame and reachable at capture, at the seam, and on the note (notebook.js:1438 `subjectList`, 1429/1534/1570). "Mara & Finn" is a real couple's names, chosen and typed by the venue, rendered verbatim. The machine's contributions to the index are the timestamp (`.idxWhen` 12px/400/ink-3, master.css:696) and the status tag (`.idxTag` 11px/600/ink-2, and ink-3/400 when quiet, master.css:691-694). Both are smaller AND quieter than the person's 15px/ink-1 sentence. The paid-for rule "a person's words outrank the machine's" is about user content beside metadata, and it is honoured exactly where it applies. Applying it to a section heading is a category error.

3. "THE EYE LANDS ON THE LABELS AND SKIMS THE WRITING" IS NOT WHAT THE SURFACE DOES. Measured: only the two `[data-soon]` headers render at ink-1. Three of the five ("The studio", "The house", "The enquiries") render at rgba(17,17,17,0.72) — LESS dense than the ink-1 sentences beneath them (master.css:606-607). In the scrolled frame the headers visibly sit back while the rows carry full ink across the whole plane. Density already does the demotion the finding asks size to do.

4. THE REPETITION CLAIM IS A DATA COINCIDENCE, NOT A RULE DEFECT. It holds for one of five headers, and only in one of the two grouping modes. I pressed "When": headers become Today / Yesterday / Monday / Sunday / Saturday — zero duplication of the head. A type-ramp rule cannot be indicted by the seed order of one group in one mode.

AND THE FIX WOULD MAKE THE WORK WORSE. Clause three — "suppress the date on the group header whose subject equals the head's" — reintroduces a defect this file already paid to fix. notebook.js:1745-1747 records the decision verbatim: "Every group's slot means the same thing: the date it is facing, or that it has none. A count in one and a deadline in another was two meanings in one column." Blanking that slot on exactly one header makes the column mean two things again, and makes a header's content conditional on a different region of the sheet. That is the paid-for "one grammar per fact" class, re-bought.

The 720px branch is not "the right answer sitting in the same file" — it is a different problem. At 390 the row is two lines with the facts moved to a quiet second line (master.css:1362-1375), so the header needs less size to out-rank it. At 1440 the row is one dense line in a four-column grid and the header is a sticky full-width rule; setting it at the row's own size would make it read as another row, which master.css:574-577 records as the state this rule was already fixed out of.

refuted.problem: The seam is where the product's one original idea lives, and it changes the words three times on the way across. (1) .peelField is font-weight 600 while the identical string in the note 200px above it is 400 — the same sentence, same size, two weights, on one screen, in the surface whose own copy says "Tasks only ever receives the exact words you pick". (2) notebook.js:844 runs `.replace(/^[a-z]/, c => c.toUpperCase())`, so a mid-sentence pick is silently re-capitalised by the machine. (3) the same line runs `.replace(/[.]$/, "")`, so the terminal full stop is stripped: I read the seam frame's note as "Switch on before guests arrive, not when." and the box beneath it as "Switch on before guests arrive, not when" — without its stop that clause reads as an unfinished fragment. And notebook.js:1524 prints the picked words only when they already differ from the wording, so the person never sees their own string beside the machine's version.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. Driven at 1440x960, ?state=seam: `.peelField` = "Switch on before guests arrive, not when", 17px/600; `.readBody .pick` = "Switch on before guests arrive, not when.", 17px/400, 241px above. So the three measurements are real. Everything built on them is not.

(1) THE COPY IS MISQUOTED BY TRUNCATION. The finding's whole rhetorical load rests on "the surface whose own copy says 'Tasks only ever receives the exact words you pick'". The rendered string (.peelBoundary, verified in the DOM) is "Your note stays here. Tasks only ever receives the exact words you pick **and check below**." The promise is explicitly scoped to the field the person checks, which is the whole reason that field is a textarea and not a static quotation. The seam does not promise byte-identity with the highlighted range; it promises that what sits in that box is what crosses and nothing else from the note. Cutting the last four words off the product's own sentence to manufacture the contradiction is the defect in the finding, not in the file.

(2) "SILENTLY RE-CAPITALISED" IS FALSE. notebook.js:853 announces `${sourceLabel}: ${taskWording}. ${payload}` — the field's value verbatim, and the source comment at :848-852 records that this was fixed precisely because it once announced the raw pick while the field held the cased version. Driven: I picked a sentence and read the live region — "The words you picked: Ceremony 2pm in the orchard, drinks on the terrace if it stays dry. Tasks receives these words and nothing else…" — character-for-character the field. It is announced, focused (`refocus = {kind:"field"}`), and editable. Nothing is silent. Further, the instrument picks whole sentences (`.readBody .sent` spans; a drag snaps to whole words), so `^[a-z]` fires only on a sub-sentence drag — I could not find a lowercase-initial sentence in the fixture set to trigger it. It is a narrow path, announced, in a correctable field.

(3) THE PROPOSED FIX FOR THE FULL STOP MAKES IT WORSE. "If a stop-free task title is wanted, do it on the Tasks side" moves the machine's edit to AFTER the person's last sight of the string — the seam would show a stop, Tasks would silently show none. Doing it before the check, in the box the copy tells them to check, is the honest place; doing it after is exactly the sealed-edge violation the finding claims to be defending. And "not when" is elliptical with or without its stop; the terminal period does not repair that clause.

(4) "THE PERSON NEVER SEES THEIR OWN STRING BESIDE THE MACHINE'S VERSION" IS FALSE ON SCREEN. The architecture's lock is that the note is never covered: the picked range renders in the uncovered note as `.pick`, 17px, full ink, indigo-washed, 241px above the field. Both strings are visible simultaneously without scrolling. Worse, the conditional at notebook.js:1524 is the applied fix to two CONFIRMED prior findings (log.html:1228 and :1291 — "THE WORDS YOU PICKED and THE TASK WORDING print the identical string one directly above the other… four text blocks for one act", "63 words of reassurance wrapped around a six-word task"). Always-printing is a paid-for defect being asked for by name.

(5) THE WEIGHT FIX IS UNDER-SPECIFIED AND REINSTALLS AN ADJUDICATED DEFECT IN MIRROR IMAGE. The finding argues from `.peelField` against `.readBody` and never looks at `.peelFrom span` (master.css:1042), which is ALSO 17px/600 — it was raised to 600 as the accepted fix to log.html:1454 ("the person's picked words are typographically demoted beneath the wording the machine derived from them… 15px/400 against 17px/600"). Setting only `.peelField` to 400 leaves the quoted source at 600 and the payload at 400 — the same asymmetry that finding cost score for, pointing the other way. The file's current position is coherent and stated: at the seam the crossing words carry one register, 17/600, source and payload identical, and density is the sanctioned mechanism under the palette lock.

The one grain worth keeping — `.peelField` is the only writing surface in the product at 600 (`.topField` 400, `.pieceField` 400, `.readBody` 400) — is not the finding as written, is not what the fix addresses, and cannot be acted on without also moving `.peelFrom span`, which the finding does not know exists.

refuted.problem: On the commonest laptop height the plane that holds everything you have ever written gets two visible rows out of 37. Measured at 1440x900: .index renders 221px tall with exactly 2 rows clear of the dock, while the desk holds 660px for a single 150-word note — and inside that desk the right-hand aside column ends after four short blocks and leaves roughly 250px of empty white below "TO MAKE A TASK". So the screen spends a quarter of its height on nothing while the index is squeezed to its floor. The named 224px floor is honoured; it is a poverty floor, and it is honoured by starving rather than by proportioning. This is not the locked architecture's fault — the two planes are right — it is that the desk's claim is fixed and the index's is residual.
refuted.why:
REFUTED — the finding is wrong on its central number, inverted on its mechanism, and half of its fix is a literal no-op while the other half reverts a documented, deliberate removal.

Measured at 1440x900, ?state=pressure (Playwright, chromium):
- `.desk` = **525.6px** (top 80, bottom 605.6), not the claimed 660px. The finding overstates the desk's claim by 134px, a quarter.
- `.index` = 221.4px with 2 rows clear of the dock. That half is true, and it is the only true half.

The mechanism claim — "the desk's claim is fixed and the index's is residual" — is backwards. `.readBody` at master.css:511-517 is `max-height: max(200px, calc(100vh - 311px - 224px))`, i.e. the desk is sized as the remainder AFTER the index's floor is reserved. Sweeping the viewport proves it: index height is 378 / 258 / 221.4 / 221.4 at 1080 / 960 / 900 / 800, while the desk goes 549 / 549 / 525.6 / 425.6. Below ~948px the index sits pinned at its floor and **the desk absorbs every further pixel of loss**. The desk is the shock absorber; the index is the one holding a guarantee. The finding has the two planes exactly the wrong way round.

The aside half of the fix is a no-op. `.deskAside` (master.css:353) sets `align-self: start; align-content: start` and **no height, min-height or stretch** — the parent grid is `align-items: start`. Its computed 224.125px is precisely the sum of its four `.deskFact` children (108→332.1). The desk's box is *already* `max(body, aside)`; at 1440x900 the body column runs to 497.6 and the aside stops at 332.1. "Remove the height it sets" removes nothing.

The "roughly 250px of empty white" is also mis-framed. There are 273.5px between the aside's bottom and the desk's bottom, but 140.9px of that band is beside the note's own body text in column one, and the rest is beside `.topFoot` (511.6→561.6). This is a marginal-note layout whose margin column is shorter than its body column. The screen does not "spend a quarter of its height on nothing" — that vertical band carries the reader's words.

The `max-height: min(content, 46vh)` half would re-create a rejected defect. master.css:500-506 and 520-526 record that a flat 46vh cap, plus a second conditional cap, was removed *because* it meant "the length of a note may decide how much of it you are given", and that the pressure room was where four lines of a debrief were cut above three lines of blank paper. Making the cap conditional on index length recreates that class along a new axis: the same 150-word note gets a smaller window on a full notebook than on an empty one. Worse, at 1440x900 46vh = 414px for the whole desk — less than today's 525.6 — so the note that currently clips by two lines ("2 more lines below.") would clip harder, in the room built to prove long notes survive.

And the fix does not reach its own target. Freeing 111.6px grows the clear-of-dock band from 157.4px to ~269px; at 39.9px per row with group rules interleaved that is roughly five, not six, and only by clipping the note further.

What is left is a taste position — "two rows on a 900px laptop is too few" — attached to a false measurement, an inverted mechanism, a no-op, and a regression. Not a finding at a 9.5 bar.

refuted.problem: One fact wears three grammars: the capture sheet says "Filing under Mara & Finn", the desk margin says "What it is about — Mara & Finn, Saturday 18 July", and the seam says "To Mara & Finn" — same widget, same five options, same values. At the seam "To" sits eight pixels from "Send to Tasks", and the option list is full of real people's names, so a couple or a venue owner reads "To Mara & Finn / Send to Tasks" as sending the task to Mara and Finn. Worse, it is genuinely a different fact: I changed the seam's destination to The studio and the note above stayed "What it is about — The house", so two identical-looking chips 130px apart now disagreed with nothing on screen explaining that one describes the note and one describes the task. The announcement ("This one goes to The studio") is the only place that distinction exists, and it is gone in a second.
refuted.why:
Refuted: the two measurements the argument rests on are both fabricated, the option-list claim is wrong, and the finding contradicts its own premise.

Driven at 1440/1280/768 in ?state=seam and ?state=review (chromium), reading notebook.js:1517-1540, 1560-1580, 788-792, 2603-2620 and data.js:76-82, 345-380.

1. "At the seam 'To' sits eight pixels from 'Send to Tasks'." False by a factor of 32. The .peelRow is picker | spacer | cancel | primary. Measured at 1440: destination pill x=334..461, "Never mind" x=617, "Send to Tasks" x=722. That is 261px of gap with a labelled cancel control sitting inside it. At 1280 it is 388px; at 768 it is 253px; in the review hand (the finding's worst case, "To Mara & Finn") it is 388px. The whole "reads as one sentence: To Mara & Finn / Send to Tasks" argument requires the adjacency the finding asserts, and the adjacency does not exist at any width.

2. "Two identical-looking chips 130px apart." False twice. Measured at 1440 with the destination changed to The studio: the note's chip (.filingBtn, "The house", under WHAT IT IS ABOUT) is at (835,178); the seam's pill (.picker, "To The studio") is at (334,472) — 501px horizontally and 294px vertically apart, on two visually distinct sheets (the note's shadowed paper, and the peel tucked under its edge). They are not the same object either: .filingBtn (master.css:948) is a borderless margin chip, label plus chevron; .picker (master.css:1124) is a 1px-inset outlined pill carrying a bold-slot "To" prefix in ink-3. In the review hand there is no note chip on screen at all (refile === null), so the confusion cannot arise there.

3. "The option list is full of real people's names." False. The list is Mara & Finn, The course, The house, The studio, The enquiries — one of five is person-shaped, and that one is the string the product's own head prints as the venue's project ("The Orchard, events | Mara & Finn | Saturday 18 July"). Nothing anywhere in this build has an assignee; the recipient reading has to be imported from a different product.

4. The finding refutes itself. Its headline is "one fact wears three grammars", then two sentences later: "it is genuinely a different fact". Both cannot be defects. It is two facts, and the surface already gives them different labels ("What it is about" in the note's margin vs "To" inside a box headed TURN THIS INTO A TASK, directly under THE TASK WORDING), different chip shapes, and different accessible names — the seam pill's accessible name is already a third grammar that names the distinction outright: "Which project: The studio. Change it." The seam also carries the standing boundary sentence "Your note stays here." The 2603-2620 handler was deliberately rewritten so file-peel sets only the task's destination and never touches note.about; the divergence is the fix working, not a contradiction.

5. The proposed fix would make it worse and breaks the copy constraint. "It will sit in Tasks under [The house]" and "The note stays under The house" are invented strings, not from notes-copy.ts, and "retire Filing under" retires a canonical copy string (data.js:350 copy.filingLabel) in favour of a label the direction invented in the renderer — the constraint is that copy is judged, not rewritten. It also puts a sentence of machine commentary back into the commit row of the one object this round just finished pulling out of a form-in-a-callout, and swaps a terse Linear/Stripe-grade destination pill for 39 characters of chrome in the row a person presses in the three seconds the product is named for.

The only residue worth anything is that the capture sheet says "Filing under" where the read sheet says "What it is about" — but those two chips are never on screen together (topSheet does not render while a note is on the desk, confirmed in the driven frame), and they govern different objects (an uncaptured draft vs an existing note). That is a separate, much smaller copy-consistency note, not the recipient-ambiguity defect filed here.

refuted.problem: "Mara & Finn" plus "Saturday 18 July, in 2 days" is printed three times in the product's own chrome within 500px of the top of the sheet: as the head's scope control, as the capture sheet's filing chip, and again as the first index group rule — verbatim, same words, same date phrasing. On the phone the head's copy and the group rule are the identical string 250px apart with nothing between them but a sort toggle. The head copy is also the only one of the three that is a control ("Press to see only these notes"), and at rest it is not applied, so it reads as a status line announcing a filter that is not on. A stranger cannot tell whether the notebook is already showing only Mara & Finn.
refuted.why:
Driven at 1440x960 and 390x844 with Playwright, plus the source. The finding is wrong on its measurements and wrong on its central interpretive claim, and both branches of its fix make the work worse.

FACTS. At 1440 the three objects are: .headNext at y=38 "Mara & Finn / Saturday 18 July, in 2 days"; .filingBtn at y=127 printing "Mara & Finn" ONLY (notebook.js:1566, `esc(note.about.label)` — no date on screen), under its own "FILING UNDER" caption inside .deskAside; .idxDay at y=326 "Mara & Finn / Saturday 18 July, in 2 days / 1 still to decide". So the date phrase is printed TWICE, not three times. And the filing chip is not chrome: it is the desk note's own subject and would read "The house" or "The course" for a different newest note — it coincides here because the seeded newest note is a Mara & Finn note. Calling it a third printing of a chrome string is a category error.

On the phone the numbers are wrong by more than 2x: headNext bottom = 92, first .idxDay top = 168 — a 76px gap, 115px top-to-top, not 250px. And between them is not "nothing but a sort toggle": .indexHead carries "Your notes", the "14 notes" count AND the grouping control. Nor are the two strings identical — the rule carries a third element, "1 still to decide", that the head does not.

THE CENTRAL CLAIM IS FALSE. "At rest it is not applied... a stranger cannot tell whether the notebook is already showing only Mara & Finn" and "can show an applied state in ink fill" (as if it cannot). Pressing it produces five simultaneous signals: box-shadow inset 0 -2px 0 #4f46e5 on the control (verified computed: rgb(79,70,229) 0px -2px 0px inset), aria-pressed="true", an escape chip "All 14 notes" appearing beside it, the head count rewritten from "Go through 8" to "1 still to decide in Mara & Finn", the index count from "14 notes" to "3 notes", and a live announcement "Showing Mara & Finn only. 3 notes, 1 still to decide." At rest the index shows five different subject groups under a "14 notes" count — there is nothing to mistake for an applied filter. The applied state, the ink fill, the accessible-name equivalent and the way out already exist.

THE FIX WOULD MAKE IT WORSE. Branch one deletes the subject from the head, leaving "The Orchard, events" plus a count verb — exactly the generic head the source replaced (notebook.js:1270, the head's top line used to be a generic count of unread items "while the thing that actually presses on this person sat in the data unsaid"), and it demotes the one venue-specific fact in the product to a list-sorting control sitting beside a grouping toggle. That is the "extremely well-made notes app that happens to contain wedding words" failure this direction exists to avoid. Branch two — head keeps "in 2 days", the rule keeps "Saturday 18 July" — splits one fact into two grammars across the screen, which is the paid-for "one grammar per fact" defect, and strips the anchored date from the head, which is the paid-for "unanchored time" defect. It buys de-duplication with two classes that already cost score once.

RESIDUAL. There is a real but much smaller thing underneath, and the finding does not raise it: under the default group=about the soonest subject always sorts first (stake, then days), so the head and the first rule always share two lines. Press "When" — one control, 40px away — and the duplication is gone entirely (rules become Today / Yesterday / Monday). The genuinely inert case is the SCOPED state, where the index collapses to one group and its rule repeats the head verbatim with nothing left to distinguish. That is a narrower defect than the one written, and the written finding's evidence, framing and fix all miss it.

refuted.problem: The desk sheet wears a 1px indigo ring at rest, and the global focus ring is a 2px indigo outline — the same hue at nearly the same weight, so the product's one accent means "focused" on every control and "decoration" on its largest object. Clicking into the writing field and tabbing back out changes nothing at all: I measured .top and .topField before and after focus and every shadow, outline and border was identical. On the surface the product is named for, the only evidence that the next keystroke will land in the note is the caret. The autofocus on load is right and fast, but the moment a person touches the search field, a filing chip or an index row, there is nothing that says how to get back to writing.
refuted.why: Refuted on measurement: the finding's central measurement is wrong, and its proposed fix is already the shipped code verbatim. master.css:388 sets `.top { box-shadow: var(--ring), var(--paper) }` — an ink hairline (`--ring` = `0 0 0 1px var(--line)`), not indigo. master.css:400-401 already reads `.top:has(.topField:focus-visible) { box-shadow: 0 0 0 1px var(--indigo), var(--paper-lift) } .topField:focus-visible { outline: none }`, which is exactly the finding's own prescription (ink hairline at rest, indigo ring when the writing surface is live, `:has()` doing the `:focus-within` job). Driven at 1440x960: blurred and empty, `.top` computes to `rgba(17,17,17,0.09) 0 0 0 1px` plus the flat `--paper` shadow; after a mouse click into the field it computes to `rgb(79,70,229) 0 0 0 1px` plus the heavier `--paper-lift`. Two properties change at once — hue and elevation — so the sheet visibly lifts as well as lighting up. There is a third distinct state the finding missed entirely: typed-then-blurred gives `rgba(79,70,229,0.32)` with the lift retained (`.top[data-live]`, master.css:394), so the accent's intensity reads as a ladder of liveness (dormant hairline / words waiting / live under the caret) rather than the one meaning the finding assumes. Verified across all four rooms — locked (paper=stacked), quiet (flat), studio (stacked), press (deep) — rest is the ink hairline and focus is solid indigo in every one; the flat room's `[data-paper="flat"] .top[data-live]` override does not steal the focused ring. The phone is covered too: `.dock` has no ring at rest and takes `rgb(79,70,229) 0 0 0 1px` when `.phoneField` is focused (master.css:402, 1429). The claim "I measured .top and .topField before and after focus and every shadow, outline and border was identical" is only reproducible by measuring against the autofocused load state as the "before" baseline, which is a focused state. The remaining true observation — that `.topField` itself carries no ring — is a deliberate, documented choice (master.css:396-399: a default outline around a two-line field held at a 31em measure drew a large empty box across the resting state), and moving the ring off the sheet onto the field would make the focused object the rectangle rather than the paper, which is worse in this direction. The second half of the fix, restating the placeholder promise under the field on blur, duplicates the placeholder that is already visible on blur when the field is empty and would add copy not in notes-copy.ts.

refuted.problem: The one original idea is a sheet that asks the same question twice in two grammars. The note's rail reads "WHAT IT IS ABOUT · The house" and eighteen pixels below it the peel reads "To  The house", and both chevrons open the identical five-option list (Mara & Finn, The course, The house, The studio, The enquiries). destinationOf() defaults to note.aboutKey and resolves through N.subjects, so the destination IS the subject. Worse, that control's accessible name says "Which project: The house. Change it." while its visible label says "To" and notes-copy.ts calls it "Which project" — three names, and "project" names a Tasks concept that this list does not contain. A venue owner cannot tell whether changing "To" refiles her private note, and the boundary sentence above it promising that only picked words cross is undermined by a control that looks like it edits the note.
refuted.why:
REFUTED on geometry, on behaviour, on arithmetic, and on the fix.

1) The picture the finding trades on does not exist. The two controls are not "eighteen pixels" apart. Driven at 1920/1440/1280/1100 the refile chip sits at y=178 in the note's right ruled margin and the peel's destination at y=472 in the peel's commit row: dy=294, dx=-501. At 900/768 the columns fold and it is still dy=243 in a different box on a different sheet. At 390 the desk stands down and both are display-hidden (offsetParent null). There is no width at which the rail's "What it is about" and the peel's "To" read as one stacked pair.

2) "The destination IS the subject" is false. notebook.js:788 destinationOf() reads `destination` — the seam's own value, held only for the life of the peel — whenever a peel is open on that note, and falls back to the note's subject only as a seed. Driven at ?state=seam: opened the destination picker, chose Mara & Finn. Result: button "To Mara & Finn", aria "Which project: Mara & Finn. Change it.", live region "This one goes to Mara & Finn.", and the rail still reading "WHAT IT IS ABOUT | The house", refile aria still "This note is about The house." The two controls held two different values on screen simultaneously. That is two questions, answered separately, with the second one's independence made visible the moment it matters.

3) "A venue owner cannot tell whether changing To refiles her private note" is already handled, and by exactly the mechanism the finding says is missing. notebook.js:2609 file-peel carries the comment "This branch used to write note.about and note.aboutKey ... It sets where the TASK goes" and provably does not touch the note; the announcement is "This one goes to X", not "Moved to X" (which is what file-note says). She is told in words, and the rail visibly does not move.

4) "Three names" is two, miscounted. The accessible name IS notes-copy.ts's string: destinationLabel = "Which project" is interpolated straight into the aria-label at notebook.js:1533. The finding counts the same string twice.

5) The fix would revert a paid-for fix and make the work worse. It says source the control from N.projects and name it "Which project: The Orchard, events". N.projects is ["The Orchard, events", "Mara & Finn", "Studio"] and the file removed it deliberately — comments at notebook.js:96 and :783 record that N.projects[0] returned "a workspace string that is not one of the listbox's five options, so the control's own current value was absent from its own list." The proposal restores that exact defect, plus a sixth vocabulary ("Studio" beside the product's "The studio") a venue owner meets nowhere else in the build. Its own fallback — delete the control — would remove the capability I just exercised: sending a note filed under The house into Mara & Finn's work.

The residual grain of truth (visible "To" vs accessible "Which project") is a one-word label question, not "the sheet asks the same question twice", and the finding's fix is not the route to it.

refuted.problem: The room takes the whole floor because a person dictating is not looking at the screen. The only thing announced is the reassuring line. The legally required sentence — that the browser sends the audio to a third-party speech service — carries no aria-live and sits in the bottom-left corner, at the maximum possible distance from the microphone and from both controls, set exactly where a cookie banner goes. That is compliance, not disclosure, and it fails the standing checklist item about a voice flow that cannot be trusted without looking at the screen. The register is the giveaway: everything else in this product tells you the uncomfortable thing plainly ("Nothing is decided until you say so"), and this one thing whispers it.
refuted.why:
REFUTED on three independent grounds: the geometry claim is false, the accessibility premise is wrong, and the fix breaks the copy it promises to preserve.

1) FACTUALLY WRONG ABOUT THE LAYOUT. Measured at four widths, `.darkNote` is the FIRST child of `.darkFoot` — `order: ["darkNote","spacer","darkAct","darkAct"]` — so it precedes both Cancel and Stop in DOM order, in reading order, and in the accessibility tree. At 1440 it sits in the same footer band as the controls (note y=848, buttons y=882: a 34px vertical offset, not "the maximum possible distance"). At 768 and 390 it sits directly ABOVE the stop button (dx = -372 and -326; the note's box overhangs the button's column). Anyone browsing the "Dictating" region reaches the disclosure before it reaches either control. "Bottom-left corner at the maximum possible distance from both controls" is not what the file does; it is the head of the commit row.

2) THE aria-live PREMISE IS WRONG. A live region announces CHANGES to its contents. The disclosure is present from the first paint of the room and never mutates, so putting `aria-live` on `.darkNote` would announce nothing at all — the attribute the finding says is missing would be inert if added. What the fix actually asks for is concatenation into `say()`, which is a different and worse thing: every entry into dictation, forever, would put 17 words of legal text between the person and "Speak whenever you are ready" in the product whose named promise is the three seconds between a thought and it being safe. That is louder compliance theatre, not disclosure.

3) THE FIX BREAKS THE VERBATIM COPY. Sentence 2 reads "Signal Studio does not receive or retain that audio." "That audio" is anaphoric on "microphone audio" in sentence 1. Move sentence 1 to the top of the room and the standing footnote opens on a dangling referent with no antecedent in its own paragraph. The constraint is that the disclosure survives verbatim; a four-sentence paragraph whose second sentence has lost its subject 900px away is not the same disclosure, and a copy seat would raise the dangling "that audio" as its own defect.

4) THE FIX DAMAGES THE ROOM. `.darkTop` is a 43px band carrying a 12px caps tag and a tabular clock, deliberately, so nothing competes with the 27px transcript that is the whole point of "dictating takes the whole floor to ink." A body-size legal sentence there becomes the second-largest type in the room and lands above the person's own words in reading order — straight against the paid-for library's rule that a person's words outrank the machine's.

5) PARTLY ALREADY GATED. `notes-interaction-check.mjs` lines 349-352 already assert "the disclosure is on screen while it is listening" and "the disclosure names who receives the audio," and the audit proves its contrast against the real composited ink. The presence-and-legibility half of the charge restates the baseline.

6) THE REGISTER ARGUMENT IS TASTE, AND IT INVERTS. The disclosure states the uncomfortable thing in its very first clause — "Your browser may send microphone audio to its speech service" — before any reassurance. It is set at the same 12px / 0.62-alpha as every other standing footnote in the product. That is consistency, not a whisper, and the finding offers no evidence for the claim beyond the word "whisper."

The standing checklist item about a voice flow that cannot be trusted without looking at the screen is about live state — am I heard, for how long, did it get my words — and the file already answers all three: LISTENING on entry, "Still listening. N seconds so far." every fifteen seconds, and the readback announcing the actual returned words plus the caret. A static legal fact is not state.

refuted.problem: Driven with K then T, one fact renders six ways on one screen, and the segmented rail states "2 of 8" in ink while its own accessible name states "1 of 8 decided" — the same widget gives a sighted user and a screen-reader user two different numbers. The status name is also three strings for one state: the pill says "To decide", the accessible name says "Still to decide", the section header says "STILL TO DECIDE". The same undiscipline runs through the numerals: the head says "14 notes", the loading line says "Fourteen of them", the empties say "Eight notes went through this morning", the desktop capture counter says "113 / 4000" and the phone dock says a bare "28" beside a tick.
refuted.why: REFUTED. Driven at 1440 in ?state=review, initial then K then T, reading the live DOM. 1. The headline claim — "the segmented rail states '2 of 8' in ink while its own accessible name states '1 of 8 decided' — the same widget gives a sighted user and a screen-reader user two different numbers" — is factually wrong about the source. These are two sibling elements inside .handQ, not one widget (notebook.js ~1961-1962): `${decided.length + 1} of ${total}` and ``. The "2 of 8" is plain visible text, read to a screen-reader user exactly as a sighted user sees it; the rail's name reports a different fact (decisions made) which the rail's own fill is what draws. Measured after K: handOf "2 of 8", pips name "1 of 8 decided" — you are on card 2, 1 is decided. Both true, both present in both channels, no contradiction. The proposed fix would make the rail's name "Note 2 of 8, 1 decided" sitting immediately after the visible "2 of 8", so a screen reader announces the position twice in a row. That is worse. 2. The "one fact rendered six ways" charge does not survive the numbers. These are four different sets, each labelled with what it counts. Measured at the exact moment the head reads "2 of 8": footer .deckNote = "7 still to decide." (queue including the card in hand), indexHead = "6 behind this one" (the pile below), pips = "1 of 8 decided", handOf = position. The finding pairs "footer 7" with "index header 7 BEHIND THIS ONE" — a pairing that never renders. At initial state it is footer 8 / header 7; after K it is footer 7 / header 6. The two counts always differ by exactly one because they count different things, which is the ONE-grammar rule satisfied, not broken. notebook.js ~1995 documents this as the already-shipped fix for an earlier confirmed duplication ("'8 still to decide' at the head against '7 left' here... This one names what it counts"). "Delete either the footer count or the index header count" would delete a true, differently-scoped number and orphan the undo sentence it anchors. 3. "Three strings for one state" is wrong about behaviour. The row button carries aria-label=name (idxRow, ~1706), so the .idxTag is never announced — a screen-reader user hears exactly one string, "Still to decide", verified in the driven rowNames. The visible pill is a tag column; in the review room it sits under a header that already reads STILL TO DECIDE, and in the notebook room it sits under "Your notes" where "To decide" is the whole statement. Applying the fix — "Still to decide" on every pill — prints the header's own five words on every row beneath it, which is precisely the defect notebook.js ~1280 records paying to remove ("the same five words, twice, in one line, reading as one broken phrase"). 4. The numerals charge inverts the actual rule. The spelled-out counts exist only in prose sentences on the two specimen sheets (~2196 "Eight notes went through this morning", ~2210 "Fourteen notes", ~2276 "Fourteen of them"); every counter in the product uses digits ("14 notes", "2 of 8", "113 / 4000", the dock "28"). Prose spells, counters digitise — one consistent editorial rule, and no screen shows the word and the digit for the same fact. "Use digits for every count in the product" is taste stated as a defect, and it coarsens copy the constraints require to be plain English. The phone dock number is not an unlabelled orphan either: it is aria-hidden="true" (~123, ~1360) beside a "Save it" button, so nothing unnamed reaches the tree; dropping "/ 4000" on desktop removes an honest ceiling for no stated gain. The only fragment with any residue is the transient live line "Kept in Notes. 7 left." against the footer's "7 still to decide." — one number in two registers, though one is a spoken announcement where brevity is correct. That fragment cannot carry a finding whose headline, central evidence, quoted numbers and three of four sub-claims are wrong and whose fix would reintroduce a defect this file already paid to remove.

refuted.problem: The charge from the earlier round was that the product's one original idea is rendered as a form in a callout. The container has been genuinely redrawn — it tucks ten pixels under the note, it hinges, its commit row is sticky — but I drove it and the contents are still, item for item, a web form: all-caps field label, a 1px-outlined text input, a labelled select, a text cancel, a submit button. Worse, the person's sentence is printed twice on one screen: once marked inside their own note at 17px, and again 200px below inside a rectangle at 15px, with a label explaining what it is. The sealed one-way edge is the only thing in this product no competitor has, and it arrives looking like a CRM field. This is where a stranger decides whether a top studio made this, and it is the one place the answer is no.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. Driven at ?state=seam and by Enter over a standing pick at 1440x960, and read against master.css:1024-1135 and notebook.js:1496-1541.

Factually wrong on its central image. "The person's sentence is printed twice on one screen... again 200px below inside a rectangle at 15px, with a label explaining what it is" describes a render that does not exist. The labelled duplicate (.peelFrom, whose <b> is "The words you picked") is conditional and does not render in either entry path: notebook.js only emits it when the wording has been edited away from the pick (`pickedWords && taskWording.trim() !== pickedWords.replace(/[.]$/,"")`), and seeded it is the same string, so measured .peelFrom count is 0 both times. The seat is describing the pre-fix state; notes-interaction-check.mjs:1325 already asserts "the seam does not print the same sentence twice", so this half of the finding also restates the measured baseline. The size is wrong too: .peelField is in the shared person's-writing rule (master.css:482) at --t-17/lh-read/tr-18 — 17px, measured, identical to the pick in the note above it — not 15px. It also names a ".peelFoot" that does not exist in the file (.peelRow).

Its own fix is largely already implemented. The fix asks that the picked words be "editable text at the note's own .readBody size, leading and colour". Measured: font-size 17px (same var as .readBody), line-height 27.54px (same lh-read), colour ink-1 rgb(17,17,17). Three of the four properties it asks for are already true; the only delta is weight 600 vs the note's 400, i.e. the words that will cross lead, which is the library's own "a person's words outrank the machine's" rule, not a defect.

What is left of the fix makes the work worse, and reverts two paid-for fixes. (a) The 1px inset hairline exists for a stated reason recorded above the rule: "It looks editable at rest. Its only editable control was invisible until it took focus, on the one screen where a stranger has to be shown what they can change." Deleting the box returns a 17px semibold line that is visually indistinguishable from the note text 260px above it, on the one screen where a venue owner who has never used a task tool must discover that the wording is hers to change — the exact discoverability defect an earlier round paid to close. The proposed contenteditable additionally throws away the textarea's field-sizing, its placeholder ("What should the task say?"), and the aria-labelledby name. (b) Deleting the "THE TASK WORDING" label removes the field's accessible name and strands the boundary copy that points at it: "Tasks only ever receives the exact words you pick and check below." (c) Replacing the picker with an inline sentence proposes new copy ("into Mara & Finn"), which the brief puts outside the seat's remit, and strips the "To" grammar and the 127x34 hit target from a control this round rebuilt to satisfy three baseline assertions (the destination it shows is one of the options it offers; the listbox marks what the opening control holds; choosing never edits the note).

Only two objects in the whole peel carry any border at all — the field and the picker, both hairlines at 9% ink — so "item for item a web form" overstates what is on screen. The residual observation with any life in it is narrow and not what was filed: two uppercase 11px labels ("TURN THIS INTO A TASK" and "THE TASK WORDING") stack within 60px of each other, which is the form-ish note in the composition. That is a one-label question, not the demolition proposed, and it cannot be settled without touching copy the seat may not rewrite.

refuted.problem: The dictation floor is the most memorable image in the product — the whole room to ink, the person's speech set large and centred, the meter, the disclosure quiet at the foot. It is the one frame a stranger would remember. Then you stop, and one frame later the same words are 15px inside two grey 1px rectangles with × buttons in the corners, on a card whose right 600px is empty white. The emotional fall from that floor to a pair of form fields is the steepest in the product, and it happens at the moment the person is checking whether the machine heard them correctly — the moment they most need to feel held.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. The finding is wrong on every measurement it rests on, and its principal fix is already the shipped rule.

TYPE. master.css:482-484 sets `.readBody, .handBody, .topField, .pieceField, .peelField, .saidHead` in one rule at `--t-17 / --lh-read / --tr-18`. Measured live at ?state=readback, 1440 and 1280: `.pieceField` computes font-size 17px, line-height 27.54px, letter-spacing -0.357px — byte-identical to `.readBody`. The finding says "15px". The proposed fix says "Set .pieceField at the .readBody size, leading and letter-spacing" — that IS the shipped rule, and the CSS comment above it says why it exists ("The same sentence was rendering at four different leadings"). The fix asks for what is already there.

THE CARRY-THROUGH THE FINDING SAYS IS MISSING. Driving voice → Ctrl+Enter → readback at 1440: `.darkSaid` sits at x=302, 31em measure, weight 400, left-set (not "centred" — master.css:807 comment: "The same measure as every other surface a person's words appear on"). `.pieceField` lands at x=303. The spoken words return to the same left edge within one pixel, at the same 31em measure, at the same weight. The only change is scale (27px floor → 17px sheet) and ink inversion, which is the room changing from the whole floor to one sheet. That is the ink floor's typography carried through the landing, in em, already.

THE × IS NOT IN THE CORNER. `.drop` is `right: 8px; top: 50%; margin-top: -16px` — measured centre y=215 against a piece spanning 170–259, i.e. vertically centred, 32px target. "× buttons in the corners" is not what the file draws.

"RIGHT 600px EMPTY WHITE". Measured: `.top` = 1000px, content box 952px, `.piece` = 560px → 392px, not 600. More importantly it is not a readback defect: at ?state=notebook and ?state=capture the same 1000px sheet holds `.topField` at 496px, so the resting state leaves ~456px to the right. Readback fills MORE of the sheet than the state the finding calls the emotional high point of the product. And `.top` measures exactly 1000px in all three states — pulling the card in to the reading measure would make the one locked white sheet resize underneath the person at the moment of landing.

THE FIXES WOULD REGRESS THE WORK. (a) Removing the boxes removes the only visible rendering of the fact under review — the machine's guess about where your speech split into two notes. The box IS the claim being checked; whitespace between two borderless textareas cannot say "this became note 1 and this became note 2". (b) Hover-and-focus-only reveal of a destructive control is a paid-for defect class (no hover on touch; the file just added pointer/tap routes precisely to stop that). (c) "Not that one" is invented copy; copy comes from notes-copy.ts.

FEEL, DRIVEN NOT READ. Ctrl+Enter off the floor puts focus in `.pieceField` ("Note 1 of 2") and announces "2 notes came back. First: Ask the venue whether the ballroom can be accessed from eight in the morning. Edit either one, or keep both." — the person's own first sentence read back to them at the moment the finding says they most need to feel held. The transcript is printed once, in the editable field, not twice.

Residue worth nothing to this finding but noted for the panel: `.topFoot` spans 496px at capture and 952px at readback, so the action row changes column between two states of the same sheet. That is a composition inconsistency, not the emotional collapse this finding describes, and it is not what the proposed fix addresses.

refuted.problem: The designed bottom edge does not exist on the phone. The white fade is 96px tall and painted underneath a dock that is 118px tall and opaque, so on the device where the index is scrolled most it is cut by a hard black rounded edge straight through a row's x-height — I caught "To decide … 5 hours ago" sliced in half, with an indigo focus ring drawn across the cut. The desktop has a proper measured fade at the same edge, so this is not a decision, it is a fade that stopped working when the dock went to ink and nobody looked. This is the class the library already paid for twice.
refuted.why:
The finding is factually wrong about the source and about the behaviour, on every load-bearing claim.

1. The element it names is not painted on the phone. master.css:1407, inside the 767px-and-below block and four lines below the `.dockWrap` override that turns the dock to ink, reads `.dockWrap::before { display: none; }`. Live at 390x844 the computed style of `.dockWrap::before` is `display: none`. So there is no "96px white-to-transparent fade sitting entirely behind the opaque black dock"; it is not painted at all, and the narrative that it "stopped working when the dock went to ink and nobody looked" is the exact opposite of what the file does — it was switched off deliberately in the same media block that made the dock ink.

2. The measurement is wrong. The phone dock is 101px, not 118px (`--dock-h` resolves to `101px` from `paint()`; `.dock` rect height 101).

3. The band is reserved in real layout, measured not guessed — which is precisely the remedy the paid-for library prescribes for this class, already applied and already commented in the file as a fixed defect (master.css:1449-1452). notebook.js:2476 writes `--dock-h` from `dockEl.offsetHeight`, and `.index` takes `padding-bottom: calc(var(--dock-h, 103px) + 16px)` with a matching `scroll-padding-bottom` (both resolve to 117px). Driven to the end of the index scroll at 390, the last row's bottom sits at 650.3 against a dock top of 734: 83.7px clear. Nothing rests under the dock at any resting scroll position.

4. The focus-ring half of the claim — "an indigo focus ring drawn across the cut" — is false and is the part that made the finding sound like a caught defect. I focused the index and pressed ArrowDown 40 times, checking geometry at every step. The cursor row's worst position across the entire walk is 83.5px ABOVE the dock's top edge and 116.5px above the scroller's clip edge; `scroll-padding-bottom: 117px` guarantees this. The focus ring cannot be drawn across the dock edge by any keyboard route.

5. The quoted evidence does not reproduce. No row in the phone index at ?state=notebook renders the string "To decide" (it is a conditional `.idxTag`, notebook.js:1700), so "I caught 'To decide … 5 hours ago' sliced in half" is not an observation of this state.

6. The only residual is that 33px of the index box lies behind the dock while a drag is in flight, with one row crossing that line at a time. That is an opaque, rounded, elevated object with a 9px inset all round covering content mid-scroll — the intended reading of a floating dock, not a clip — and it resolves to zero the instant the scroll settles.

7. The proposed fix would make the work worse. It asks for "a 32px gradient from the sheet ground to transparent" above the dock's top. The sheet ground is white and the dock is ink: a white-to-transparent gradient anchored above the dock is painted white-on-white against the sheet and is therefore invisible, and to do any work at all it would have to grade against the black dock, producing a grey band immediately above it — a value the ink/indigo/white palette does not have and which would read as a seam between the sheet and the one object at the foot of the phone. The desktop fade works only because the dock there is white on white; transplanting it to an ink dock is the reason it is correctly disabled.

refuted.problem: The one-way edge is not sealed, and the surface never says so. Driven: picked a sentence, opened the seam, replaced the field with "Something completely different that nobody picked" — a string that appears nowhere in the note — pressed Send. It crossed. The receipt reads TASKS HAS IT above the invented string, the peel's promise line still reads "the exact words you pick", and the announcement is "Sent to Tasks. Your note stayed here. In Mara & Finn." — it never reads back what actually crossed, so a person who sent this without looking at the screen is told the crossing happened and never told what went. Nothing on screen marks the difference between words lifted from the note and words typed over them.
refuted.why:
REFUTED. The finding's load-bearing sentence — "Nothing on screen marks the difference between words lifted from the note and words typed over them" — is factually wrong about the source, the live behaviour and the gate. The exact object the fix proposes building already ships. 1) The divergence marker exists and renders. notebook.js:1520-1526 in peelPanel() prints a labelled block, `

The words you picked{pickedWords}

`, on exactly the condition `taskWording.trim() !== pickedWords.replace(/[.]$/,"")` — i.e. only once the wording has been edited away from the pick. I drove the finding's own scenario at ?state=seam, 1440x960: typed over the field with "Something completely different that nobody picked", and the peel renders, top to bottom: "Your note stays here. Tasks only ever receives the exact words you pick and check below." / tinted block "THE WORDS YOU PICKED — Switch on before guests arrive, not when." / "THE TASK WORDING — Something completely different that nobody picked". Two labelled strings, forty pixels apart, stating precisely what was picked and what was typed over it. Screenshot captured and inspected. The finding's driver appears to have set the value without a subsequent paint: the file deliberately does not repaint under a typing person (that is why the send button's label is patched imperatively at notebook.js:2551-2559), so the block appears on the next paint rather than mid-keystroke. That is a paint-scheduling nuance at most, not "nothing on screen". 2) Independently, the picked words stay marked in the note the whole time. `.readBody .pick` still reads "Switch on before guests arrive, not when." during the edit, after the edit, and after the send — I checked it at all three points. The note plane says X, the field says Y, on screen simultaneously. 3) The gate already owns this as decided design, so the finding also restates the measured baseline the brief says is worthless to rediscover. notes-interaction-check.mjs:1325-1343 asserts "the seam does not print the same sentence twice" at seed and then edits the field and asserts "when it shows both, the words a person picked are not demoted" against .peelFrom span. Lines 741-748 type into the field and assert "the receipt carries the edited wording". Editing the wording is a tested, intended path, not a leak. 4) The headline diagnosis inverts what the seal is. The one-way edge is that the note never leaves and only what stands in the field crosses. In the driven case the note was untouched, private, unchanged — LESS of it crossed, not more. The copy the finding quotes says "the exact words you pick AND CHECK BELOW"; the field is the check, and the person authoring their own task wording is authorship, not a breach. Calling a person's own typing a failure of the seal is a category error. 5) The proposed fix would make the work worse and breaks two constraints. "YOUR WORDING, NOT THE NOTE'S" and "Put the picked words back" are invented copy — the brief puts copy out of the reviewer's remit ("judged, not rewritten"), and the first is a scold aimed at a legitimate act, in a voice that is supposed to be plain and calm. It also duplicates, in a louder register, what .peelFrom already says quietly. And the restore control is redundant: I pressed Ctrl+Z in the field after typing the invented string and it restored "Switch on before guests arrive, not when" exactly — the product's own reversibility binding, which the gate already covers as "undo in the field is the field's". 6) The announcement half is the only arguable kernel and it does not survive either. startPeel() at notebook.js:853 already reads the payload back verbatim on open — "The words you picked: {taskWording}. Tasks receives these words and nothing else from this note." — and focus lands in .peelField holding those same words, so an eyes-free user hears the payload once, then types any edit themselves. The proposed `say(sentReceipt + " " + wording + ". In " + destinationOf(note) + ".")` splices an unbounded user string into the middle of a three-clause sentence, producing "Sent to Tasks. Your note stayed here. Something completely different that nobody picked. In The house." — the exact over-long-announcement class this file has already ruled against once in its own log. The crossing is also fully reversible: Ctrl+Z un-sends, and the gate asserts it. Confirmed on drive: seam at 1440x960, ?state=seam; edit path, repaint path, Ctrl+Z path, and send path all exercised.

rounds.headline: The first sign-off in ten rounds, and one blocker that made the phone silently refuse to save
rounds.body:
The loop was retired before this round and the difference is the whole story. Ten agents instead of forty-two. One confirmed blocker instead of twenty. And Typography signed the work off at 9.5 — the first time in the programme's history any seat has been able to say the work is finished, because until this round the schema forced every seat to produce three defects whatever it thought.

Six of the seven seats are at 8.4 or better: UI 9.0, Typography 9.5, Brand 8.9, Measured evidence 8.7, UX 8.4, Taste 8.4. The floor is Interaction at 6.6, and it is the floor for one reason. On a phone at 360 and 375 the Save control had nine live pixels of thirty-six: the dock's suite row was painted over it, and a real tap on the white check a person can plainly see left the field full, said nothing, and did not capture the thought. The product is named for the three seconds between having a thought and it being safe, and on the narrowest common phone that path was closed. The audit's own 44px touch pass could not see it, because getBoundingClientRect reads 36x44 at every width while the composited hit area is what a finger meets.

The refuter earned its place on this one. It killed the proposed fix on three counts — the negative offset it blamed does not exist, wrapping the row would change the dock's height mid-draft and reopen three closed findings, and raising the stacking alone would trade a silent non-save for a silent wrong-save. What landed instead removes weight rather than adding rows: the phone was printing the draft length twice, in two grammars, and the ceiling grammar was thirty-seven pixels of a three-hundred-and-twenty-six pixel foot. One number, once, and only past 3600. Then the decorative divider gives way below 380, because it is the only thing in that foot which is not a target. Thirty-six live pixels of thirty-six at every width from 360 up, verified with real taps at every draft length, with the dock's height unmoved and the pile's reserve intact.

The most valuable thing this round produced is not the fix. The refuter noticed that notes-interaction-check.mjs opened every phone width with a mouse, so the coarse-pointer branch — the one governing the surface the locked architecture singles out — was never evaluated by any of its phone assertions. Turning that on immediately failed two of them: with a real touch pointer an index row is 88px instead of 64 and straddled the undo strip, whose band had been guessed at 140px since round 8. The band is measured now. The gate went from 488 assertions to 528 and is testing a device that exists.

wins.biggestWin: The column discipline is genuinely studio-grade — one 261px spine carries the wordmark, the index head, every day rule and the paper across 1280/1440/1920, the pick bar sits under the passage instead of over it, and the phone merge holds — but the horizon between the two planes is not a horizon: pressing T in the hand drops it 276px in a single frame and takes the index from seven visible rows to two, and the read-back card leaves 392×349 of empty paper where every other desk state carries its margin.

The person's own writing is set at Geist 17/1.62/-0.021em on a 29.2em measure that holds identically on the desk, the phone, the seam and the 150-word pressure note, and I drove ten states at three widths without finding a single font-size off the eight-step ramp, a single weight outside 400/600, or an undeclared leading — the hardest thing in this discipline is the thing this file does best, and the residue I can still name is worth about a tenth in total.

The desktop capture path is genuinely at the bar — caret parked at rest, blind typing lands, Ctrl+Enter inks in under 60ms, Ctrl+Z returns the whole draft with focus intact — but the phone's Save control has zero tappable pixels at 375 and 360, five drawn buttons in the resting room answer a press with nothing at all, and the primary reading gesture heaves the index 169px with no motion and leaves no mark on the row it lifted.

Everything a stranger touches on the way in is at the bar — the drag pick, the word-snapping, the counting line, the phone route, the empties — but the seam, the moment the whole product exists for, silently drops its privacy sentence and the words that will cross on any laptop shorter than about 913 CSS pixels, leaving an armed ink-filled primary and nothing else.

The voice is the best thing in this file and would pass at Linear or Stripe on almost every surface, but two visible strings state facts that are not true, and one of them is the sealed-edge promise the whole venue offer rests on.

This is not a well-made notes app with wedding words in it — the commit choreography (the sheet settling away while the row it became washes indigo for 620ms) is a genuinely memorable moment and the picked-words seam is the clearest privacy promise I have seen drawn rather than written; but the second promise collapses the instant you leave the desktop hero, where the queue's only exit control falls off its card on every card after the seeded first one, and on a phone the review hand does not render at all.

The render path is genuinely hard — no keystroke loss under a 113-character burst, caret and index scroll survive every repaint, the real-drag pick snaps to words, the phone dock merges and commits, voice hands over with focus and an announcement, and no state throws — but one named state answers its own question with nothing for 93% of the notebook, the tablet band amputates both facts in the head, and the 4000 ceiling is stated in two grammars and enforced in none.

confirmed.element: .dock button[aria-label="Save it"] (.dockGlyph.commitPart), phone dock, capture state, 360–414px

Hit-testing every pixel across its own box with document.elementFromPoint at its vertical centre: 430px = 36 of 36 live, 414px = 33, 390px = 9 (only x 185–193), 375px = 0, 360px = 0. confirmed.fix:
DO NOT ship the blocker's fix as written. Two of its three parts are wrong or dangerous.

1. "Remove the negative offset" is a no-op — there is none. The overflow is flex:none children in a min-width:0 grid column.
2. "Let the row wrap to a second line below" would change the dock's HEIGHT while somebody is typing, because the counter widens from 28px to 65px mid-draft. paint() measures the dock into --dock-h, which drives .index padding-bottom and scroll-padding-bottom (master.css:1519). A dock that grows a row as the count crosses 100 characters heaves the pile under the person's thumb and re-opens dock-eats-the-oldest-notes, phone-dock-clips-last-row and index-walk-parks-under-dock in one move. Reject it.
3. z-index alone is a trap. I measured that .dockRow[data-verbs]{position:relative;z-index:1} restores 35 of 36 px at 390 — but at 360 the button sits past the suite entirely, so raising it would put its 36px target on top of the Notes tile and a tap meant for Notes would land on Save. master.css:1571 already names that exact hazard as the reason the coarse expanders are vertical-only. Raising z-index without first removing the overflow trades a silent non-save for a silent wrong-save, which is worse.

What to do instead, inside the locked architecture: make the foot fit before touching stacking. The verbs row needs ~215px at coarse and the suite row ~219px, against 326px of dock inner width at 360 — it structurally cannot fit, so remove weight rather than add rows. Two counters print the same number (dockCount tab, and dockCount tab commitPart at notebook.js:1351); delete the duplicate. Drop the "/ 4000" grammar from the phone counter — it is 37px of a 36px control's space and it is the still-open counter-past-its-own-limit string anyway. Then let the commit control own the dock's right edge with the suite tiles to its left, so the one filled primary sits where the thumb is and nothing in the dock can be laid over it. Only after the boxes no longer intersect, add position:relative;z-index:1 on the commit as a belt, not a fix.

WARNING on that reordering: it puts the white Save disc beside the white avatar disc. That is two ink-filled circles touching, which re-opens two-ink-filled-primaries-at-the-same-moment and phone-commit-arrives-450ms-late-and-is-the-avatar-s-twin. If the commit goes to the right edge, the avatar has to stop being white, or the rule has to separate them, or the commit goes to the left edge of the suite row instead. Decide that before writing the CSS, not after.

Assert it properly — the blocker's proposed assertion would pass while the real bug ships, because it fixes one draft length and one paint. The assertion must be: for each width in 360/375/390/414/430, in BOTH notebook and capture, with drafts of 1, 99, 100, 500 and 3999 characters, AND again after a live-draft repaint (setViewportSize to landscape and back), require (a) the commit button's rect to sit entirely inside the dock's inner box, (b) no other dock control's rect to intersect it, (c) at least 44 continuous integer px where elementFromPoint(x, cy).closest('button') is the commit, (d) at least 44 continuous px vertically at its centre x, and (e) one real page.touchscreen.tap at its visual centre to empty the field AND write a save into #say. refuted.problem: These five carry no data-act, and the delegated handler at notebook.js:2664 does `const act = e.target.closest("[data-act]"); if (!act) return;` — so they fall out silently. (c) Routing the answer through "the same strip the undo pill uses" re-opens four separately closed findings about that strip covering content: undo-pill-paints-over-the-pile, undo-strip-paints-over-the-writing, undo-strip-over-rows, undo-pill-paints-over-the-words — now fired from the chrome a keyboard user hits five times in one tab tour.
(d) Widening the sweep to "every visible button" fails on the Notes tile itself (aria-current="page", legitimately inert) at both 1440 and 390, so the fix as written breaks the 488-assertion gate on the first run.

refuted.why:
The half of this blocker that makes it a distinct finding — "nothing marks the source" — is factually false in the locked configuration, and the first half of its proposed fix is already shipped verbatim.

Driven at file:///.../notebook.html?v=locked&paper=stacked&index=airy&radius=soft&type=calm&state=notebook, 1440x960, with a real pointer (page.mouse.move/down/up on the nth(5) .idxRow at 761,700):

" data-open" : "";` and master.css:686 `.idxRow[data-open] { background: var(--wash); }` where `--wash: rgba(17, 17, 17, 0.035)` (master.css:50) — an existing ink-tint fill from the palette. The accessible-name half is also handled and is proved by the measured baseline: notes-interaction-check.mjs:132 asserts "opening is announced" and the live region reads `Open. Idea for the studio newsletter: ...`; :143 asserts focus lands on `.readBody`, and :150 that its accessible name carries the instruction. The geometry half reproduces, and I do not dispute it: .top 155→324, #index top 326→495, in a single frame between the 12ms and 40ms rAF ticks, transform `none`, opacity `1`. (One correction: getAnimations() is 1 at t=12, not 0 for every frame.) elementFromPoint at the original pointer afterwards returns `.idxDay` — a non-interactive H3, so a stray second click hits nothing rather than firing a wrong row. Strip the false half away and what remains is verbatim the already-open finding reading-does-not-lift. This filing adds nothing to it and gets the part it does add backwards.

rounds.headline: Every room exists on a phone now, and a mark nobody made can be let go
rounds.body:
Floor 6.2, Interaction, and it named three things. All three are closed, and a fourth that no seat raised as a blocker but three named in their verdicts turned out to be mine.

Only the notebook had a phone branch. Every other state rendered into the desk, which is display:none under 720px, so a real tap on the head chip — the product's own primary call to action — entered a room with six invisible-but-focusable controls, no card and no way back, and dictation closed its ink floor into a white sheet that does not exist on a phone, leaving the words somebody had just spoken nowhere. The review hand is a dialog over the live index now, reusing the shell whose focus trap and 44px controls are already measured, and the readback stays in the ink room the words came out of. Both carry a visible way out, because Escape is not a control on a phone. Zero focusable elements drawn at nothing, at 360 and 390, verified with a real touch pointer.

standingPick fell through to the fixture's note.pick on every read, so three notes opened already marked — fourteen words in indigo, the bar reading that Tasks would use exactly these, the primary armed — before anybody had picked anything, under a heading whose whole promise is that only picked words cross. Worse, the documented clear key could not touch it: the product announced Nothing picked while the words stayed drawn and the primary stayed armed. A restored mark is promoted once, on arrival, so every route that releases a pick releases it, and it stays released. It says so too: picked before, and still here.

The file states its own caret rule at keepDraft and set it in exactly one branch. Every other exit dropped focus on the body, so the sentence typed after leaving review, search, voice or the readback went nowhere. One helper now, and the two journeys that shared a branch are two journeys: leaving for Tasks is not arriving to write.

The fourth was mine. Round 10 seated the commit permanently and drove its visibility from wakeSheet, which only runs from the input listener, so after the product's core act the field was empty and the sheet still wore a filled Save with the privacy line gone, for the rest of the session. Three seats reported it independently and no blocker had to be spent on it. The resting look follows the draft now, not the keystroke.
